events.title: Trump eases Russia oil sanctions, but is Europe still buying Moscow’s gas?
events.summary: Analysts say Russia will benefit most from US sanctions waiver. United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order waiving newly-passed Russia sanctions, claiming the move is in the US’s “national interest”. Earlier this month, Trump also announced a deal to bring stocks of Russian diesel into global markets, in a bid to drive down energy prices that have spiked during the US-Israel war on Iran. The US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027. Trump’s embrace of Russian energy has angered Ukraine, European partners and many US officials, who say the move rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war against its neighbour. Ukraine’s President Volodmyr Zelenskyy slammed Trump’s diesel deal as “a gift” to Russia’s President Vladimir Putin that will help fund his war effort. While European countries have also criticised Trump’s embrace of Russian energy, the US president has accused them of “hypocrisy”, as figures show that European Union countries continue to import Russian gas. In his executive order on Friday, Trump called off numerous planned Russia-related sanctions days before they were due to take effect, including duties on Russian goods and penalties for buying the country’s oil and gas. The now-blocked measures were part of legislation passed in Congress with bipartisan support last month , named after the late US Senator Lindsay Graham, an outspoken critic of Russia. They would have included up to 100 percent tariffs on all goods brought into the US from the five top importers of Russian crude oil or gas, including China and India. They could also have imposed equal penalties on countries deemed to have knowingly bought oil or gas from Russia 30 days after the law’s implementation, or to be among the top five countries helping Moscow circumvent sanctions on sales of its oil. The waiver will hold until the Trump administration believes “further action is appropriate”, according to the executive order. US Congressman Don Beyer, a Democrat from Virginia, said the sanctions waiver amounts to a “surrender to Putin” that “betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent”. Vasily Astrov, an economist at the Vienna Institute for International Economic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the Russian government will likely be the greatest beneficiary because the easing of sanctions means Russian oil will not have to be further discounted. He estimated that about 60 cents of every extra dollar in the price of a barrel of Russian oil would “end up in state coffers”. Russian official Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, hailed the US decision to waive the sanctions as “an important and truly historic moment”. Other beneficiaries include major importers of Russian oil and gas, such as China and India, who are now less exposed to the risk of secondary US penalties. While Trump hopes the measures will also help bring down oil prices for US consumers before November mid-term elections, experts say that is less certain. Addressing the US’s recent diesel deal with Russia, EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis said it is unlikely to have a significant impact on global prices. According to Trump, that deal would bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel into US and global markets “immediately”, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November, and 1 million tonnes afterwards. “If we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks,” Dombrovskis told the AFP news agency. Which countries still buy oil from Russia? China and India are the largest buyers of Russian crude oil, purchasing 6 billion euros ($6.74bn) and 3.6 billion euros ($4.04bn) worth respectively in September, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank. Hungary and Slovakia, the landlocked EU members that have exemptions to the bloc’s ban on Russian crude, also remain big customers, buying a combined 290 million euros ($326m) worth of the commodity in September, said CREA. Turkiye imported 172 million euros ($193m) worth of Russian crude oil the same month, the think tank added. Since the end of 2022, the largest importers of Russian oil products, which include diesel, have been Turkiye, China, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Singapore. Saudi Arabia imported the most Russian oil products in September at 534 million euros ($600m), followed by Turkiye with 321 million euros ($361m), China with 304 million euros ($342m) and India with 161 million euros ($181m). Is Europe buying increasing amounts of gas from Russia? “The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel,” European leaders said in a joint statement adopted following a two-day European Council meeting in Brussels this week.

events.title: The US Army is growing its space forces. They're already in combat.
events.summary: Soldiers with the Army's 1st Space Brigade unload equipment from a helicopter during training on Fort Carson, Colo. on Jan. 31, 2025. Brooke Nevins/US Army The US Army is expanding its ranks of soldiers specialized in space warfare. Army space personnel are already deployed to the Middle East, where the US has been fighting Iran. More than 600 enlisted soldiers joined the new specialty this year, with more growth planned. The US Army is expanding its ranks of soldiers trained for space warfare, a growing military specialty that is already supporting American combat operations in the Middle East. The service established a new enlisted space operations branch in June, creating a dedicated career field for soldiers whose work involves satellites, communications, and the ability to disrupt an adversary's use of space. While the Space Force and its Guardians oversee a broad range of military space operations in support of the entire US military, the Army has its own dedicated specialists focused on supporting its ground forces with satellite communications, navigation, and other capabilities. Some space soldiers are already deployed in the Middle East , where American forces have been fighting Iran. Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, the commander of US Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington, DC, this week that roughly 2,500 soldiers from his command are deployed to US Central Command's area of operations. That figure includes both air-defense formations and space specialists. "Space is really embedded in every single echelon there," Rafferty said, speaking of the job's growing prevalence throughout all levels of military decision-making. Those space soldiers' responsibilities can range from helping ground forces access satellite communications and navigation systems to disrupting adversary space capabilities, known as "space interdiction." Officials did not provide specific examples or further details on the work being done. For soldiers on the battlefield, such help is essential for communicating with nearby units and gathering intelligence on enemy movements. The growing importance of space as a domain of warfare, alongside land, sea, air, and cyberspace , prompted the Army to expand its specialized workforce. Command Sgt. Maj. Rickey Jackson said at AUSA that the service reviewed several thousand personnel files for its new enlisted space operations branch. The 600 soldiers ultimately selected for the new job came mostly from intelligence, communications, and air-defense specialties, though the career field is open to troops from other backgrounds. The service plans to continue growing its formalized space community, with around 1,700 space soldiers by the end of next fiscal year. "When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch between the enlisted and the officer side is a significant contribution across the service," Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, who oversees the integration of emerging space capabilities into Army operations, said during the event. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I'm a real estate agent building a $480,000 backyard home for my mom. I still made these costly mistakes.
events.summary: Shalini Karnani Bonjour in her California backyard. Courtesy of Shalini Karnani Bonjour Shalini Bonjour is building a 1,100-square-foot ADU in her backyard so her mother can age in place. The project is taking longer than she expected and is going over budget. Bonjour shared the five biggest lessons she's learned during the process with Business Insider. After her father died in 2024, real estate agent Shalini Karnani Bonjour moved her mother from Michigan to California to be closer to her and her family. "My husband and I didn't feel comfortable having her so far away, especially when it came to her day-to-day needs," Bonjour, 50, told Business Insider. Later that year, the family bought a home with a backyard large enough to build an accessory dwelling unit for her mother. In 2025, they broke ground on a 1,100-square-foot ADU. But what was expected to be a six-week project has dragged on for months and cost the family thousands more than expected. "The whole process has been difficult because there are so many things to manage," Bonjour said. "You're trying to keep the project affordable, keep your neighbors happy, and stay on track. I can only imagine how overwhelming this would feel for someone without any insight into the process, because it is a huge undertaking." Here are five hard lessons Bonjour has learned from the project, from choosing the right contractor to budgeting enough money for unexpected challenges. A bad contractor can make or break a project The ADU during the early stages of its construction. Courtesy of Shalini Karnani Bonjour At first, Bonjour thought she had found the right architect for the project. They designed the ADU and even promised to guide her through the permitting and construction process. But they didn't follow through. Bonjour said hiring the wrong person was one of the "biggest mistakes" she's made during the project. Although she found someone to take over the project after interviewing about 10 builders, mistakes made by the original architect have made construction more difficult. "Watching my builder try to translate that original designer's plans is like trying to fit a square peg into a round hole," she said. "It's basically like he was working off somebody else's recipe." Understanding local permitting and construction rules is essential Solar panels being installed on a rooftop. Hispanolistic/Getty Images Every city has its own rules for building ADUs , and some are more complicated than others. In her part of the Coachella Valley, Bonjour had to secure permits for the roof, electrical work, plumbing, HVAC, and solar panel installation. "The city was pretty tough on solar," Bonjour said. "The first two electrical inspections were fine, and then on the third inspection, they determined we needed solar panels. Getting solar here in the desert is its own job. Researching the proper solar companies and their packages was another." Building a home can test relationships Shalini Karnani Bonjour in her California backyard. Courtesy of Shalini Karnani Bonjour While the family waits for the ADU to be finished, Bonjour, her husband, their son, and her mother are all living in the main house . It's been difficult sharing space, especially the kitchen. "My mom loves to cook, so having her own kitchen will be really important to her," she said. "She was making a recipe and said, "It'll be different when I have my own stuff." I think the whole thing is bittersweet, but once she sees her finished kitchen, she'll feel different." Construction has caused headaches for the cul-de-sac, too. Because the neighborhood's electrical transformer is outdated and overloaded, the local utility needs to upgrade it before the ADU can be connected. The work has involved digging up Bonjour's driveway and those of two neighbors. "Our neighbors had to deal with the inconvenience of their driveways being out for a week and a half," she said. "My contractor and I are trying to be as considerate as we can and get the best people to do the work as quickly as possible. Thankfully, the neighbors have been gracious and nice along the way." You have to be careful with your budget Wood for home construction. ArtMarie/Getty Images Bonjour's family budgeted $480,000 for the construction of the ADU. Of that total, they set aside $100,000 as a contingency fund. "As a realtor, and as someone who's always telling people to ask all the questions, I also hate to be caught by surprise," Bonjour said. "With the contingency budget, you build in extra money that you hope you won't need. It's something everyone should consider, whether they're building a million-dollar home or a small casita in the backyard." Unfortunately, unexpected costs, like hiring replacement contractors and installing a new electrical panel and solar panels, have exhausted the reserve. Bonjour said the extra expenses have trickled into the family's day-to-day life, making it harder to justify things like family trips and upgrading the main home. "I wish I had allocated it differently, but again, I think that planning with the right people at the onset would have saved so much headache and time," she said. "We'll have to wait on upgrading the home. That's kind of annoying, but that's where we're at. Lesson learned on that one." Give yourself grace; it's all a learning process Karnani Bonjour. Courtesy of Shalini Karnani Bonjour If she had to do it all over again, Bonjour says she would make different decisions. "I'm a professional, so I hold myself to a higher standard of asking questions and being informed," she said. "I like to have good relationships with the builders, contractors, and vendors. In some ways, I feel like I should have known or seen what was going wrong, and that becomes really hard to kind of wrestle with." She still tries to give herself grace. For all its challenges, she believes building the ADU has been the right decision. "We know that having Mom in proximity is right for our family," she added. "We've learned some lessons along the way as homeowners, as a realtor, as a child, as a mom who's growing old herself." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds
events.summary: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation US corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth. Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy group found . US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation. The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius, described it as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States. In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has been in effect “dismantled ”. The law will come into effect in December. Lobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States. It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026. The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union and Cargill. Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings. Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House. Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen , the two sides released a joint statement that promised the US special treatment with regard to the EUDR. The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggest financial and trading companies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”. Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance. “Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.” Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitals arguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European market because it would raise costs for US producers. In an opinion piece published in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.” US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR. The American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ...

events.title: The US Army needs to get rid of old explosives near its new artillery ammo plant. They're too dangerous to move, so it's blowing them up.
events.summary: The service broke ground on a 155mm artillery production line at the plant earlier this year. US Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Emilio Murphy The US Army will detonate 68 barrels of unstable explosive material at an ammunition production plant. Officials determined the lead azide couldn't be relocated and are in contact with residents on environmental concerns. The facility is also home to the Army's new 155mm artillery production line, which began construction earlier this year. The US Army will detonate dozens of barrels of unstable explosives at its ammunition plant in Iowa after determining the material couldn't be safely moved, according to a public affairs official. The lead azide the service needs to get rid of has been stored at the site for almost 20 years and is no longer needed for ammunition production . The detonation will occur near the service's new 155mm artillery production line, construction of which began in July. The Army informed residents of nearby Middletown, Iowa, this week that it would detonate 68 barrels of lead azide sometime in November. Army Explosive Ordnance Disposal teams will execute the detonation. "There are 68 barrels of lead azide in two earth-covered magazines, and that material was on site for potential production," Justine Barati, deputy director of public affairs for the US Sustainment Command, told Business Insider. "When we realized that we would no longer need that material or use that material, then it becomes hazardous waste." A team of experts recommended a controlled explosion to destroy the lead azide, and that decision was elevated to former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for approval. Barati said the 155mm facility is on the other side of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The Army anticipates a four-hour delay to construction at the facility on the day of the detonation. The Army asked Middletown residents near the plant to temporarily leave their homes and is offering the Army Reserve Center as a place to stay during the detonation. About 55 homes are expected to be affected by the detonation decision, Barati said. Local residents can assess any property damage afterward and file claims with the Army. The Iowa newspaper The Hawk Eye first reported on the detonation and town hall with residents. Lead azide is a highly sensitive and toxic material used as a primary explosive component in some weapons that can pose environmental and health risks. Barati said that prior to and after the detonation, the Army will test air, water, and soil in the area. Residents agreed to give the service access to their properties for the checks. The Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is a critical production facility for medium- and large-caliber munitions. Earlier this year, the Army began construction of a new production line for 155mm ammunition , replacing the plant's World War II-era M795 artillery production line. The new facility was designed by the Army's Combat Capabilities Development Command's Armament Center and MSM North America to produce different types of 155mm ammunition with the capacity to surge manufacturing for wartime demands. 155mm artillery shells have become a high-demand munition amid recent conflicts. The US has ramped up production after providing millions of rounds to Ukraine. Concerns about the state of US ammo stocks have risen as the military assesses its readiness for future wars. events.title: Giorgos Tsetis: no one is personally accountable for AI. This must change
events.summary: For almost a decade, I led a company whose products people swallowed. If our hair growth supplements caused harm, I was responsible. Not just morally – legally. It kept me awake at night. And that was a good thing. Personal legal responsibility is a powerful tool. It prompts corporate leaders to take the safety of their products seriously, giving consumers confidence in those products. It’s not currently something causing AI leaders to lose sleep. It should be. Some might think introducing another layer of accountability would stifle innovation. My own experience building what became a multi-billion-dollar company says otherwise. In my industry, the law has long held that the people in charge are personally for the safety of what their companies sell. That accountability was essential to building the consumer trust I needed to make my business a success. It could do the same for AI leaders. Today, I invest in AI and AI-enabled companies through Great Things™, a new investment model, and my family office. My investments include frontier AI companies such as Anthropic and xAI, infrastructure and compute-related companies such as Positron AI, and AI-enabled science and health platforms such as Lila, which uses AI to accelerate discovery. I believe AI technologies, if used safely, can help solve some of humanity’s toughest problems and the potential I see in these companies is truly exciting.So I’m putting my capital behind them because I want them to succeed. But as an investor, I’m part of the ecosystem that makes AI innovation possible. And I’ve observed a gap: personal legal accountability. It’s a gap that needs filling. Executives are currently shielded behind their companies, with corporate financial penalties for misconduct or negligence often amounting to a fraction of their turnover and valuations – just another line item. Responsibility that stops at the corporate entity isn’t responsibility. It’s an expense. Meanwhile, AI leaders can make decisions from which they personally stand to make billions while risking nothing personally if their mistakes expose us all to danger. That asymmetry is indefensible. It’s not that nothing is happening. The rules around AI are evolving fast. States across the US are introducing their own AI laws, and Congress is weighing legislation that would impose safety requirements on frontier AI companies. At the end of September, leaders of several of the biggest AI companies went to the White House and signed an accord committing to internal risk controls, independent audits and board-level oversight of safety. These are welcome steps, as are the safety frameworks leading labs have published. But both the safety frameworks and the accord are voluntary, and when it comes to AI, voluntary isn’t enough. Nothing yet holds the people at the top personally legally accountable. We have built a legal system in which it is mostly companies that pay but rarely the people who lead them. An AI executive who misstates revenue to investors can be held personally responsible. Yet decisions that could contribute to anything from an individual suicide to large-scale cyberattacks and geopolitical destabilization are made without personal legal jeopardy. We have already seen where that leads in another segment of the tech industry: social media. With AI, the stakes are potentially much higher. As I know from building Nutrafol, personal liability changes how you run a business. A safety checklist tells you what to test; personal exposure makes you worry about what isn’t on the list. You drive your teams to identify the risks, test for them and put safeguards in place before they become a problem. You make sure problems reach you early rather than allowing them to get smoothed over on the way up. And you’re willing to slow down or say no, even when money or a competitive edge is on the table, because your name is attached to what happens next. I recognize that asking for personal liability for AI leaders is a significant step. But AI is unlike any other industry. A supplement reaches the people who choose to buy it. AI is becoming embedded in all our lives, whether we’re boarding a plane or turning on the lights. We are all “customers” of AI’s products. AI technologies are built into the systems that we depend on, from power grids to hospitals to the classrooms where our children learn. A single failure could ripple across a city, a country or beyond. And unlike almost any other product, the people building AI have warned that it may one day escape human control. Extraordinary risks call for extraordinary accountability. To be clear, I’m not arguing that AI executives should be punished for every failure. Just as I could not guarantee that every one of my products was perfect, no one can guarantee that an AI system is safe. But when leaders know their systems pose serious risks and ship them – or release them – anyway, when they inadequately fund their safety teams or ignore their warnings or when they hide problems from regulators and the public, there should be consequences. Not just for the company. For the individuals behind those decisions. Whether that accountability is civil or criminal is not for me to say. Where the thresholds sit, which harms count, who audits what – that’s for legislators, lawyers, technologists and ethicists to decide. But whatever obligations they land on, a named senior executive should be personally responsible for meeting them. When the people at the top know the risks, what they do next should carry real personal stakes. I believe AI has the potential to transform everyone’s lives for the better. But like everyone, I’m concerned about its dangers. Personal legal responsibility focuses minds on safety, builds public trust and helps ensure that the race among AI leaders to come out on top doesn’t come at everyone else’s expense. It’s a standard long applied to those making products that go into human bodies. It must now be applied to those making products that could shape the future of humanity itself. events.title: Susan Dell is the one running the Dells’ $10 billion giving operation—and her biggest bets are on kids, health care, and UT Austin
events.summary: Michael Dell is the sixth-richest man in the world with a net worth of about $232 billion. He and his wife, Susan, have given away about $10 billion of that fortune—and she is calling a lot of the shots on where the money goes. She is the co-founder and chair of the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, established in 1999. The organization currently manages more than 800 projects worldwide each year, particularly in the U.S., Africa, India, Israel, and their home state of Texas, where they live on a sprawling 33,000-square-foot estate . The organization’s focus areas are education, jobs and livelihood, and health—causes she’s cared about deeply since childhood. Her father was a surgical oncologist and “sparked her lifelong passion for health,” the foundation says. As a girl, she would even stop strangers at the grocery store to tell them not to smoke. “People matter to her,” Janet Mountain , head of the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation, said in a statement . And because people matter to her, solutions matter to her.” Mountain also previously served as an executive at Dell before joining the foundation in 2003. Recently, Susan has focused largely on the foundation’s livelihood pillar through the Dells’ commitment to Trump Accounts. In December 2025, the couple committed $6.25 billion to provide $250 contributions to 25 million U.S. children. The donation is intended to benefit children age 10 and under who aren’t eligible for the federal government’s separate $1,000 contribution for children born between 2025 and 2028. The Dells’ money will go to children in ZIP codes with median incomes of $150,000 or less, giving millions of families a chance to start building wealth early. “We believe that when children have a future that they can see is worth saving for, then that will help build hope and opportunity and prosperity for generations to come,” Susan said during the White House announcement in December. From Texas to beyond The couple initially considered limiting their contribution to Texas, Michael explained at the event, before deciding to expand the initiative nationwide. But their home state has long been central to the Dells’ philanthropy, particularly when it comes to health care. In April, the Dells became the first donors to surpass $1 billion in lifetime giving to the University of Texas at Austin. Their latest commitments will support a new advanced research campus, an AI-focused medical center, scholarships, student housing, and expanded supercomputing capabilities. That milestone builds on decades of Dell investments in health care across Central Texas. In 2013, the foundation committed $50 million to establish Dell Medical School at UT Austin, along with another $10 million for local health care initiatives. “A medical school at UT Austin further establishes Central Texas as a center of excellence for family health and research,” Susan said at the time. The foundation has also supported Dell Children’s Medical Center , which opened in 2007, and the Dell Pediatric Research Institute , helping expand access to specialized children’s care and medical research in the region. Beyond her philanthropic work, Susan had a career of her own. A fashion entrepreneur , she founded three labels, including luxury brand Phi (which closed during the recession ). She’s also an endurance athlete who has competed in marathons, triathlons, and the Ironman World Championships in Hawaii. In 2018, she was inducted into the Texas Women’s Hall of Fame for helping families recover from Hurricane Harvey. She and Michael committed more than $43 million to rebuilding and recovery across 41 counties. In 2025, she and Michael also received the History-Making Texan Award, recognizing their contributions to the state and beyond. And despite decades of philanthropy, Susan has long viewed the foundation’s work as far from finished. “The reality is, you know, we’re just getting started,” she said during a 2017 discussion about the future of philanthropy. events.title: My husband retired just as we became empty nesters. Now we're together nearly 24/7, and it's been a strange adjustment.
events.summary: The author and her husband are spending a lot of time together after retiring and becoming empty nesters. Courtesy of Susan Teresa When my husband and I became empty nesters, he retired, too. We used to have busy, individual lives, but now we are always together. It took a lot of adjustment and honest conversations, but we're learning to navigate our new normal. My husband and I have been married for 26 years, together for 32. That's more than half my life. I thought we'd experienced just about every version of our life together. Then we became empty nesters . And then my husband retired. We're now together 24/7 with nowhere else we need to be, and I realized that all these years, I'd never spent this much time with him. Since the day he brought home his office belongings , I've caught myself thinking more than once, " Oh, you're still here? Our home feels different now Without school schedules or workdays organizing our lives, we have more unstructured time than we know what to do with. We navigate quiet hallways lined with unoccupied bedrooms. We now split the responsibility for coddling our cat, who suffers from separation anxiety. We announce, "We're back," to the furniture and the cat, forgetting we left the house otherwise empty. Our aching hearts inspired us to collaborate on a shared list of silver linings. We drafted wish lists, imagining what we could do now that we no longer had to accommodate five personalities with varying interests. While we shared many ideas and dream list to-dos — things like traveling to Tuscany for cooking and painting retreats — we hadn't anticipated that our day-to-day would also require attention and planning. The trouble with together-time all the time Throughout our marriage, my husband and I had always noted how similar his parents and mine were. Connected at the hip, one parent was seldom without the other. We, on the other hand, prided ourselves on allowing each other space. We'd spent decades insisting we weren't like them — valuing independence, traveling separately , and encouraging each other to pursue our interests. Then, when my husband retired, we instantly became our parents. With freedom to do whatever we wanted, we fell into the rhythm our parents had modeled: together all day, every day. Sometimes you really can have too much of a good thing. I'm an introverted writer who loves spending time in my rich inner world. He's an extroverted adventurer always on the go — kayaking, swimming, walking on the beach, sometimes all three in the same day. One day, the realization that we had to structure our time hit hard. I'd been sitting at my writing desk when my husband opened the door to ask what we were having for lunch. Not wanting to be rude, I talked with him for a moment, then asked for a few minutes to finish my thought. He left. I stared at my screen, hands still on the keyboard. My thought was gone. While we enjoy being together, we're learning the importance of agreeing on when to be together and when to allow each other space. We're creating a new rhythm Mornings offer the perfect opportunity to plan our day over coffee, breakfast, and a card game — usually rummy. Between playful attempts to end each other's winning streaks, we check the weather, compare plans, and decide what we'd like to do. Our morning ritual helps shape our lives now that external demands no longer impose structure on our time. Unless we have plans with friends, mealtimes serve as natural meeting points. An unexpected result: his cooking is improving. I'm now enjoying gourmet meals in the middle of the day, and again at dinner. He gets to run around outdoors, while I get to lock myself in my attic feminine sanctuary and write. In the evenings, we wind down together. After sharing a home-cooked meal, we enjoy a movie or simply each other's company. We're embracing new opportunities to grow together Now that we're home together most of the time, honest communication, negotiation, and compromise have become essential tools. After decades of countless demands on our time, we're now free to choose how we spend it. We're not always perfect. Some days, I join him outdoors when I'd rather stay home. Sometimes he interrupts when I'm in the flow. I'm learning to ask for space when I need it. He's learning that he can pursue his desire to travel — even without me. After 32 years, I never imagined we'd have to learn how to spend time apart. Having all the time in the world together doesn't mean we have to spend every minute of it that way. These days, staying happily married sometimes means knowing when to leave each other alone. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The debt crisis won’t be solved by debt relief alone. Developing countries need a growth reset
events.summary: Leaders like President Mahama of Ghana are building the architecture for a new kind of cooperation – a global reset anchored in country-led growth powered by domestic resources and private investment. On its face, however, this inspirational message seems in sharp contrast to economic reality. More than half of developing countries face liquidity and financing challenges that are making it difficult to finance basic expenditures, let alone the investment needed for growth. As global borrowing costs soar, the current crisis of fiscal space and affordable financing risks morphing into a new wave of full-blown debt crises. It is not hopeless. Working together, the international financial institutions, borrower and creditor countries, and private actors have the power to prevent a wave of crises and enable countries that have ambitious investment and reform plans to pivot to a higher and sustained growth path. As finance leaders gather in Bangkok for World Bank and IMF Annual Meetings, will they rise to meet the moment? Even before the latest spike in global borrowing costs, most developing countries faced unprecedented debt service burdens. Following a series of global shocks, the average developing country now spends more than ten percent of its revenue on interest on debt, [nearly double the burden a decade ago], crowding out investment for growth. In ten countries, interest payments eclipse the entire public investment budget. Debt acts as a ceiling on private investment, further stifling growth. The results are stark. In the decade to 2015, real per capita incomes in Sub-Saharan Africa grew by about a fifth. In the decade since, they haven’t grown at all. This is about to get worse. A wall of Covid-era, low-cost external borrowing is coming due just as global borrowing costs have skyrocketed. Meanwhile, sources of affordable financing have evaporated. In the status quo, international financial institutions have been an essential lifeline. But while the IMF and MDBs have provided countries with enough to avoid widespread default, they have stopped short of what is needed to get countries back to the growth or enable them to rebuild resilience. And since G20 creditors have continued to pull money out, much of the new multilateral funds have effectively gone back out the door to pay back creditors. China, for example, shifted from a net provider of finance to a net extractor over the last decade. As post-Covid debts mature, a record share of poor countries net-repaid the IMF in 2026 – a drain set to widen by 2030. Absent action, around 40 of the world’s poorest countries will face a stark choice: make further sharp cuts to spending at significant cost to growth and human lives, or finance government deficits and debt rollovers through exorbitant private borrowing that is likely to lead to eventual default. Both roads lead to crisis: debt-to-GDP will spiral upwards because growth is falling, because debts are rising, or both. Living standards stay stagnant and social unrest keeps rising. The IMF itself has recognized this problem. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva recently told G20 finance ministers that “high refinancing needs and rising debt-service costs are constraining many developing economies… limiting their capacity to finance critical spending on infrastructure, health, and education, which undermines growth and, in turn, debt sustainability.” Counterintuitively, for most countries, drawing a line under this crisis doesn’t require a debt initiative. It requires a growth initiative. Long overdue improvements to the debt restructuring process remain crucially important for the handful of countries that need debt stock reduction. But more than 40 countries currently struggling with financing and liquidity challenges do not have debt stocks that require imminent restructuring. Rather than waiting until they need a restructuring, we need a new toolkit that restores sustainability through dedicated support for growth. We need a reset that replaces a piecemeal drip of financing with a coordinated and decisive surge. We need creditor countries to recognize that supporting this surge – rather than using it to exit – is in their interest: that growth is the surest way to get repaid. And we need support for countries to ensure that future private debts are spent on growth enhancing investments, more transparently managed, and less shock prone. The Rockefeller Foundation has just published a policy proposal – developed in partnership with leading experts – that details how a Growth and Investment Reset could work. The Reset is not fundamentally a question of money but of political will. Resources already positioned at international financial institutions, combined with innovative financing mechanisms developed over the past five years, mean that this Reset could cost donors very little – a small fraction of the large-scale restructuring that will ultimately be needed if we don’t act. As finance leaders meet in Bangkok, they should urgently discuss how to end the cycle of dependency. High-ambition leaders building a new model of development deserve a high-ambition international financial system with the capacity to enable them to get there. The window is still open. But it is closing rapidly. The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: There be monsters: what Odysseus can teach us about innovation when maps fail
events.summary: The Various-Minded Leader . I have long thought that The Odyssey is the greatest work written on innovation leadership. Christopher Nolan’s recent film reminded me of another time when the world was awash in ambiguity and leaders needed to navigate the perilous voyage across unfamiliar territory. Over 30 years ago, before I had published any of my books on innovation, I was asked to make a presentation to the Aspen Institute as part of a summit on “Tomorrow’s Corporation.” The august speakers included an Oxford don, a Harvard strategy professor, a New York Times reporter, and … me, the lone representative for the young and technologically adept, unencumbered by conventional wisdom. The implied theme was the disruptive effect of the rapidly emerging internet and the imminent dislocation of the familiar commercial landscape. I called my talk “How Far to Ithaca?” I started with a simple proposition: There is no data on the future, and that’s where innovation happens. As such, the greatest obstacle to genuine transformation is getting stuck in the planning cycle. You know, the meeting about the meeting, the report about the report. The better, and the new, are seldom found in the safe harbor of the planning meeting. They are discovered well beyond the bounds of the strategic map, where the winds shift, the old answers sink, and the pilot must find the way by dead reckoning. Then I advanced my central thesis: Odysseus as the archetype of the modern leader, driven off course by outrageous fortune and forced to adjust his plan as he went along. To describe this form of active and adaptive creative thinking, I coined a term: creativizing . The presentation at Aspen was a shipwreck, but somehow the term made it to shore. In the decades since, I have studied this problem as a business school professor, written books about it, and worked with organizations trying to innovate when the old answers no longer work. Along the way, I have come to understand creativity as more than something we possess. A noun. It’s something we practice. Creativizing suggests that the act of creation is generative. A verb. We Martinize our cocktail attire, winterize our vehicles, and modernize our organizations. The suffix transforms a condition into an action. Creativity in action becomes creativizing . Like many of my generation, I first met our intrepid hero, Odysseus, in tenth-grade English, where culture was poured on thick, accompanied with Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar and Whitman’s Leaves of Grass . Our teacher, Mr. Johnson, declared that “The Bible and The Odyssey are the cornerstones of Western civilization.” That may have been a slight overstatement, but it pointed in the right direction. He read us the invocation that opens the epic, asking the Muse to tell the tale of the “various-minded man.” But what did that mean? After the class struggled with the question, Mr. Johnson suggested that Odysseus was a “clever man.” Such a small word for such a large character. Creative, quick, and devious come to mind. Clever people figure things out. They move around obstacles, sometimes following the rules, sometimes working around them, and sometimes inventing new rules. Different Monsters Require Different Minds That brings us to today. Many of us thought we knew the way to our own Ithaca: earnings, market share, sustainability. But there be monsters along the routes we once took. These forces, many with us since antiquity, are seldom factored into the course: plagues, wars, calamities. Nothing goes according to plan. The Cyclops, Polyphemus, renders the strength of Odysseus’ crew insufficient, much as expertise that took a company decades to develop can suddenly be commoditized. AI appeared faster and bigger than most of us anticipated, even in its nascent form. The ten years you spent perfecting a proprietary process can now be replicated by an upstart with an AI algorithm. And they can do it before lunch. Our old maneuvers are no match for it. Business models and strategies have a shelf life and go sour like milk left out too long. When more of the same won’t work, look at what you have at hand with new eyes and act in novel ways the monster couldn’t imagine. You don’t defeat the Cyclops by becoming a bigger Cyclops. You beat him by seeing what he can’t. That’s creativizing . The Sirens seduce Odysseus’ men with their sensuous song much as synthetic intelligence tells us exactly what we want to hear. Certainty is an aphrodisiac. It attracts us with plausible opportunities. It plays to our preferences. We get what we desire, even if it means our undoing on the jagged shore of misfortune. Ask your favorite AI engine about an acquisition you think makes sense, and watch it come back with a cogent and persuasive case for why you are right. It’s your personal echo chamber, supporting all the nonsense you already believe. Odysseus, understanding the real danger, had his crew plug their ears with wax and had himself lashed to the mast, ordering the men to ignore his pleas to be freed. The most dangerous voice is the one telling you what you most want to hear. Before you can outsmart the monster, you must outsmart yourself. That’s creativizing . The most dangerous monster may be the one that doesn’t appear to be one at all. One who is alluring and enchanting, like the nymph Calypso. She offers our intrepid hero comfort, sanctuary, and the possibility of immortality. She’s a legacy business, a dominant market position, a prestigious institution. She is the expertise that made you successful. And as you linger, your motivation wanes until you fade into Kodak or Blockbuster or Nokia . You become a story of the past. Like Odysseus, you lose yourself in the ease of where you are until you choose to leave before circumstances make the choice for you. That’s creativizing . Yet the greatest of these monsters is Poseidon himself, the great disruptor, the earth-shaker and master of the stormy seas. He is change itself, arriving in forceful shifts: geopolitics, competitors, regulations, and, sometimes, technologies like AI. It is foolish to provoke him and more foolish still to ignore him, for he is constantly changing the conditions of your voyage. Odysseus survives them all, not because he is prescient, but because he can actively adjust his thinking to meet the circumstances. That’s creativizing . What Would Odysseus Do? Odysseus was making it up as he went along. He rarely knew exactly what he was doing. The winds of fate will do that to a leader. What makes Odysseus the great hero of the epic is that he knows how to proceed when he doesn’t know. This is the practical discipline of moving ever onward in the face of ambiguity. That’s creativizing . So, what does the various-minded leader do when the map runs out? Like Odysseus, start with a few simple questions. 1. Where is my Ithaca? Have a clear sense of what you are trying to achieve, but don’t confuse the destination with the route to it. Persist toward Ithaca,

events.title: Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act, citing national interest
events.summary: Trump invoked the Graham Act’s national-interest waiver to suspend new duties on Russian goods and major Russian energy buyers, along with other sanctions and restrictions. The waiver came two days before the law’s implementation deadline and follows a separate temporary easing of sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The moves have drawn praise from a Russian envoy and criticism from Democrats. President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving parts of a recently enacted package of sanctions aimed at curbing Russia's ability to prosecute its war against Ukraine. "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States," Trump wrote in Friday's order. The House passed the Russia sanctions bill on Sept. 16, and Trump signed it into law two days later. The bill was introduced over a year ago, and its primary backer was the late Lindsey Graham , a veteran Republican senator who represented South Carolina. Titled the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 , the legislation targeted Russia's economy, intending to penalize the country over its continued full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The act required the president to increase duties on all Russian goods imported into the U.S. by up to 500% no later than 30 days after enactment. It also required Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries including China and India that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas. Trump's latest order waives these two parts of the Graham Act and comes two days before the law's implementation deadline. However, the order preserves existing sanctions on Russia under earlier executive orders. The law could also sanction Russian leaders, officials, and financial institutions, and expand sanctions on Iran. Oil sales revenue is critical to funding Russia's war effort. The move also comes a week after the Trump administration temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027 to ease a supply crunch caused by the war in Iran. High fuel prices are a sensitive issue for voters ahead of midterm elections on Nov. 3. Trump's Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. "The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's economy envoy, said in a post on X. "The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," Dmitriev added. But Trump's opponents have criticized the move. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat who also drafted the Graham Act, condemned the latest waiver. "Donald Trump confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug & the enablers of Russia's war machine & against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, & our European allies," Blumenthal said in an X post. Speaking to reporters in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the U.S.-Russia diesel agreement could set a precedent for further sanctions relief, while highlighting Ukraine's continued reliance on U.S. military technology and intelligence despite efforts to develop alternatives. "Sanctions will be lifted after gas," Zelenskyy said. "They will be lifted on something else. Then this will come to the banking system, certain individuals, chemical industry." Earlier this week, reports emerged that Ukraine has restricted SpaceX's Starlink military application, Starshield. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the U.S. government and president were ultimately responsible for any curbs on the network.

events.title: I'm a Walmart store manager at 23. I worked hard to get this life and started as a cashier — here's my career journey.
events.summary: Kiley Pulley transitioned from cashier to store manager within seven years. Kiley Pulley Kiley Pulley became Walmart's youngest US store manager at 21, starting as a cashier at 16. Her former store manager helped her through her succession plan and interviews. Pulley emphasizes learning daily and adapting for career growth. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kiley Pulley, a 23-year-old Walmart store manager in Buckeye, Arizona. It has been edited for length and clarity. In 2019, when I was 16 years old, I started working at Walmart as a part-time cashier. I wanted my own money, and figured, why not just get a job? My sister and my mom were already working there, and it was also right down the street from my high school. It was easy for me to get out of school and walk to work. Over the next few years, I moved through different roles, from cashier to stocker to online fulfillment. Then, when I turned 18, I became an academy trainer, and six months later, a digital team lead. When I became a team lead in mid 2021, it hit me that I wanted to stay at Walmart full time and make it my actual career . At 19, I became an operations manager, and right before I turned 22, I became the youngest store manager at Walmart in the US. People ask me, "How did you do it?" My answer is to show up and learn something new every day. Here are six things I've learned along the way. I realized I could help people by hiring them Originally, I wanted to start either my own nonprofit or my own business and help out the homeless population; then I realized that I could do all that through Walmart. I could make a difference through the people that I hire and the impact that I have on my associates at the store. When I became a team lead, I was making good money, and I also really liked it. I started actively working toward becoming a store manager. I got on succession plans and was on monthly calls with our market manager. When I became an operations manager, I led multiple projects in our market to get myself ready to become a store manager. I'd also ask to cover for store managers when they'd take off work; that way I could gain additional experience that was needed to be promoted. I remember thinking, I'm going to be a store manager at 21. I'll be the youngest in the company. I had to learn that my words carried more weight As an associate, I was friends with everybody. I could joke around with everyone. When I became salaried, everything changed. One of the biggest learning points for me has been the way I talk and how to engage with people from different cultures. Changing my tone and limiting the joking and playful attitude felt necessary as a leader in the building. At the time, setting new boundaries for myself made me feel more confident in my new role and even now in my current role. I was a little nervous when I first went into a salaried position. People said I might have issues managing those older than me, but I've never had problems with my team not respecting or listening to me. I also made my social media profiles private. I think connecting on social media can make it harder to separate between being someone's manager and being their friend. I had to learn how to delegate Getting out of the "if I want it done the right way, I'll do it myself" mindset was a big learning. I realized not everyone's going to know everything that I know, and if I really want to delegate and get tasks done , I'm going to have to teach and train. A big part of being an academy trainer and team lead is training your associates. Once you get to operations manager, you kind of have to step back and expect your team leads and academy trainers to do that same thing. I had to learn that if I delegated, things could get done faster or more efficiently. I had to learn to be a servant leader When it comes to my associates, if they need something, whether that's ordering the supplies or putting in tickets for them, I want to do that. I want to advocate for them. I know it makes them more productive, but they'll probably be happier coming to work , too. Also, everyone likes the appreciation of, "Hey, thank you for doing this today," or "Thank you for going above and beyond on this." I had to learn to have work-life balance When I first became salaried, I was always on the clock. I stopped going to the gym, and I sacrificed some time with my fiancé and family. I'd stay at work and say, "They need me." It was my fault; the team didn't need me that badly. Now, I'm doing better. When I get home, I'm not spending the whole day looking at metrics or constantly texting my team. I've gone back to the gym. I learned to take a step back and trust my leaders to do what they need to do. I trust that they know what they're doing. I think there's always going to be some event you could miss out on. That can be hard to juggle sometimes, but I'm lucky enough to have a fiancé who's also career-focused and driven, so we kind of use each other as motivation. I realized I could build a career without giving up on school I went to college for business and ended up dropping out when I got my salaried position. I told myself that I'd get back into college when I got my first store. My old store manager was the one who promoted me through all of the hourly supervisor roles. She even prepped me for my first salaried role. She sat in the office reading interview questions with me. Every time I'd say the word, 'um,' she'd say, "Nope, restart." She was constantly there for me, and even still having her as someone to go to has been great. My market manager has also known me since before I started promoting. Every time I think I'm too young to be in this room, he's always in my corner. I'm now enrolled in Live Better U , a program where Walmart pays for certain bachelor's degrees. I'm getting some of my foundational courses, and then I plan to get my college degree. Keep pushing to learn more For teenagers starting out, I encourage them to do a good job and learn as much as they can. Companies are constantly changing, especially with technology. It's important to adapt and not be comfortable with what you already know. When I look at my future at Walmart, I told myself I'd get to market manager at 27 or 28 — that's my short-term goal. Then, long-term, my goal would be regional EVP. One thing I always remind myself is that I worked hard to get to this life, so I can't be upset now that I have it. Maybe we don't have time to do all the fun things right now, but if we work hard through our 20s, thinking about where we might end up when we're 30 or 40 keeps me motivated. events.title: Egypt boosted by Moody's upgrade as inflation eases and investor confidence grows
events.summary: Moody's Ratings has raised Egypt's sovereign credit score due to easing inflation and growing business confidence as the country introduces economic reforms . The upgrade to B3 was underpinned by efforts focused on fiscal consolidation and structural reforms, which have helped reduce government debt and interest burdens, the New York-based ratings agency said on Friday. A B3 rating is still six notches below investment grade, which makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funds when the need to borrow arises. But the upgrade pulled Egypt out of the "substantial risk" level. "Stronger revenue collection and expenditure restraint have supported [Egypt's] progress," analysts at Moody's said. Cairo's shift to a flexible exchange rate and tighter monetary policy has strengthened external buffers and the economy's capacity to absorb shocks, they added. "The government's ability to sustain this credit-positive trend despite a challenging external environment and higher oil prices highlights the durability of the improvement, rooted in increased policy effectiveness," Moody's said. The agency also gave Egypt a positive outlook, noting sustained fiscal discipline and continued reforms that have performed better than expected. That could be further driven by "stronger growth, more effective revenue collection and a faster decline in domestic borrowing costs as inflation eases and investor confidence strengthens", it added. Fitch and S&P Global affirmed their ratings on Egypt last week, with both referring to the country's progress. Egypt has been battling economic challenges and elevated inflation, but the government has taken steps to counter their effects. "The reform of Egypt's monetary policy framework since March 2024 has strengthened the sovereign's ability to absorb external shocks," the Moody's analysts said. "The unification of the foreign exchange market and adoption of a flexible exchange rate reduced foreign currency distortions, eliminated chronic foreign currency shortages, and allowed the currency to adjust to changes in capital flows without depleting official foreign-currency buffers, unlike in 2022." As a net energy importer, Egypt was forced to introduce fuel-saving measures as the war in Iran drove up oil and gas prices, adding to inflationary pressures and the cost of living. Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, Capmas data show. Higher inflation might prompt a policy reversal at the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates. But the Arab world's most populous nation has been able to weather the economic fallout from the regional conflict relatively well, helped by policies centred on exchange-rate flexibility, energy price adjustments and spending controls. "The resilience of the updated macroeconomic policy framework has been tested by the sharp rise in oil prices and a confidence shock," Moody's said, referring to the decision by authorities to adjust domestic fuel and electricity prices, use expenditure contingencies and energy-conservation measures, and expand targeted social support rather than reversing energy price reforms. "These measures limited the fiscal consequences of higher commodity prices and helped preserve macroeconomic stability," the agency added. In July, Egypt was able to unlock about $1.8 billion in funding after clearing the latest review from its expanded economic programme with the International Monetary Fund .

events.title: Solar power booms in Philippines as war on Iran spikes energy costs
events.summary: With Southeast Asia’s largest electricity bills rising even higher, Filipinos invest in rooftop panels. Philippines solar power boom: Iran war spurs demand for renewable energy sources Manila, Philippines – Keith Cantera and his family have been thinking about having their own solar power grid at home for years. But spending up to $5,000 for solar panels was nothing to scoff at, so they put the idea on the back burner. It all changed this year when the United States-Israel war on Iran rattled global energy markets and sent electricity prices soaring. From paying a monthly bill of about $150 before the war began in late February, Cantera said his family went to forking out as much as $220. Eight months later, they are having solar panels installed on their rooftop. “The cost is about the same as paying our electric bills for three or four years based on the current rate,” Cantera said. “But in the fifth year, we’ll have recovered our investment, and electricity will essentially be free.” Cantera is one of a growing number of Filipino homeowners turning to solar power in a country that had Southeast Asia’s highest electricity costs even before the war. They were comparable only to Singapore, where the average income is more than 10 times higher. A report by the energy think tank Ember estimated that rooftop panels had nearly doubled in the Philippines since early 2025. And in the first months of the war from March to May, the rush for solar power led to $407m in panel imports, according to government trade data from China, where most panels are manufactured. The Philippines became the biggest single overseas market for that period. Only the Netherlands bought more, but it redistributes them to the rest of Europe. Lexus Grepo, CEO of the solar power supplier Solarmaxx, can attest to the boom. “There is a 30-day wait because solar panel shipments can’t keep up,” Grepo said. “In March, we had 40 projects, which was almost triple our monthly clientele. Since then, we have been setting up 25 to 30 systems a month.” Grepo does not expect demand to slow down even if tensions in the Middle East ease and shipping routes for energy supplies reopen. “I think people now realise that the world is an unpredictable place, so they have to be ready for any eventuality. Filipinos now see that they don’t necessarily have to be at the mercy of the global energy market.” The Philippines, one of the few countries in the region where electricity is not subsidised, relies on imported coal and gas for more than 70 percent of its power mix. The value of its currency, the peso, which has slid to a record low of more than 63 to the US dollar, is making these imports even costlier. In late March, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr declared a national energy emergency in response to the war ⁠and what he described as the “imminent danger” posed to the national energy supply. Still, electricity rates have continued to increase. The shift to solar is also partly driven by anger at electric companies that have come under scrutiny for charging customers for so-called system losses, which include illegal connections. Cantera said learning about having to pay for someone else’s electricity consumption was the last straw. “Who would agree to paying for something that you did not use? It’s not like the money we spend for electricity just fell from heaven,” he added. But while the soaring demand is real, the upfront cost of a solar power system is still too high for most Filipinos. The government in March launched a new initiative offering loans for residential rooftop installations, but these are available only to public sector workers. What officials hope can bring power rates down for the majority of people are the dozens of renewable energy projects in the pipeline, including a 3,500-hectare (8,650-acre) solar farm north of the capital, Manila, that is projected to be the largest in the world. When fully operational, the project is expected to generate 850 megawatts of electricity for 2.4 million households. But some consumers said such projects could take years to complete, leaving them with ballooning electricity bills unless they take action themselves. “It’s just so unpredictable nowadays. You have the impending El Nino weather pattern. There’s still war, the continuing fuel price hikes and so much more,” Cantera said. “So why not utilise a natural resource?”

events.title: Tesla is taking $250,000 deposits for a Roadster with SpaceX thrusters. The FAA says it isn’t an aircraft
events.summary: The flying car just got a little closer to reality. Tesla’s long-awaited Roadster drove upside down along a curved ramp, launched into the air, rolled 180 degrees using bursts of compressed air and landed on its wheels during a livestreamed demonstration Thursday at SpaceX’s rocket test facility in McGregor, Texas, near Waco. Moments later, it used its thrusters to leap over a lineup of Tesla vehicles , including a Cybertruck and a Tesla Semi. “Turns out the future does have flying cars,” CEO Elon Musk wrote on X afterward. Getting one into customers’ garages is another story. When Tesla first unveiled its second-generation Roadster in November 2017 , flying wasn’t part of the pitch. The company promised an electric supercar that could accelerate from zero to 60 mph in 1.9 seconds, seat four people and travel 620 miles on a single charge . Tesla began taking $50,000 reservations—or $250,000 for one of 1,000 limited Founders Series cars—and targeted a 2020 launch. That date came and went. Musk has repeatedly treated the sports car as a lower priority than Tesla’s other projects , while also blaming supply chain shortages for earlier delays. On Tesla’s October 2024 earnings call, he thanked “the long-suffering deposit holders of the Tesla Roadster” and explained that the car was “not just the icing on the cake, it’s the cherry on the icing on the cake.” Tesla now says production will begin in 2028—eight years later than originally promised. Three versions, one that flies The Roadster that took the stage Thursday is a radically redesigned car, built around the SpaceX thruster package Musk first floated in 2018 . It comes in three versions: Performance, a “road ready” two-seater with active aerodynamics and a fan-driven suction system; Thrust, a two-seater that adds rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters for sub-one-second acceleration to 60 mph; and Rocket, an invitation-only single-seater with 10 thrusters arranged around the car that can briefly take flight. Tesla engineering vice president Lars Moravy said the thrusters run on about 600 liters of rechargeable compressed air. Tesla claims a top speed of more than 230 mph. The redesign also comes with compromises. The original four-seat sports car now seats no more than two, and Tesla now promises a range of more than 300 miles —less than half the 620 miles it touted in 2017. The airborne spectacle was a prototype demonstration, not a test of a production-ready vehicle. It showed only brief aerial maneuvers, not sustained flight, and Tesla hasn’t said how long or how far the Roadster can actually stay airborne. Tesla states on its website that the Rocket version is “not approved for public road use.” It’s also unclear which regulator, if any, would oversee its flying features. The Federal Aviation Administration told CBS News and Politico that the vehicle doesn’t meet its definition of an aircraft, meaning the agency wouldn’t need to certify it as airworthy. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, which oversees vehicle safety, largely relies on automakers to certify that their cars meet federal standards. The Transportation Department said in a statement that NHTSA “will continue to monitor the situation.” Musk, for his part, isn’t pitching the Roadster as a safe car. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car, OK?” he said during the reveal . A halo car, not a moneymaker Securing a spot in line won’t come cheap. Tesla is asking for a $50,000 reservation payment for the Performance model and a whopping $250,000 for Thrust. The flying Rocket version is available by invitation only, with no publicly disclosed reservation fee. Tesla has yet to announce final prices for any of the three versions, and it hasn’t said what will happen to customers who put down deposits on the 2017 version. Despite the hefty reservation payments, the Roadster is unlikely to become a major revenue source for Tesla. Unlike its mass-market vehicles, the niche sports car won’t sell in large volumes. At Tesla’s 2023 annual shareholder meeting , Musk said the Roadster was “definitely not gonna be a huge contributor to revenue.” Wall Street agrees: The Roadster “will not move the volume or revenue needle,” Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a research note, according to CBS News . Its value may lie elsewhere. TechCrunch described the Roadster as a “halo car” for Tesla—a vehicle meant to showcase the company’s technological ambitions rather than a volume seller. The reveal also came days before Tesla reports third-quarter results, which analysts say matter far more to investors. The last car you drive yourself The Roadster also occupies a curious place in Tesla’s future. As the company shifts its focus toward autonomous driving and humanoid robots, Musk has said the Roadster will eventually be the only manually driven car Tesla makes. Yet Thursday’s demonstration had no one behind the wheel—just a mannequin in a SpaceX spacesuit, a nod to the “Starman” dummy that rode Musk’s original Roadster into space in 2018 . Musk said the car operated autonomously for safety reasons. For a company increasingly focused on taking humans out of the driver’s seat, the Roadster reminds us that driving can still be part of the attraction.
