events.title: ‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?
events.summary: Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last I nside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy. A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King. “Resilience” was the buzzword at one event after another, after six months in which sky-high oil prices and geopolitical chaos have made less of a dent in the global economy than first feared. Growth has not fallen off a cliff, buoyed up by the AI investment boom; stock markets haven’t crashed. “We had Covid, the war in Ukraine, supply-chain shocks, the war in Iran, and the alarm bells go off. And yet we haven’t had that massive synchronised crisis. So I think there’s this feeling that a lot of countries are sort of defying gravity at all income levels,” said Clemence Landers, the vice-president of the Washington-based Center for Global Development. Yet the IMF was also keen to remind delegates that the resilience of the past six months had been bought at a cost and may not last. The message – “Resilience under strain, urgent choices” – leapt out from the front page of its flagship publication, the World Economic Outlook (WEO). According to IMF experts, the cost of the energy support measures governments have put in place to protect their citizens from soaring oil prices, as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, has been an extraordinary 0.5% of global GDP. It said many countries would be unable to sustain support on this scale for much longer – and some had already begun to phase out subsidies, exposing the public to more of the costs of the conflict. The IMF urged governments to limit the costs and let market signals do their work, by sticking to temporary, targeted measures, rather than across-the-board subsidies. Aside from how to cope with the practicalities of a conflict that has persisted far longer than many governments had hoped – and whose end point remains elusive – the IMF was also keen to highlight two pressing risks. The first was what it sees as the unsustainable state of the public finances, particularly in the world’s richest countries. The WEO projected the highest budget deficits this year for advanced economies since the depths of the Covid pandemic. That means government debt in these countries is expected to keep rising – from 108% of GDP last year, to 115% of GDP in five years’ time. “Public debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from ageing populations, climate change and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks,” the WEO said. Anxiety about spendthrift governments appears to have been one factor driving the recent sell-off of government bonds – pushing up yields, or interest rates, to their highest levels in decades; though it also reflects higher expectations for inflation and growth. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva , lamented: “Too many countries, they did not use the post-pandemic recovery to rebuild fiscal buffers, and each new shock has pushed debt levels higher.” Fretting that this leaves governments exposed when the next shock comes, as well as pushing up the share of tax revenues required just to service debt, Georgieva repeatedly implored governments – not least Washington – to tighten their belts. “What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she said. It seems a message unlikely to land well with voters buffeted by one shock after another. The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, did not bother to travel to Bangkok to hear it; nor to oversee the meeting of G20 finance ministers, of whom he is formally the chair this year. The UK chancellor, John Healey, stepped in to chair the meeting instead. He spent much of his brief time in Bangkok stressing the importance of standing shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine – which the US has notably not been doing of late. Russia’s delegation was allowed to attend the G20 meeting, to the deep discomfort of UK delegates. The UK received a positive review from Georgieva and her colleagues, for setting out a plan to balance the books; though she conceded the bond markets had not rewarded its prudence. “The UK is actually one country where action to reduce the deficit has been taken decisively,” she said. Asked why the UK’s bond yields have not fallen accordingly, Georgieva said London’s status as a global financial centre tended to put the UK under additional scrutiny.

events.title: In nearly 2 decades of leading philanthropy at the Milken Institute, I’ve never seen a tidal wave like the one that’s coming
events.summary: There is a third wave of philanthropy coming to shore. It could be the tide that lifts society’s most important boats, but it will take understanding the currents, careful navigation, courage, and community.    In 2026, the world witnessed the largest initial public offering in history when SpaceX raised $75 billion, achieving a $1.77 trillion valuation. But those massive figures may soon be eclipsed. The two leading artificial intelligence labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, are both racing to IPO in the coming months, each with estimated valuations of at least $1 trillion.   The massive valuations of AI labs mean that thousands of tech workers are suddenly becoming wealthy. It’s estimated an additional $37 billion will flow to the philanthropy sector annually. The question before these tech employees should not be what this wealth can buy, but rather what it can do.  In my nearly two decades of leading strategic philanthropy at the Milken Institute, I have spent ample time with philanthropists, their families, and financial advisors, helping identify how their wealth could be used amid economic booms and busts. Just last year, I spent time interviewing several ultra-high-net-worth families as they grappled with how to transition their legacy of giving to the next generation. What I’ve come to learn is that philanthropic potential has never been greater than it will soon be. In 2026 alone, US charitable giving rose to $617 billion . This new capital only has a track record of exponential growth. If used strategically, it can be leveraged to unlock $1.5 trillion in catalytic capital or guide trillions in annual government funding. Let us embrace this historic moment with some tested principles of wayfinding in philanthropy.  I’d like to address directly those who are set to garner this new, unfounded wealth for the first time. There will be a litany of ways to use this capital. The first step is to establish an identity of how to give that represents your core values. Some of the best philanthropy starts from a place of personal connection.  Next, these new wealth generators must lean into the complexity of today’s most pressing problems – those that feel nearly impossible to solve, such as closing the hunger gap, estimated on the low end of $33B annually, to managing plastic pollution, estimated on the low end of $50B annually.  Just as AI now allows us to find connections, patterns, anomalies, and insights more quickly than ever before, that spirit and mindset can be brought to tackling housing insecurity, climate change, poverty, and so many other multifaceted problems. These challenges aren’t solved with single interventions, but rather by systems-based solutions that may require careful choreography of complementary approaches – research, building novel partnerships, policy change, awareness campaigns, social movements, or impact investment into commercial solutions.   Philanthropy can rewire and transform systems. It is society’s risk capital and can be deployed strategically to derisk solutions so other types of funding – from the government to the capital markets – can flow in. Through our work at the Milken Institute, we have seen time and time again the power of philanthropy to derisk – from advancing unproven, early-stage medical research to identifying and testing novel technologies created by entrepreneurs from around the world with no commercial track records – and creating investable opportunities for other financing that can bring pioneering solutions to market and at scale.  The philanthropy journey can be lonely, but there is an opportunity for connections to learn and grow together. Giving circles are the fastest-growing form of philanthropy, having tripled from 2016 to 2023 . At the Milken Institute, for example, we have several opportunities for philanthropists of all backgrounds to gather, connect, and meet on a peer level to learn from one another and explore ways to pool resources to achieve maximum charitable impact. This is a welcome opportunity to invite this new cohort into the fold. There is a perception that philanthropy is outdated. That it is solely about garnering positive press, and that nonprofits are not equipped to drive the change we need. However, true philanthropy, as I’ve come to know, is not as simple as writing a check, but when done with intention, can lead to real-life, impactful change.  The exact timeline for when these AI companies go public is still in flux, but there is no doubt that new wealth will be coming online soon, and some of it is already here. This is a call to action for this new cohort of captains to continue the legacy set before them by decades of philanthropists. This could be one of the largest infusions of new philanthropic capital in a generation. It must not go to waste. The seas are too stormy, and the stakes are too high.   So as this third wave of philanthropy comes to shore, let’s rally around these new philanthropists. May they find their North Star, set off with the courage and curiosity of our history’s greatest explorers, embrace the unknown and unimaginable, and find out not just where they can go, or what they can buy, but what they can do to make the world a better place.    The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: The wealthy boomer problem is metastasizing—they got 38% richer over the last 3 years as Gen Z and millennials under 35 got wiped out
events.summary: A fat stock portfolio and an expensive car can both make you feel rich. Over the past three years, though, they did very different things to Americans’ finances. The Federal Reserve’s latest Survey of Consumer Finances revealed a striking split: Median net worth rose roughly 38% for households headed by someone 75 or older between 2022 and 2025, while falling 23% for those headed by someone under 35. Both figures account for inflation, according to an analysis by Nick Maggiulli, chief data officer at Ritholtz Wealth Management and author of The Wealth Ladder . The Wall Street Journal first reported the age split in a short post on what it called “the gold standard for measuring household wealth,” which the central bank releases every three years. Americans 55 and over now hold roughly $140 trillion, about three-quarters of the nation’s net worth, Fortune reported this month , citing a Bank of America Institute analysis of the Fed data. The oldest households finished the period with a median net worth of $504,600, up from $366,288 in 2022, measured in 2025 dollars. For the youngest households, it fell from $42,725 to $32,820. The oldest group now has roughly 15x the wealth of the youngest, compared with about 9x three years earlier. Across all families, inflation-adjusted median net worth rose just 2% between 2022 and 2025, reaching $215,900. That modest national gain concealed sharply different experiences at opposite ends of the age spectrum. The findings also echo an argument Yale law and history professor Samuel Moyn made in an interview with Fortune this summer about his book, Gerontocracy in America : The concentration of wealth among older Americans is not merely a matter of who has had longer to save. In his account, it also shapes whose interests the economy and political system serve. Moyn describes an “oldigarchy,” in which older, disproportionately wealthy Americans hold outsize influence. His book argues that “aging Americans control the biggest bank accounts and stock portfolios,” and that “the old rich have pulled away from everyone else.” Asked about the latest Fed figures, Moyn responded by email that they further prove his thesis. “The question is whether the age correlation of the haves versus have-nots with the older versus the younger is fair,” Moyn ventured. “And it isn’t. So this is a case of the older getting richer, not just the rich getting richer.” “The boomers have created a new American system of rule, which reserves power—including in the form of wealth—for later life,” he told Fortune . “And that is the wrong time for power, including in assets and resources.” The Yale professor added that he does not expect the pattern to end here. Boomers, he wrote, “lucked out in acquiring a lot early and enjoying several asset bubbles along the way,” but the issue is older asset owners in general. “The pattern will increasingly be wealth concentrated towards the upper end of the age spectrum.” A bracket full of boomers The 75-and-older bracket is not purely boomers, to be sure. Households headed by someone that age in 2025 were born in 1950 or earlier, so it also includes the Silent Generation; the under-35 bracket mixes Gen Z with younger millennials. The survey also does not track the same households over time. Still, the youngest and oldest groups stood out. No other age bracket recorded a change in median net worth larger than 6% in either direction, according to Maggiulli, writing in his blog, Of Dollars and Data . Boomers help explain why the oldest group’s gains look so large. Wealthier boomers aged into the 75-and-older bracket between surveys, lifting its median. Comparing households aged 72 and older in 2022 with those aged 75 and older in 2025, Maggiulli calculated a smaller—but still substantial—21% increase. That follows a birth cohort, not the same individual households. The youngest households’ decline followed an unusually large pandemic-era gain. Their inflation-adjusted median net worth rose from about $18,000 in 2019 to nearly $43,000 in 2022—a roughly 140% jump that Maggiulli calls the largest on record—before falling to roughly $33,000 in 2025. Even after the setback, young households remained wealthier than their counterparts were before the pandemic. With stimulus checks gone and student loan payments back, Maggiulli suggests the drop may partly be a return to normal. But the figures still suggest that young adults up to age 35 feel 23% poorer since 2022. The crucial distinction, Maggiulli argued, was ownership—not just how much people owned, but what they owned. Older households had more of their assets in homes and financial investments. Younger households were less likely to own a home and had a bigger share of their assets sitting in the driveway. As investments rose and vehicle values fell, those different starting points mattered. Housing helps explain why. The share of under-35 households that owned a home fell from 38.5% in 2022 to 35.6% in 2025. Nearly two-thirds of young households therefore did not own an asset that accounted for a substantial share of homeowners’ wealth. Maggiulli recalled that back in 2021, he argued that millennials weren’t poorer than previous generations , and the data eventually proved him right . “But things feel different with the youngest households, many of whom are Gen Z,” he added, citing the worst job market for recent college graduates on record and housing reaching its least affordable in 40 years . Older households that built wealth over the last few years didn’t necessarily have to do anything differently, Maggiulli continued. “Their wealth gains came from appreciating assets. There’s nothing wrong with that. But many younger households may not get the opportunity to build wealth in this way.” The old rich pull away When Fortune first talked to Maggiulli , in August 2025, about his book The Wealth Ladder, he said there’s “something weird” going on in the economy, a problem of too much affluence and numbers that do not always match how people feel. “The economy wasn’t built to handle this many people with this much money,” he told Fortune . More recently, he described an “ upper-middle-class trap ,” in which even high earners find themselves working harder to buy declining-quality products and services. His latest analysis gets at another version of that disconnect: Rising asset prices can make the economy look prosperous while leaving younger households behind. If you already have a house and a portfolio, your wealth can grow without much additional effort. If a large share of what you own is your car, the same economy can deliver a very different result. The divide also fits a longer-running pattern. A 2025 paper submitted to the National Bureau of Economic Research by Edward Wolff found that average wealth among households under 35 fell from 21% of the national household average in 1983 to 16% in 2022. events.title: The Saudi Arabia airport attacks have made Middle East travel more unpredictable. Here's what to know.
events.summary: Riyadh's airport is closed until at least Saturday. Bernd von Jutrczenka/picture alliance via Getty Images Riyadh airport, one of the busiest in the Middle East, has been closed for a week after missile attacks. The US State Department has told Americans to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia. Delta has also suspended the launch of a new route to Saudi. Here's what to do if you're affected. Travel to Saudi Arabia and the broader Middle East is looking increasingly unpredictable this fall after a series of Houthi attacks on airports, including in the capital, Riyadh. The latest attacks killed 13 people and wounded hundreds last Saturday. Another strike the following day killed one person and injured about a dozen more. Flights to and from Riyadh have been suspended all week, and while the airport is set to reopen on Sunday, this has yet to be confirmed. The Houthis , an Iran-backed Yemeni militant group, control territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route linking the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. They have been attacking Saudi infrastructure amid an escalating regional conflict. Saudi Arabia has supported Yemen's internationally recognized government in the country's civil war, which began in 2014. Many airplanes continue to fly over eastern Saudi Arabia, including on routes to hubs in Qatar and Dubai and onward to East Asia. The US State Department told Americans to reconsider travel to Saudi Arabia because of the risk of missile and drone attacks, armed conflict, and terrorism. It also warned of "potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions." The UK's Foreign Office similarly says there is a heightened threat to airports and other infrastructure across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh, Jeddah, and Abha. On Monday, Delta Air Lines postponed the launch of its new Atlanta-to-Riyadh route, which had been due to begin on October 23, until March 2027. "Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long term," the airline said. It came after the Federal Aviation Administration warned US airlines on Sunday that the threats could pose risks during overflights, takeoffs, and landings in Saudi Arabia. Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation-risk company, said that unannounced missile launches through civilian airspace can pose a "latent hazard to flight operations at all altitudes," including from a malfunctioning missile, debris, and sudden route diversions. It also said further attacks on Saudi aviation and energy infrastructure are likely in the short term. What should you do if your flight is canceled? First, check your airline's app or website before going to the airport. The flight may have been canceled or automatically rebooked. Delta has issued a waiver for customers traveling to, from, or through Riyadh between October 23 and March 26. Eligible passengers can change their flight without paying a change fee, or cancel for a refund or credit. The rebooked trip must begin by May 31, 2027. Other airlines may offer their own waivers, but the terms can differ. It would be sensible to keep anything you would need for an unexpected overnight stay in your carry-on, including medication, a phone charger and power bank, toiletries, and a change of clothes. You should also avoid tight self-booked connections. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Trump waives new Russia sanctions in the "national interests"
events.summary: President Trump waived new sanctions on Russia late Friday night, saying it was in the "national interests" to hold off on the sweeping levies under the Graham Act that he signed just last month. Why it matters : Trump is easing American pressure on Russia despite a bipartisan chorus calling for him to do the exact opposite. It comes a week after his surprise deal to let Russia sell diesel internationally, which Republicans have condemned as loudly as Democrats. It also puts Republican candidates making their final midterm sprint in the position of having to defend the president's warmer relationship with a country voters overwhelmingly see as an American enemy . Driving the news: The White House released the text of an executive order late Friday night detailing the implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed in September. The bill, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, imposed broad new sanctions on Russia and countries that do business with it, including buyers of its oil. The order notes that the law allows the president to "waive the application of any sanctions provision with respect to a foreign person, any restriction with respect to a person, and any duty." "I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order. What they're saying: Democrats quickly blasted the waiver. "Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) posted on X. "These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, & everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) said on X. The big picture: The waiver caps a historic week in recent U.S.-Russia relations, where Trump abruptly eased pressure on multiple fronts. Whether it was the diesel deal, or a fight over Ukraine's ability to use Starlink to defend itself against Russian munitions, or a public denial of Russian involvement in the Iran war, Trump has spent the last few days shifting America's position on an old foe. The bottom line : The louder the bipartisan anti-Russia chorus gets, the more Trump doubles down on pulling back the pressure.

events.title: Walmart sees current diesel prices wiping out $2.9 billion tariff refund by end of 2027, Deutsche Bank says.
events.summary: Walmart is expecting up to an additional percentage point of inflation due to fuel costs in 2027, according to Deutsche Bank. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Walmart is bracing for billions of dollars in additional fuel costs due to higher diesel prices. The company previously said it would put much of its $2.9 billion tariff refund toward lower prices. Now, higher fuel costs are likely to erase that benefit, and other retailers are likely to follow. Just when US shoppers might have thought they dodged the tariff jab, energy costs are coming in with the right hook. Deutsche Bank says Walmart executives are now expecting the added cost of higher diesel prices to wipe out their total expected benefit from tariff refunds and push prices back up, according to a Thursday analyst note following a meeting with Walmart CFO John David Rainey. "Elevated diesel is pressuring WMT directly through transportation costs and indirectly as suppliers pass through higher costs, including on petroleum-linked products," the analysts wrote. "Elevated diesel costs are beginning to flow through to consumer prices" The company is now expecting an additional half to one percentage point of inflation in 2027, the note said. At that rate, additional fuel costs this year and next year will completely erase Walmart's $2.9 billion tariff refund. Walmart said in August that it had been putting the bulk of that tariff refund money toward lower prices for shoppers . "Like other retailers, we are not immune to sustained increases in fuel and transportation costs, but we work to minimize their impact," a spokesperson told Business Insider. The spokesperson also said that many of Walmart's current discounts and holiday deals are time-bound, after which some prices may return to regular levels. "That should not be characterized as a broad-based price increase," the spokesperson said. Beyond Walmart, which runs one of the most efficient supply chains in all of retail, the energy impact could be even more pronounced. The Deutsche Bank analysts noted that competing retailers are also hiking prices in similar categories, leaving Walmart with the relative low-price advantage. The bank also upgraded its rating of Walmart's stock. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: As Israel blocks PA funding, the West Bank’s healthcare system is failing
events.summary: Hospitals across the occupied West Bank have been hit by a funding shortage. Beit Jala, occupied West Bank – Khaldoun Atwan starts each day in the oncology ward at Beit Jala Government Hospital, not knowing what barriers will come his way. The Nabi Yunis checkpoint in Halhul seems to be “always closed”, so the head of the daytime oncology unit at the hospital leaves his car and finishes the commute from Hebron by taxi. list 1 of 3 Palestine weekly: Gaza marks year of ‘ceasefire’ with more Israeli killing list 2 of 3 Israeli forces raid Palestinian NGOs in occupied West Bank list 3 of 3 Gun-wielding Israeli settlers terrorise fruit pickers, observers “More than once, by God, I found the mirror broken. I found the wiper broken,” he said about his journey through an area where settlers are now active. Traversing a dizzying array of gates and checkpoints opening or closing at will, he does not know whether he will reach the hospital, whether his patients will, or whether the drugs they need will be on the shelf when they do. Beit Jala is the only government hospital in Bethlehem governorate, home to some 320,000 people. Inside his tiny, spartan office, Atwan is struggling to keep up with his cancer patients who have regressed because they missed crucial appointments or essential drugs needed for their chemotherapy treatment. Not even during the second Intifada, he recalls, was drug supply an issue. Now, it’s inescapable. “Everything’s short … whatever’s available we give,” he said. “It’s a disaster.” The Palestinian Authority (PA)’s finances have collapsed over the last three years due to a reduction in international aid and disruptions in Israel’s transfers of tax receipts. Israel’s actions in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, including widespread road closures, checkpoints and a series of settler pogroms against Palestinian communities, have also impacted the economy. As a result, the occupied West Bank’s healthcare system is rapidly deteriorating, with staff receiving just half their salaries, while the PA can’t pay for essential medications. Alongside others nervously pacing in the courtyard, an older cancer patient from a village in Bethlehem governorate stood at the entrance of the hospital, weighing with his son what to do. “Every month they do their best, the doctors and the cleaning staff, but they aren’t provided with anything,” he said. Ministry clinics are now operating part-time, with doctors seeing well more than 100 patients a day when they are. Now, even a doctor’s visit is rushed and unaffordable: “If we want to go to the doctor for a checkup, we need 200 shekels [$65],” said an older cancer patient. “It’s not a story of there being no staff,” said Iyad Dari, the attending physician at the dialysis unit at Beit Jala. Getting paid only half their salaries, “the government employee is working just two or three days a week, because he hasn’t got enough to come in for his full hours,” he added. As a result, the hospital ends up covering emergency cases only. “At first, [patients] were [angry]. But now everyone understands: Everyone’s suffering,” Dari said. The medical supplies crisis in Beit Jala and across the West Bank is the result of Israel’s withholding of tax revenues earmarked for the PA, an action spearheaded by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “This crisis is very predictable, and we saw it coming 100 percent,” said Milena Ansari of Physicians for Human Rights Israel. Even before the genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Israel was periodically withholding tax revenues, endangering the Ministry of Health’s coffers, Milena said. According to Yosef Ojra, an internal medicine specialist at Beit Jala, the withheld revenues have depleted the Health Ministry’s funds to pay medical suppliers, who are now withholding their services. The ongoing borrowing of supplies between the public and private arms of healthcare has greatly strained private clinics, pharmacies and hospitals. Hisham Amle, an oncologist at the hospital, said shortages are “an old problem, not a new one”, but that about 90 percent of important items – for chemotherapy, above all – used to be there. Now, even immunotherapies and biologics are missing, and cancer treatment runs on an unbroken chain. “If the patient misses a session or two, he’s lost all the treatment before it,” he said. “When I first took over the department, the drugs were available,” said Atwan, the lead oncology nurse. He then began to list all the crucial drugs he was now missing for his patients. “There’s not one single complete protocol I’ve got.” Khuloud Dweib, the hospital’s director of pharmacy, said the ministry recently managed to obtain eight previously missing oncology drugs and four biologics. This should be enough for between a month and a half and two months. But many other drugs are still out of stock, she said. Unlike in Gaza, Israel is not blocking medicines from entering the West Bank, Ansari noted.

events.title: Sudan’s army claims dozens of RSF fighters killed in Nyala attack
events.summary: Rapid Support Forces accuse army of killing 30 civilians in attack on Nyala’s busy livestock market. The Sudanese army says it has killed dozens of fighters from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in a series of air attacks on the southwestern city of Nyala, but the paramilitary group says the military has killed civilians. The targets of Friday’s attack were RSF positions and command centres in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state and the seat of the paramilitary group’s self-declared administration, the army said in a statement. list 1 of 3 Drone strike kills 30 people in Sudan’s Blue Nile region list 2 of 3 At least 72 Sudanese miners killed in air strike: Rights monitor list 3 of 3 Conflict, drought increasing risk of famine in Sudan: Monitor However, the RSF said the army carried out a drone attack on a busy livestock market, killing 30 civilians, including 17 women and five children. The group has not confirmed or denied whether separate attacks by the army killed some of its fighters and destroyed its command centres. Separately, the human rights group Emergency Lawyers said in a post on X that a market was hit on Friday in Nyala and the drone used was “affiliated” with the Sudanese army. Reporting from the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, Al Jazeera’s Almigdad Alruhaid said on Saturday that the fighting between the army and RSF has “intensified”. “In South Kordofan, a source in the Sudanese government told Al Jazeera that the RSF carried out drone attacks on mining sites with the exchange in fire intensifying in many parts of Sudan in the past 24 hours.” The army has repeatedly targeted the Darfur region in western Sudan with drones to try to retake territory controlled by the RSF, which holds most of the area. This month, Sudanese military chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan promised to seize “every inch” of territory under RSF control. The Sudanese civil war began in 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people. The United Nations has described the situation in Sudan as the world’s worst humanitarian crisis.

events.title: IMF urges support for poorer nations facing high inflation, war spillovers
events.summary: Low-income countries spend up to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, IMF chief says. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has a responsibility to help poorer nations struggling with rising debt, high inflation and price shocks caused by war spillovers, the head of the global lender says. Speaking as the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok wrapped up on Saturday, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said discussions with global policymakers showed both “optimism and worry”. list 1 of 3 AI fears are being weaponised list 2 of 3 Can Yemen’s government forces sustain their offensive against the Houthis? list 3 of 3 Israeli raids and arrests in southern Syria push population to the brink “Optimism from the resilience of the global economy, the promise of AI, the dynamism of Asia,” Georgieva told reporters. “But AI is also recognised to be a source of worry and so are inflation, high levels of debt, wars, climate risks.” Georgieva said vulnerable nations are missing out on the AI investment boom that is driving growth in richer countries while at the same time dealing with higher borrowing costs. Higher global interest rates mean low-income countries now spend 8 to 14 percent of their revenue on debt repayments, up from previous years, she said. “I can tell you that people everywhere, but especially in poorer countries, don’t like inflation. Inflation is like a tax on the poor,” Georgieva said. The warnings came as low-income, oil-importing countries take the strongest hit from rising global energy costs. Prices have soared since February when the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran , leading to retaliatory strikes in the Middle East and disrupted oil and gas flows. “Escalating conflicts ‌and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security,” said a statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chairman of the International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC). The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender. Georgieva said her organisation has a responsibility to help countries restructure debt if needed to assist with domestic resource mobilisation, bring in international finance and create conditions for private investment. Such countries need to set spending targets that prioritise growth and protect the most vulnerable people, she said, adding that the IMF has a “relentless pursuit of more resources for low-income countries”. “When we do our best, it translates into better lives for people,” she said. Georgieva also said the IMF plans to back Iraq “very firmly” with a requested loan programme while talks with Lebanese authorities are making progress. “We will get to Iraq both money and policy support,” she said. “In the case of Lebanon , we are in very intense discussions with Lebanese authorities. We have made significant progress towards the programme. We have still a bit more work to do together, and I’m confident we will be successful.”

events.title: Google Labs’ ‘secret society’ way of thanking its most valuable employees
events.summary: Josh Woodward is the vice president of Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio. Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images Google Labs leaders use ominous meeting invites to surprise and thank top staff. It's a "secret society" ritual for the most valuable employees, Google Labs chief Josh Woodward said. Woodward called the meetings "pretty fun" during an appearance on "Lenny's Podcast." An unexpected meeting invite with the boss is often the kind of thing that sends employees spiraling. For Google Labs staffers, though, it could mean top brass are about to tell you how great you are. Speaking on a recent episode of "Lenny's Podcast," Josh Woodward , the vice president of Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio, described the surprise appreciation meetings as a kind of "secret society" ritual for the team's most valuable employees. "We'll basically like put an invite on someone's calendar, and we'll just, you know, it looks kind of scary because there's like four or five leaders on the team," Woodward told podcast host Lenny Rachitsky, adding that there's no agenda given. "And then they show up, and we take turns. We go around the circle, and we just tell them why we appreciate them so much for being on the team," Woodward said. Woodward called the sessions "pretty fun" and said employees are regularly surprised to learn what the meetings are about. "I always start the meeting with like, 'This is not a bad meeting. This is a good meeting,'" he said. "Your mind may assume the worst, but we're actually doing the opposite. These are some of the most valuable people." The surprise recognition meetings are one of the ways Google Labs celebrates the often unflashy work behind its AI products , according to Woodward. He said the team also has a tradition of handing out quirky awards to employees. There's the "TPU harvester" award, which consists of a "little miniature rake" from Etsy as well as a cash reward, for staffers who optimize Google's AI chips, known as Tensor Processing Units , Woodward said. "A few of us wanted to figure out a way to reward people who do the grungy work of efficiency and reclaiming TPUs, harvesting TPUs, so we can build the next features and fuel our growth," he said, adding, "we kind of turned it into this big celebration." Employees who fix small product flaws or "paper cuts" receive a golden Band-Aid, Woodward said. And those who find surprising ways to push AI models toward new capabilities can become an "LLM whisperer," earning them a giant set of ears and a "really nice" mechanical keyboard. "We're trying to find like ways to kind of like I don't know encode the value in these like dorky symbols, but that means something," he said, explaining, "We're always coming up with weird stuff like this." events.title: Houthis strike Yemen’s Aden: What that means
events.summary: Armed group has hit the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the city’s airport as war spreads across the region. The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have fired missiles at the presidential palace in the southern Yemeni city of Aden, killing five people and wounding 16, on Thursday. On Friday, two missiles landed on the grounds of Aden International Airport as a passenger plane prepared to take off for Cairo. After the Houthis seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014, the internationally recognised government of Yemen decamped to Aden with the backing of a Saudi-led coalition of Arab countries. The latest attacks come as Yemen’s war , largely frozen under a 2022 truce, has reignited and become another front in the wider regional conflict involving Iran. So what has happened in Aden, and why does it matter? The Houthis hit the Al-Maashiq Presidential Palace with five missiles, according to Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani. Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said the dead and wounded included guards and civilian employees. The government said Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani and other officials were safe, but two of his bodyguards had been killed. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had struck what he called the “Saudi military operations headquarters” in Aden. On Friday, two missiles landed on the airport’s grounds, according to the Aden Security Department, which blamed the Houthis. It said it was the second attack on the facility in less than a week. Yemenia Flight 612 to Cairo was preparing for takeoff. Al-Eryani said the missiles landed about 500 metres (1,600ft) from the aircraft. No casualties were reported. Al-Eryani called the strike “a direct threat to the lives of passengers and aviation crews”. The Houthi-run Saba agency claimed the group was targeting a military headquarters and weapons depots inside Badr Camp, a military site next to the airport. Why are attacks on Aden significant? Aden is the interim capital of Yemen. The government moved there after the Houthis took control of the capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. The al-Maashiq Palace is the internationally recognised government’s headquarters and its seat of power. The Houthis currently control much of the country’s north and west. Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi coalition supporting the government had largely ended following a 2022 ceasefire. But in September, the Houthis launched a lightning offensive along the Red Sea coast, seizing territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea. Nearly two weeks ago, government forces launched a counteroffensive dubbed “Operation Dawn of Yemen” with Saudi air support, but have so far failed to reverse those gains. Saree said the Houthi attacks on Aden were part of the group’s declared policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”. In December 2020, an attack on Aden airport as a new cabinet arrived from Saudi Arabia killed at least 22 people. A second attack hit the palace where ministers had been taken to safety. The coalition blamed the Houthis, who denied responsibility. On Thursday, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, blamed Iran for having “encouraged” the escalation. He said the Iran-backed Houthis had rejected an offer to meet for talks in Oman when the latest round of hostilities began. Tehran denied the claim on Friday. “The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said. Baghaei said Iran “has always been ready to use its good offices to help end the hostilities”, offering again to mediate. Canada’s embassy in Saudi Arabia condemned the palace attack and called for “an immediate de-escalation of hostilities”. “We stand in solidarity with the internationally recognised Government of Yemen and the Yemeni people,” the Canadian embassy in Saudi Arabia said in a post on X. On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including those affecting civil aviation and energy infrastructure. The governing council of the UN’s International Civil Aviation Organization also condemned recent attacks on civilian airports and aircraft in Saudi Arabia. On October 9, Hans Grundberg, the UN special envoy for Yemen, told the UNSC the country had slid back into “full-scale war”. What is happening in the wider conflict? Fighting resumed in July, ending a 2022 truce. Last month, the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most important waterways. Since the Strait of Hormuz was closed by Iran in March amid US strikes, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on sending oil exports to the Red Sea via its East-West pipeline instead.

events.title: This CEO is on his 4th chief of staff in 5 years — by choice
events.summary: Covista CEO Steve Beard recently hired his fourth chief of staff. Eric Ogden Covista CEO Steve Beard treats the chief of staff role as a rotating post, not a permanent job. He said the first one he hired told him he talked too much in meetings — feedback he welcomed. The downside, Beard said, is having to replace someone performing at the peak of their abilities. Most chiefs of staff don't stick around for very long. Covista CEO Steve Beard sees that as a feature, not a bug. Since taking the helm at the healthcare education giant five years ago, Beard has appointed four chiefs of staff, with a few months of overlap between hires to preserve continuity. He treats the role as a leadership rotation rather than a permanent job, bringing in people with backgrounds that match his evolving needs. His first chief of staff specialized in finance, the second in strategy, the third in technology, and the fourth, who started recently, in management consulting. "Each of my chiefs of staff has looked different because I've been in a different place in my own journey at the time that they've come on board," Beard told Business Insider. "It really is defined by the leader and the moment." The median tenure for chiefs of staff is 2.3 years, a length that reflects both the job's intensity and its potential as a springboard to more senior positions, according to a 2024 report from McKinsey. That is also roughly the amount of time Beard said he considers appropriate for the job — and long enough for those in it to advance their careers afterward. His first chief of staff moved into a CFO role at one of Covista's universities , and the second became a vice president overseeing the company's business-to-business operations and clinical partnerships. The third is preparing to become a vice president of enterprise pricing. "It takes about one year to really get in a groove," said Beard. "By the time you're approaching three years, that's a pretty grueling pace." The demands of the job help explain why. Beard oversees five educational institutions that train students for careers in healthcare. Most weekdays, he said he's at his desk around 7 a.m. and leaves after 6 p.m. His chief of staff works closely with him throughout, starting with a 15-minute meeting to review priorities and prepare for what's ahead. They stay in close contact when apart and occasionally travel together. Beard said a key part of the job for his chiefs of staff is to give him honest feedback about how he interacts with his executive team, clients, investors, and others. He recalled how his first chief of staff told him he was talking too much in leadership meetings. He began holding back, allowing others to share their views before weighing in. "I found that I actually learned more by listening to the conversation amongst the team," said Beard. When he's ready to bring on a new chief of staff, Beard said he taps a variety of channels to identify potential candidates , including his own network, traditional search, and Covista's existing employee base. Of the four he's hired, two came from within the company. Beard said he looks for people who can influence without relying on authority, build strong relationships, bring a fresh perspective, and move comfortably between strategy and execution. Once on board, Beard said he asks his new right-hand advisors to take a fresh look at his routine and suggest modifications or improvements. One reorganized his executive team's meeting cadence, another introduced AI into office workflows, and his newest chief of staff is leading a five-year retrospective on his tenure to help shape the company's next chapter. Beard's revolving-door strategy isn't without drawbacks. He said replacing a chief of staff means giving up someone who is performing at the peak of their abilities and starting over with someone who needs time to build the same rapport and shorthand. "You do have to slow down to speed up a bit," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I went to see why Silicon Valley can't stop laughing at Elizabeth Holmes
events.summary: Extend booked out a theater at AMC Lincoln Square. Henry Chandonnet/Business Insider Tech companies and venture capital firms are hosting private screenings of the Elizabeth Holmes doc. I went to one hosted by the AI startup Extend. Attendees I talked to said they looked at Holmes more as a joke than a product of their industry. Elizabeth Holmes is a black mark on Silicon Valley's reputation. And yet its residents are lining up for the documentary about her. Tech companies across the US are hosting screenings of " You Can See Everything ," the documentary from Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim about Holmes and her fiancé, Billy Evans. Venture capital funds are bringing their founders to the movie. There are Luma events upon Luma events . The irony, of course, is that Holmes makes tech look bad. She sold big dreams with her medical testing company, Theranos, which eventually came crashing down. Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors of hundreds of millions of dollars. (She has long said that she is innocent.) Holmes is the exemplar of Silicon Valley's hucksterism. She's who much of America points to when they call founders liars or scammers. So, what's with all the tech love? I went to a Thursday screening of the documentary hosted by Extend, an AI documentation startup, to find out. Inside the Extend screening A swarm of techies crowded outside theater nine at New York's AMC Lincoln Square . The screening was set to start at 7. By 6:40, a crowd had formed to talk shop and admire Extend's custom stickers. Outside the theater door, I met Bo Lau, the event's organizer who works in developer relations for Extend. Lau recently moved to New York and said she didn't want to watch the documentary alone. So, she posted about it on X — and it helped that she already had a following on so-called "Tech Twitter." "I was like, 'What if I just turn this into a work event so I can expense it?'" Lau said. The event got 1,400 RSVPs for about 120 seats, she said, and she's flying to San Francisco soon to host another screening. The tickets were given out free, so Extend got no benefit other than brand awareness, she said. Extend gave out free stickers before we entered the theater. Henry Chandonnet/Business Insider Why was it so popular? Lau said that Holmes was a source of fascination within Silicon Valley, and that Fielder's "awkward humor" matched the awkwardness of tech . Filing into the theater, I heard my seatmates chat about AI and which tech companies let you work from home . On a brief social media scroll before my three-hour Do Not Disturb, I spotted Lau's recent project: a simulator of Holmes' desk. Holmes' X account responded: "Impressive project." Laugh lines, reflection time This was my second time watching the documentary; the first was at New York Film Festival . The reactions among the techier crowd were mostly the same. There were lots of laughs, both at Fielder's discomfort and Holmes' oddities. The crowd didn't react strongly to (mild spoiler alert) the big, AI version of Holmes that her fiancé creates after she goes to jail. That struck me as curious; maybe the tech crowd is already used to AI replicas . There was also a much stronger gasp at the reveal of who's running Holmes' X account. That wasn't shocking; the attendees found out about this screening through X, after all. The crowd talked about AI and corporate benefits before the documentary started. Henry Chandonnet/Business Insider We walked to a local wine bar, sipping cocktails while debriefing the film. Two techies that I talked to were split. One came away feeling bad for Holmes, then feeling bad that he felt bad for her. Another thought the film certified that Holmes was a true and utter psychopath. I asked: Why is tech so comfortable laughing at Holmes? Her boastful visions don't sound too different from those of the current crop of young AI founders . Maybe it was because the crowd was mostly in their 20s, not yet working in startups when Holmes' reckoning came. Or Holmes has been detached from her Silicon Valley roots. The techies seemed to view her as more a product of the media — the books, the tabloid stories, the Hulu show — than of their own industry. One attendee put it to me bluntly: she's turned into a meme. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: IMF to accelerate talks with Iraq and Lebanon as Mena support grows
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund is to advance discussions with Iraq and Lebanon as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa, its managing director has said. Baghdad had approached the Washington-based fund for a potential programme, as the IMF continues to look at opportunities in the region, signalling it will be ready for any nation that may seek its assistance, Kristalina Georgieva said. "We will support Iraq very firmly. We would get Iraq both money and policy support," she said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand on Saturday. She also noted IMF support in Egypt and Jordan. "We are in very intense discussions with the Lebanese authorities," she added. "We have made significant progress towards a programme. [There is] still a bit more work to do together and I'm confident we will be successful." Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. But Baghdad has been driving efforts to boost its standing. Last month at the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi appealed to the world to invest in Iraq as he pitched his economic and anti-corruption plans. Lebanon, meanwhile, is heavily reliant on imports, making it more exposed to shocks such as the disruption to shipping and energy supplies caused by the regional war. Beirut is also still dealing with the effects of the economic crisis that began in 2019. That was one of the worst in modern history, according to the World Bank, which also projected Lebanon's economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026. The IMF said this month that it would assess any potential changes to Lebanon's bank resolution law to ensure they were consistent with international standards. On Wednesday, the governor of Lebanon's central bank, Karim Souaid, told Bloomberg that he was expecting a "breakthrough" by the end of 2026 in IMF talks on the law, which stipulates it would repay depositors whose savings were entangled in the country’s financial collapse. "Programmes for Iraq and Lebanon would go a long way," Ms Georgieva said. She also acknowledged efforts by governments in the Gulf, whose pursuit of reforms have allowed them to "cushion the impact of the shock that has impacted them". "It would've been much worse if ... many of them have not done reforms and been building buffers," she added.

events.title: I lost my job right before having my first child. My wife and I took the opportunity to level up our side hustle.
events.summary: Rachel Calaj and Felipe Rochi run a camcorder rental business for weddings. Felipe Rochi Felipe Rochi lost one of his jobs while his wife was pregnant with their first child. They decided to take the leap and grow their side hustle — a rental camcorder business — together. As new parents, the two of them split the tasks involved in running the business. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rachel Calaj and Felipe Rochi, a married couple in their 30s. Together, they run a wedding camcorder rental business that they started as a side hustle. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Rochi: I'm an SEO supervisor. I also had a second job in the SEO space, but I was terminated this summer, in early June. Calaj: I've been a school psychologist, typically hired through an agency to work for a district on a contract basis. We found out we were pregnant last December, and my contract ended in May. We were trying to think throughout that time what we would do next year. Felipe lost his job before our baby shower Calaj: As a first-time mom , I wanted to stay home with my child. We were trying to see if Felipe's two jobs would be enough for me to do so. Then, he got terminated the day before our baby shower. It was a very sad moment for us, but we still had a great time at the baby shower, even if it wasn't the best timing. Rochi: Unexpectedly losing my job and her contract ending around that time impacted our income significantly. Calaj: It changed everything for us; it was a turning point. We were in the middle of buying baby clothes and all the things that you need. Rochi: I applied for a decent number of jobs . You never hear back from jobs fast enough. You're just waiting to see if you got it. My dad owns a cleaning business, so we considered asking him for work in the meantime. With a kid on the way, we were thinking about anything I could do. Calaj: I reached out to the district that I worked for the previous year to see if I could do some flexible, part-time contract work. We were trying anything we could to have extra income at that point. We turned an idea into a new income stream Rochi: In April, I saw videos of somebody renting camcorders to people to record their weddings, and then editing the footage for them. I immediately thought it was a really cool idea. My brain started to spin. Before even telling Rachel, I created a website and a TikTok account for our business, Pass the Cam, and posted a few videos just to see if it could work. I've tried a lot of side hustles over the years, including starting a newsletter that sent people entry-level remote job postings and creating a product called DooBagz, a bag dog owners could clip on to hold a used poop bag. However, they didn't work out. Calaj: With this camcorder side hustle, I could see real momentum behind it from the start. Felipe hit the ground running, and when our first order came in, I was so excited. The couple had their first clients in May and have had nearly 100 clients since then. Felipe Rochi Our first orders gave us hope we could do this Rochi: We were at T.J. Maxx one Friday night when somebody reached out and said their videographer canceled and she needed our camcorders the next weekend. I was like, "Oh snap, I have to ship this out ASAP." I bought a Sony 4K camcorder and memory card from a camera store nearby for around $1,100, including the warranty, picked it up on Saturday, and bought a random box to ship it to her. Because we didn't have the money to pay an editor right away, and we were trying to pay off the camcorder I'd just bought, I edited the footage she sent back, since I have a little bit of experience with editing. She loved it. That first client was in May, before I lost my job. By the end of the month, we had gotten two more clients. It gave me something to fall back on when my termination happened in June. I said, "Hey, I got a couple of clients out of this, so why not try this more?" I was still applying for jobs, though, because a second job felt more secure than betting on a side hustle . Calaj: Of course, there was still some uncertainty. You always wonder whether something will take off or eventually fizzle out. We've had nearly 100 clients since we started Rochi:  Our goal is to reach 100 clients by the end of 2026. We're nearly there, and we still have some months to go, so I think it's possible. We've made over $50,000 in net volume since starting in May, about half of which was in September alone. I see more camcorder rental businesses showing up compared to when we started, but with millions of weddings a year in the US, I believe there's room for everyone. We try to price our packages slightly lower than our competitors, run almost monthly promos, and include everything without charging for add-ons. We actually dropped the prices for our two most expensive packages in order to stay competitive. Our packages are $429 for our starter package, $699 for the core package, and $899 for our deluxe package. They differ in terms of the type and number of camcorders, the length of edited video, and additional attachments like microphones and lights. Calaj: I handle the operations side, like managing bookings, handling shipping logistics, ordering packaging, hunting down the best deals on boxes and stickers, and growing our camcorder inventory. The cameras are probably the biggest expense that we have at this moment, but it's been worth it so far. My husband leads marketing and is the main point of contact for every couple we work with. He takes care of the camcorders themselves, making sure each one is working properly and set up with the right settings before it ships. He also works with our editors and reviews their work, so everything we send out is top quality. On top of that, he manages our finances , making sure we're smart about what we earn and how much we reinvest back into the business. Rochi: Sometimes overbooking happens, or we don't have enough inventory. I think that's all part of learning a new business . Their business has grown to have multiple camcorders and editors. Felipe Rochi We wish we'd had something like this at our wedding Rochi: Some might disagree with our ways, but we know how expensive weddings already are. Calaj: When we got married about four years ago, we did more of an elopement-style wedding with our close friends and family because we were starting off in our careers. We had disposable cameras; we still have those pictures around our house. To hear that wedding videos can now cost thousands of dollars — it's just an insane amount. We both said that if camcorder rentals were around when we got married, it would be a really cool thing to do. It's really sweet looking at the videos; it just feels very homey. Rochi: The coolest part is hearing back from the couples over text or in reviews. We became new parents in August Calaj: It's definitely been hard to be new parents , but we love it. events.title: ‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes
events.summary: The entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacy D avid Agus’s first encounter with Elizabeth Holmes at a health conference came as a shock. The Holmes he met in the green room was personable and pleasant. The Holmes he interviewed on stage was altogether different. “The accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,” Agus, a medical oncologist , recalls by phone from Los Angeles. “It was as if I had met a person and then interviewed a separate person. That transition from the green room to the stage – I had never experienced something like that before.” Holmes is not like you or me. She was still a teenager when she founded Theranos, touting technology capable of performing medical tests using only a few drops of blood. She cultivated a distinctive persona: blond hair, an unblinking gaze, a husky voice and a black turtleneck worn in homage to Apple co-founder Steve Jobs . Holmes mesmerised investors and board members including Rupert Murdoch, Larry Ellison, Carlos Slim and former secretaries of state Henry Kissinger and George Shultz. She became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire. But it was all an illusion, a confidence trick built on a scam. Holmes’s shining career ended in disgrace and imprisonment. Margaret O’Mara , a history professor at the University of Washington in Seattle and author of The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, says: “You can’t make this stuff up. If some screenwriter had tried to manufacture this out of whole cloth people would be like, no, this is an unbelievable story. Yet it’s real. Who’s the real Elizabeth Holmes? That’s a question that still hasn’t been answered .” Perhaps the answer lies in You Can See Everything , a reality-bending documentary, released in the US on Friday, in which Holmes goes eyeball-to-eyeball with the absurdist comedian Nathan Fielder, who directs along with Lance Oppenheim. It was filmed in the 34 days before she was due to report to federal prison camp Bryan in Texas to begin her 11-year sentence for wire fraud and conspiracy. That fate seemed unthinkable in 2003 when, at the age of 19, Holmes dropped out of Stanford University and established Theranos , promising to revolutionise the multibillion-dollar blood-testing industry by using microfluidics to run hundreds of tests on just a few drops of blood. She found a receptive audience among investors who wanted Silicon Valley to deliver more than Facebook friends. O’Mara explains: “ She stands out in her ascent as a female entrepreneur at a time when men were dominating the scene and she was doing something that was in tech but seemed to be change-the-world-tech. “The techlash wasn’t brewing yet but, where there was criticism of Silicon Valley, it was like: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people and all you’re doing is building apps? Why don’t you do something a little more meaningful?’ And: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people, but they all seem to be men.’” O’Mara adds: “She was going against gendered expectations but also, to become the female Steve Jobs, she made herself less feminine and also made herself less young.” Holmes ran the company with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, a businessman 19 years her senior, while keeping their romantic relationship a secret. Together they raised $945m. Theranos had published no peer-reviewed data but Holmes was a charismatic and persuasive presence in boardrooms. Agus, a professor of medicine who is chief executive of the Ellison Medical Institute , comments: “You know how you go into a room and there could be 10 people at a table and everyone’s having a discussion? All of a sudden one person speaks and the entire room goes: ‘Yeah, I’ll go that direction.’ She had that ability. “I saw how she was able to sway people. That characteristic is great if you’re a Steve Jobs. That characteristic is very difficult in health because we should be data-driven, not swayed by personalities.” By 2014 Theranos was valued at $9bn. Holmes was named the youngest female self-made billionaire in the US with a net worth of $4.5bn by the time she was 30. She was celebrated on magazine covers and in power lists. The New Yorker wrote : “Although she can quote Jane Austen by heart, she no longer devotes time to novels or friends, doesn’t date, doesn’t own a television, and hasn’t taken a vacation in ten years. Her refrigerator is all but empty, as she eats most of her meals at the office. She is a vegan, and several times a day she drinks a pulverized concoction of cucumber, parsley, kale, spinach, romaine lettuce, and celery.” The heady atmosphere seduced elder statesmen such as Shultz, who had served as a bridge between Washington and Silicon Valley during the Ronald Reagan era. Despite no specialist expertise in laboratory diagnostics, he joined the Theranos board in 2011, when he was in his 90s.

events.title: The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time | Jeffrey Ingold
events.summary: The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution … D o you remember the last time you were lied to? I certainly do. I was tricked by the North Finchley Vue, which sold me and my boyfriend tickets to a 7.15pm showing of The Odyssey. Guess what was playing at 7.15pm? A car advert. Ten minutes later, it was a trailer for the horror film Werwulf. Then there was an advert for Vue – as if I wasn’t already there. The film was half an hour late to its own showing when it finally started at 7.45pm. I am sick and tired of cinemas getting away with such treachery. I don’t want to follow in the footsteps of my friend, who knows that the ads at her local run for 22 minutes so slinks in at just the right time. I shouldn’t have to do mental maths because I am being lied to by cinemas. We are all the victims of their predatory time-wasting system. If you went to see a play and the ticket said the show started at 7.30pm, you’d rightly be annoyed if after 20 minutes the performance still hadn’t started. Yet when it comes to watching movies, we’ve collectively accepted that it’s fine for them to start later than advertised. Which also means we all put up with people coming in late, shining their phone torches and bumping into you because they tried to show up when the film actually starts. Now that almost a third of wide releases run over two hours and pre-show advertising and trailers last for 20-30 minutes, something’s gotta give. I say films should start on time. I know a better moviegoing experience is possible. I grew up in Canada, where our cinemas played their films at the ticketed time and the ads started earlier. When my family showed up 10 minutes late to The Fellowship of the Ring, we missed the entire opening sequence explaining the history of the rings of power. We deserved that! A brave senator in Connecticut tried to tackle this injustice in 2025 with a bill that would “ require the disclosure of accurate movie start times in advertisements and listings ”. However, it was watered down to a mere “working group” after pushback from cinema operators. They warned they’d lose vital revenue if advertisers pulled back because people started skipping the pre-show entirely. Erin Brockovich wouldn’t have given in so easily. How can we succeed where the Connecticut senator failed? Simple: we also get rid of assigned seating. Say goodbye to paying £26 for an Ultra Lux recliner if you want the best view. It’s a flat fee no matter where you sit. Welcome to the Hunger Games of cinema seating. If you want a “good” seat for a film, you have to earn it by showing up early. Exactly like when I was young, the ads and trailers will play before the start time so the film can begin promptly. Arrive on time, after the trailers, and you might be stuck in the front row, but that’s on you for avoiding the ads. I’m just a cinephile, standing in front of a movie theatre, asking it to respect me and my time. Why is that so hard? Jeffrey Ingold is a freelance journalist covering LGBTQ+ issues, music and culture

events.title: Stinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewer
events.summary: Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem T he leafy south London neighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. But there is something foul in the air of this corner of the capital – and for once it’s not the traffic fumes hitting bicycle riders. A toxic stench thought to be caused by untreated sewage stuck in Thames Water drains has been emanating from the subterranean depths for months, most likely caused by the summer’s lack of rain. The stink is so acrid that the Bicycle Nation shop has had to bar some customers and its mechanics have been forced to work on the pavement outside. The owner of the shop, Tamas Polocz, has repeatedly complained to Thames Water since the smell first hit the shop in June and caused his colleague Nick to vomit. Last week the troubled water company told Polocz it accepted that a mains sewer directly beneath the shop was to blame, but it has yet to offer him and his team of 11 any date for resolving the problem. Polocz and his colleagues have been left fearing for their physical and mental health after repeated exposure to the gassy stench. And the outlook for the business is bleak. The odour comes in putrid wafts that occur at least five times a day, according to a “smell chart” used to log the time and duration of each incident with a description. The words used include “cabbage”, “teargas”, “onions”, “spicy BBQ” and repeated references to “shit”. When the Guardian first arrived at the shop there was a whiff of rotten eggs but not enough to stop mechanics working inside and customers milling about. But within minutes we were overpowered by a repulsive gas that hit the back of the throat and left us scurrying outside, gagging for air. “It’s unbearable,” said Polocz. “You can’t be in the shop when it comes.” He added: “It has a really strong physical presence. This is a smell you take home with you. It’s in your hair, on your skin, sometimes it feels it’s inside your skin. When you go home and cough, you taste it again.” The ordeal comes after record-breaking temperatures and drought prompted calls for a radical overhaul of an outdated sewage system , just as the Great Stink ushered in new sanitation in the Victorian era. Thames Water initially suggested the Herne Hill smell was due to a gas leak. But extensive tests by the local gas supplier ruled that out. Polocz said he had been battling the company every week. “Thames Water have always tried to push me away, or blame others. When they finally accepted liability last week I just broke down. But we still don’t have a date for fixing it.” The exact cause of the stench remains unknown, but a Thames Water engineer told Polocz it was likely to be linked to the lack of rain. The engineer also told him that a cast-iron ventilation pipe that had previously drawn odours away from the shop had not been replaced. Experts warn that during dry periods, untreated sewage builds up in pipes with no rainwater to flush it out. Microbial activity in the sewage causes foul-smelling gas to be emitted in wafts , in a similar process to the one that causes flatulence in human digestion. Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, said: “It sounds like methane and it’s probably unsafe working conditions. Biological processes are cyclical just like in your digestive system, which is why sewer smells come in wafts.” When Polocz woke up to rainfall, he was hopeful it would flush away the stench. “I looked out through the window at home and thought, oh good, but it didn’t make any difference. Even after the rain there was still the smell. Maybe the rain will eventually clear it, but we don’t know. Something is happening down there that is pushing the smell up.” Evans said: “The first flushes of rain will probably make things smell worse because it just stirs things up. It needs a lot of rain to clear. There might be some blockage there but it’s impossible to know without a proper inspection.” Harriet Talbot, a board member of Bicycle Nation, said: “You can’t run a business relying on the weather.” She helped set up a webpage asking for customers to sign up for a collect and repair service to help the shop survive. Polocz said the shop was currently unsustainable because staff had to evacuate so frequently. “We have to do half a day in the shop and half outside on the pavement. But now the cold weather is coming, we can’t keep doing that.” And the stress from the stink is taking its toll. Polocz said: “I’m 49, but today I feel 62-ish. We have guys calling in sick. It affects you both physically and mentally.” Polocz said he laid in bed at night worrying how he would be able to keep the shop going. “The last thought of the day and the first thought of the day are now both the same,” he said.
