events.title: China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
events.summary: The concept of ‘paying to suffer’ soars in popularity, with simulated disasters proving a modern twist on visiting sites of historic tragedies W hen Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods. “I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China . “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.” She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario. Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.” Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”. Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments. At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster. “I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.” It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations. The offerings are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake. Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country. In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis. “The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction. In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside. In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck. “I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.” Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered. In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres.

events.title: Darwin accountant trades tax for cane toad taxidermy
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'More to life': Darwin accountant trades numbers for cane toad taxidermy Mithram Selvaratnam transforms cane toads into souvenirs sold at Darwin's Mindil Markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) There are 531 dead cane toads in Mithram Selvaratnam's Darwin backyard freezers. By Christmas, some will be wearing Santa hats. The former accountant runs an unusual souvenir business, which sees him doing everything from sandblasting and whitening crocodile skulls to gutting and stuffing dead toads. Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam now sells taxidermy cane toads and crocodile products at Darwin's markets. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) It's a far cry from the life he envisioned for himself when he left Malaysia to study accounting in Australia 16 years ago. "When I grew up it was all about the rat race," he said. The decision to leave it all behind came to Mr Selvaratnam after working full time as an accountant in Melbourne. "I was doing that corporate life, 9 to 5, stuck in the office, and I just felt like there was more to life," he said. Christmas-themed cane toads are being prepared for the festive season. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Word of Mr Selvaratnam's dilemma got out to his Darwin-based aunt, who offered an unexpected solution. For decades she had been selling curries at the iconic Mindil Markets and a neighbouring stall had put his Territory souvenir business up for sale. That was in 2017 and the transition from spreadsheets to stuffed toads hasn't always been smooth sailing. Mr Selvaratnam was initially purchasing the toads from a taxidermist in Queensland, but when the supplier decided to retire, he was left with two choices — give up the business or take matters into his own hands. Grace Ray works on a taxidermy cane toad at Mithram's Leanyer work space. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) "Before I started doing this, I could barely pick a toad up," he said. "But I thought, we have plenty of toads in the Territory, an abundance of supply, so I'll just make them myself. "I went [to Townsville] and put myself through a two-day bootcamp of learning how to do it." It was through gritted teeth and pinched nostrils that Mr Selvaratnam learnt to gut, tan, stuff and dry the warty pests before painting them with varnish to make them "look pretty". Former accountant Mithram Selvaratnam couldn't even touch cane toads until he underwent 'taxidermy bootcamp'. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Armed with his new-found knowledge, a head torch and gloves, Mr Selvaratnam began scouring golf courses and gardens hunting the pests. Community 'toad busts', like the one held recently at the Territory Wildlife Park , can provide hundreds of dead toads to Mr Selvaratnam in a single night without him having to lift a finger. Territory Wildlife Park ranger Luke Hare says toad busts aim to reduce the numbers of the pests while also educating the community of their dangers. "Cane toads produce significant risk to a lot of our native species," he said. "A lot of our natives can't tolerate the toxins cane toads have, so when they eat the cane toad, or try to eat them, often it will kill them." Mr Hare estimates that there could be hundreds of thousands of cane toads running rampant in the wildlife park on Darwin's outskirts. For Mr Selvaratnam, the park's latest haul of 531 toads has come just in time for his end-of-year Christmas orders. Soon, newly minted santa hat-clad critters will join their rum-drinking, ukulele-playing and occasionally X-rated counterparts. The recent toad bust has filled the freezers at his Leanyer workshop. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) But cane toads aren't the only unwanted creatures finding a second life in Mr Selvaratnam's backyard. Among the tanning equipment and taxidermy tools are chest freezers full of crocodile heads. "I started with the toads and the skulls came about a year after that," he said. Crocodile teeth and skulls are also turned into souvenirs. ( ABC News: Lillian Watkins ) Mr Selvaratnam had initially been buying the skulls from a supplier, but in a case of deja vu, retirement once again threatened his supply chain. "This time I didn't go down to Queensland to learn, I just got him on the phone and he ran me through it, and from then, on experimentation, really," he said. The skulls are a by-product from crocodile farms in the Territory, and along with croc teeth, buffalo heads and other leather goods, they make up the rest of Mr Selvaratnam's unlikely livelihood. He's also recently been experimenting with other forms of taxidermy including the Territory's iconic barramundi.

events.summary: The Treasury Department said the U.S. budget deficit came in at nearly $2 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year. The U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The U.S. finished the 2026 fiscal year with a budget deficit of nearly $2 trillion, the latest measurement to underscore the extent of the country's financial stress. The $1.992 trillion figure was about 12% higher than the $1.775 trillion deficit in the prior fiscal year, the Treasury Department reported Friday. It's the third-highest annual deficit in U.S. history, behind only 2020 and 2021, when the federal government was doling out trillions of dollars in financial stimulus amid the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2026 fiscal year saw record sums for both receipts and outlays, according to a Treasury Department official. With Friday's release, the U.S. officially recorded its 25th straight fiscal year operating at a deficit. The government last recorded a surplus — meaning its revenues were larger than debts — in 2001. Friday's report offers fresh evidence of how the U.S.'s fast-growing debt pile has dragged on the nation's overall financial health. The rising debt bill has helped exacerbate angst among bond traders, who sent the 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury yields to 24-year highs last week. Social Security amounted to the biggest slice of government spending at nearly $1.7 trillion for the full fiscal year, up modestly from the roughly $1.6 trillion spent in 2025. Medicare was the second biggest contributor, costing almost $1.1 trillion for the fiscal year. By comparison, the government-run healthcare program required slightly under $1 trillion in fiscal 2025. Net interest – a calculation of the Treasury's gross interest minus the interest it receives – also topped $1 trillion for the fiscal year. In the 2025 fiscal year, net interest totaled $970 billion. Individual incomes taxes helped lessen the total deficit by bringing in more than $2.8 trillion, an increase of about 7% year over year. Corporate income tax provided $381 billion in receipts during the 2026 fiscal year. That was a decrease of about $70 billion from fiscal 2025 stemming from the tax cuts included in the One Big Beautiful Bill act passed by Congress last year. In the 2026 fiscal year, the U.S. shelled out more than $1.3 trillion in interest on the national public debt. The total owed exceeded $40 trillion earlier this year and has more than doubled over the last decade. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC in August that the U.S. can "grow our way out of" its increasing debt pile. "Our message to our allies, our trading partners, is that global growth is the way to take care of this mountain of debt," Bessent said in August. President Donald Trump pitched his plans for broad and steep tariffs as a way to drive up revenue and shrink the government's debt. The White House has pushed forward with its strategy of increasing levies on trading partners despite the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that many of those instituted by Trump were unconstitutional. The Treasury saw a record high for gross customs duties in the 2026 fiscal year, according to a department official. But the total revenue from customs took a hit due to refunds required following the Supreme Court ruling, which sent billions of dollars back to retailers. The Treasury also reported Friday that September's monthly deficit came in at $27 billion, a reversal from the prior year, when the department saw a surplus of $198 billion in the month.

events.title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
events.summary: Treasury yields remain above 5%, pushing mortgage rates toward 7.5%. The deficit was $1.99 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% from last year. AI investment is increasing competition for capital. Divided government will likely take meaningful deficit reduction off the table. Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory. Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future. The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield . The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates. In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market. If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields. But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump 's term. There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP. Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates . If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits. The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years. "My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth. AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget , a research group that advocates for balanced budgets. GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy. Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency, a moment when presidents often take on big, legacy-defining projects. But he shows little sign of wanting to make deficit reduction part of that. He pledged $5,000 checks to every adult American citizen if Republicans swept the election. In practice, Republicans are widely forecast to lose at least the House and possibly also the Senate. Such moments of divided government can sometimes produce surprising compromises, but the starting points are far apart. Rep.

events.title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test
events.summary: Apple's iPhone Duo launch-day pickup inventory sold out quickly, with some delivery estimates already slipping into late January online. The price of the first foldable iPhone reaches $3,199 at 2TB, creating a new tier above the Pro and Pro Max. Analysts say the Duo could boost Apple’s average selling prices through trade-ups, Android switchers and a halo effect across the rest of the iPhone lineup. Apple 's iPhone Duo , its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January. The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary." "We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said. Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max. The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol. But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable. Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units. That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity. "Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand. Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem. Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile. "It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said. The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated. Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500. Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share." Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year. That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity. Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply. Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term. IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards. "Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said. And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before. When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs. That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products. The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business. IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026. Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025.

events.title: 5 midterm money takeaways: Democrats have candidate cash. Republicans have Elon Musk
events.summary: Democratic candidates hold the fundraising edge across key Senate races and 13 of 21 House "Toss Ups" analyzed by CNBC. Republican super PACs are offsetting those gaps with record outside money, led by a $272.9 million quarter for the Senate Leadership Fund. Elon Musk emerged as the cycle’s biggest known individual donor, pouring more than $276 million into federal groups, including a major effort to help Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race. One of the last big campaign-finance snapshots before the Nov. 3 Election Day is now available, and both political parties found something to like. But campaign cash is flowing in very different ways — and, on balance, points to an environment more favorable for Democrats. On one side, Democratic candidates have turned into absolute cash cows, raising oodles more than their Republican rivals across Senate and House battlegrounds. Republicans, however, still have a leg to stand on from an unprecedented flood of outside super PAC cash , bankrolled by a tiny circle of billionaires led by Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk . The deluge of capital could be enough to stave off the worst of what has otherwise been a treacherous political environment for the GOP amid stubbornly high inflation and drooping approval ratings for President Donald Trump. A flurry of Federal Election Commission filings Thursday at a key deadline detailed what candidates raised and spent from July through September and give insight into many of the outside groups backing them. More of the outside-money picture comes next week with another deadline for additional filings. If Democrats want a financial case for a blue wave, start with the candidates themselves. Democratic Senate nominees put up gaudy third-quarter totals. James Talarico raised $60.2 million in Texas, Jon Ossoff brought in $33.1 million in Georgia and Abdul El-Sayed raised $30.7 million in Michigan. Sherrod Brown brought in $23.1 million in Ohio, while Troy Jackson raised $20.4 million in Maine, Mary Peltola $14.1 million in Alaska and Roy Cooper $12.2 million in North Carolina. Even in reliably red Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton raised $9.4 million . In several of those races, the Republican numbers were not even close. Ken Paxton raised about $10.2 million in Texas, Mike Rogers $9.7 million in Michigan, Susan Collins $5.2 million in Maine and Jon Husted $4.8 million in Ohio. Candidate dollars are especially potent in the final stretch because campaigns control where they go and qualify for lower television advertising rates than super PACs do. In other words, Republicans may be able to make up a $1 fundraising gap with outside money — but it can cost them more than $1 to do it. The same fundraising edge stretches into the House. Democratic candidates outraised their Republican opponents through September in 13 of the 21 House races currently rated Toss Up by Cook, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. In North Carolina's 11th District, for example, Democrat Jamie Ager raised $2.1 million in the third quarter, compared with roughly $313,000 for Republican Jennifer Balkcom . The fundraising surge coincides with a shifting map: the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter projected last week that Democrats could gain two to six Senate seats — enough to put the four-seat majority threshold within reach — and nine to 19 House seats, which would flip the chamber. While Democratic candidates dominate direct donations, Republicans are countering with overwhelming outside spending. The Senate Leadership Fund , the GOP's main Senate super PAC, raised a record $272.9 million from July through September, roughly $122 million more than its Democratic counterpart, according to FEC filings. On the House side, the Congressional Leadership Fund raised a record $94.4 million during the quarter and entered October with $156 million in cash, according to its FEC filing. That outside money is functioning as a financial backstop for GOP candidates who trail badly in direct fundraising. Texas is the most extreme example: the SLF funneled $158 million into Texas PAC, the super PAC backing Paxton, according to FEC filings. Elsewhere, Republicans have committed $15 million through the SLF to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Outside groups account for roughly 80% of all ad buys in Alaska, where the SLF has spent $14 million backing Sen. Dan Sullivan , according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The blitz allowed Republicans to hold an aired-ad advantage in seven of eight top Senate battles and 25 of 42 contested House seats rated "Toss Up" or "Lean" Republican or Democrat by the Cook Report as of Oct. 9, according to AdImpact. But polls have shown little movement in recent weeks, despite the advantage. No donor better captures the scale — or the leverage — of that outside-money advantage than the world's richest person, Musk.

events.title: Healey backs pro-growth case for Heathrow third runway after Burnham ducks issue
events.summary: Chancellor says government will study responses to public consultation, with airports being ‘big part of jobs and growth’ John Healey has said there is a pro-growth case for going ahead with a third runway at Heathrow despite the prime minister declining to back it. Healey’s predecessor as chancellor, Rachel Reeves, put approval of the long-planned runway at the heart of her “growth speech” last year, saying it would “make Britain the world’s best-connected place to do business” . However, since arriving in No 10 in July, Andy Burnham has ducked the issue of whether the runway should go ahead, suggesting it should be “a matter for London and Londoners”. A recent Sunday Times report suggested the prime minister had told the transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, that he was “unconvinced” by arguments for the megaproject. Asked for his views in Bangkok this week, Healey said the government would study responses to a public consultation, which recently closed. He appeared to strike a markedly more positive note than Burnham, however. “I think in recent decades, and this is true in Heathrow and airports right across the UK, that they have been a big part of jobs and growth. And the case for a third runway at Heathrow has always been a case for growth,” he said. Healey has insisted economic growth is his and Burnham’s “number one mission” in government. Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, has warned that investors could reassess their backing for the £33bn infrastructure project if it does not receive the prime minister’s support. “Our shareholders would like to do this,” he said earlier this week. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that … But of course we cannot wait for ever.” The airport’s owners include Qatar’s investment authority; the French private equity firm Ardian; Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, GIC. They are expected to decide in the coming months whether to apply for formal planning permission. Healey voted in favour of the third runway when the question was put to the House of Commons in 2018. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The chancellor was in Bangkok to attend the International Monetary Fund annual meetings but has returned to London to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget. The UK was praised by the IMF this week for taking action to cut its deficit, while other large economies have opted not to do so. The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged Healey to “stay the course” in his budget. On Thursday, official figures showed the UK economy unexpectedly continued to grow in August.

events.title: Katie Zacharia out as Trump's White House press secretary
events.summary: New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job just five days after starting it, a White House official told CNBC. Zacharia, who succeeded Karoline Leavitt, faced widespread criticism over her performance and came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background. President Donald Trump said Friday afternoon that he told Zacharia, "You don't have to do this if you don't want." New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving her job after just five days in the face of criticism over her performance , a White House official confirmed to CNBC on Friday. Earlier Friday afternoon, President Donald Trump told reporters that he had just suggested to Zacharia that she quit. "I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House. "'If I were you, I'd reconsider,'" the president said he told Zacharia. The White House official, who asked not to be named in order to discuss the staffing shake-up, confirmed Fox News' report that Zacharia is "transitioning" out of the press secretary role. Zacharia's five-day tenure in the Trump administration is shorter than that of Anthony Scaramucci, who in 2017 served as White House communications director for less than 11 days. That length of time became jokingly referred to as a "Scaramucci" and was used to measure the durations of other officials who served briefly. By that metric, Zacharia lasted one-half of one Scaramucci. "Records are made to be broken. But I take no pleasure in other people's pain," Scaramucci said in an X post later Friday. Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked at Trump Media & Technology Group , had faced widespread criticism in the days since she led a short and shaky first press briefing. She also came under mounting scrutiny about her legal background. Trump spoke to reporters before heading to Georgia for a political rally as he hopes to boost Republicans' electoral chances with just 18 days until the midterms. But Trump's efforts to sell his agenda have been muddled in part by Zacharia, who ended her first, and only, press briefing on Tuesday after delivering halting remarks and taking questions from just three reporters. In the less than six minutes she spent answering questions, Zacharia revealed that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to step down. That departure, and Zacharia's, follow those of a number of other high-ranking female officials in the Trump administration who have quit or been fired in recent months. Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working "You know, she's been treated very rough. And she's a nice person," Trump said of Zacharia outside the White House. He accused the media of treating her "very badly" and said that even Fox News TV host Sean Hannity, a supporter of the administration, was "a little bit tough" on Zacharia during her appearance on his show Thursday night. Hannity, after calling Zacharia's debut briefing "widely panned," had asked about her past claims about her legal work in light of reports that she never passed a bar exam. Zacharia has defended identifying herself as a lawyer, drawing a distinction between that label and calling herself an "attorney." Hannity pointed out that Zacharia had called herself an attorney in multiple social media posts. "I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record," she replied. Trump called Zacharia "an attorney" in his Oct. 9 Truth Social post announcing her selection to replace Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in late August. Zacharia's first day was Columbus Day. White House officials had defended Zacharia earlier this week. "Up and down the White House, everyone has been thoroughly impressed with Katie in just a few short days on the job," White House communications director Steven Cheung said in an X post Wednesday. "At the end of this second term, she'll be remembered as one of the all-time greats," Cheung wrote. CNN chief White House correspondent Kaitlan Collins, however, reported Friday that Trump was "embarrassed by the coverage of Zacharia's briefing and when he polled other aides about her, Zacharia had few allies willing to stand up for her or defend her performance." "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily," Trump said of Zacharia in Friday's remarks outside the White House. "And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.'" Asked if he would keep her in the role, Trump said, "I'm going to let her make that decision."

events.title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
events.summary: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange before the closing bell in New York City on Oct 16. Wall Street tumbled on Oct 16, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend. The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise. Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data centre operator’s bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%. Broadcom fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines. Investors on Oct 16 were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries. “There is some fear in the market,” said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at US Bank Wealth Management in ​Seattle. “High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk.” Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors are weighing a lower valuation for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points. The Nasdaq declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points. Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services, down 2.52%, followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology. The S&P 500 was set for its steepest weekly loss since January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June. Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla, Meta Platforms and Procter & Gamble. Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data. While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index’s median component has climbed only about 6%, year to date. About 185 S&P 500 stocks have lost ground in 2026. Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures were extending beyond energy commodities. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Oct 16 voiced optimism about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been “hanging in there” during a lingering energy shock and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation. Markets increasingly expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged in October. Barclays now expects 25-basis-point hikes each in December and January. Tesla dropped 2.5% after the electric-vehicle maker unveiled a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX. Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer on Oct 15. Its shares were down 2.9%. Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.3-to-one ratio. The S&P 500 posted 19 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 49 new highs and 263 new lows. REUTERS

events.title: Replit is no longer working with Anthropic, CEO says
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt . Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer with Anthropic. “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” Replit sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser. Under its partnership with Anthropic, Replit used the AI lab’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly. Masad’s comments were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place. There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was using Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities. TechCrunch reached back out to Replit for clarification and will update this story if we hear back. Masad shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was updated to article to include more context on Replit using Anthropic’s models. events.title: Canberra businesses battling 'multi-agency maze' to stay open, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Businesses affected by Civic construction received 'insufficient' financial relief, committee report finds Ongoing construction in Canberra's city centre has seen a reduction in turnover for businesses in the area. ( ABC News: Lily Nothling ) An ACT Legislative Assembly committee investigating the city's night life has accepted reports that "insufficient" relief has been given to businesses affected by light rail and car park construction. The country's peak hospitality advocacy body has welcomed the committee's 28 recommendations to improve the ACT's night-time economy. The recommendations include establishing an ACT Night-Time Economy Commissioner and offering "stronger temporary relief" for affected businesses. The ACT government should consider stronger relief for businesses affected by construction work and establish a dedicated night-time economy commissioner, a review of Canberra's night life has found. Restaurants and other businesses would be forced to shut their doors without more action to address car park access and construction disruptions, according to findings from the ACT Legislative Assembly committee tasked with investigating the city's night-time economy. Chris Gatfield of the Australian Hotels Association has welcomed the committee's recommendations, but says he doubts they will all be delivered. ( Supplied: Chris Gatfield ) The committee's report, made public on Friday, made 28 recommendations to improve what the Australian Hotels Association (AHA) said was "a little bit of a struggle" for the industry. "The general economic climate is really, really tough for the hospitality industry," AHA ACT branch general manager Chris Gatfield said. "That's not necessarily just related to the various infrastructure projects that are going on in the city. But the committee accepted that there had been "insufficient" relief for businesses affected by light rail and car park constructions. It recommended the ACT government "consider offering stronger temporary relief measures for businesses adversely affected by ongoing disruptions associated with major infrastructure works in the city, such as means-tested rent relief". Charcoal Restaurant owner Anna Gray says financial assistance is the only way to ensure her business survives the construction works. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) Anna Gray, the owner of Charcoal Restaurant in the Melbourne building in Civic, said her turnover had reduced by 50 per cent since parts of London Circuit closed in 2024. "Customers don't want to come because there's no parking," she said. Mr Gatfield said businesses need cash flow, but he doubted they would get it. "This will be a decision for government and so far I'm not convinced that they would be in a position to offer that kind of financial support," he said. "You really want the people who are suffering right now to be there to reap the benefits when construction is finished and people return to the city." The committee also found businesses were battling a "multi-agency maze" of red tape to stay open. Josh Dotta, the owner of Fiction nightclub (pictured), told the committee he routinely had to interact with 10 seperate government agencies. ( Facbook: Fiction Club ) Fiction Nightclub operator Josh Dotta gave evidence that he routinely interacted with 10 separate government agencies, while other stakeholders criticised the "silos" and "disconnected sections of government". "Anyone who's ever dealt with a government agency would recognise that sometimes it's very hard to get the person that you actually need to talk to on the phone," Mr Gatfield said. Although the ACT has a dedicated minister for the night-time economy, the committee said a night-time economy commissioner would support that role. The commissioner would consult the industry before major decisions, establish progress metrics, develop a more streamlined red-tape system, support culturally and linguistically diverse workers and take advice from a dedicated advisory group, the recommendations said. "We think it has legs in Canberra and if it works in other places there's absolutely no reason why it wouldn't work here too," Mr Gatfield said. Late-night venues such as Squeaky Clean, pictured during a performance by Citizen Kay, pay significantly more for a liquor licence than similar NSW venues. events.title: Coral overharvesting on Great Barrier Reef investigated by Fisheries Qld
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Aquarium industry investigated for overharvesting of coral on Great Barrier Reef Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it has investigated the overharvesting of coral in the Great Barrier Reef. Coral harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually. Fisheries Queensland does not intend to release the findings from the investigation. Fisheries Queensland has confirmed it recently investigated an overharvesting of coral on the World Heritage-listed Great Barrier Reef, but has declined to share the outcome. In the 2025-2026 fishing season the harvest of Pocillopora grandis , known as antler coral, was overfished by 30 per cent according to FishNet data. Coral harvesting is the process of collecting coral from the ocean. Harvesters are permitted to take up to 190 tonnes from the reef annually, with much of this destined for the global aquarium trade. Bright colours and interesting shapes are highly prized by 'reefers', who drive demand. But coral catch quotas have been breached several times in recent years, while some operators have been charged with fishing offences. There are quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) The ABC understands an internal investigation has now been completed into this year's exceeded quota. When questioned by the ABC, Fisheries Queensland would not send through the information about the investigations findings. Coral reef ecologist Dr Morgan Pratchett said while this particular species is not under threat, any overharvesting event is of concern. "It sends a bad message given the overwhelming international scrutiny on how this industry is being managed," Dr Pratchett said. Dr Morgan Pratchett is a reef ecologist. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) There are two quotas within the coral harvesting fishery on the Great Barrier Reef, known as individual transferrable quotes (ITC) and prescribed commercial catch (PCC) quotas. Individual quotas are where fishers are given a set amount to fish individually. Breaking these quotas can result in prosecution. PCC quotas, or competitive quotas, are where an amount is set and fishers essentially race to harvest until the quota is exhausted. Harvested coral in tanks for shipping overseas. ( ABC News: Brendan Esposito ) According to Fisheries Queensland, this can sometimes result in going over the competitive quota for a coral species, which they say is not "uncommon or unreasonable." A 2024 assessment of the Queensland coral fishery noted that despite efforts to control overharvesting, some species continue to have their catch limits exceeded. It said fisheries would consider "trip limits, increased notifications, and more individual quotas if this issue continues." Do you know more? Email angelaheathcote@protonmail.com or contact her on signal: @angeh.36 At present, several Australian coral species are banned from being imported into the EU due to sustainability concerns. Simon Miller, from the Australian Marine Conservation Society, said he was concerned catch limits are not set at the right levels. "So when you see fishers in a race to fish to go out there where they're competing against each other to catch these corals as quickly as possible, and seeing this overrun of quotas, that's really concerning," Mr Miller said. "They're meant to be some kind of precautionary catch limit yet we keep seeing them overshoot year after year." Simon Miller from the Australian Marine Conservation Society. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) The coral harvesting industry has faced ongoing compliance issues. One recent case of alleged illegal coral harvesting being pursued by the Queensland Director of Public Prosecutions involved coral collector Jardini. The case included Jardini's director Jason Coe, who currently holds five licences in the Queensland coral fishery. Coe has not yet entered a plea. Earlier in 2024, Monsoon Aquatics lead diver and skipper Tim Green was prosecuted by Western Australia Police for offences related to the collection and recording of coral and fish while harvesting on behalf of Monsoon within the Western Australian coral fishery. He was found guilty and fined almost a quarter of a million dollars. Tim Green was found guilty of offences related to the collection of coral in 2024. ( Image: Facebook ) ASIC documents show Tim Green continues to be a shareholder at Monsoon.

events.title: Why the new RTS won’t make me visit JB more often
events.summary: Journalist Rosalind Ang at a craft workshop with her husband in Johor Bahru in 2025. SINGAPORE – When I think of Johor Bahru, I think of yummy food, medicine and beauty services – all at one-third of what they would cost in Singapore. The time spent travelling to get these deals is set to decrease with the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link that is slated to begin operations in February 2027. The cross-border rail service will carry up to 10,000 passengers an hour in each direction, with a journey time of just five minutes. With this, it would seem that I’d be able to go to JB more often. But I don’t plan on doing so. I used to go there once a month with my husband, who loves JB. For what we would pay in Singapore, we can visit more upscale restaurants and enjoy a wider variety of dishes that are harder to find in Singapore, such as herbal bak kut teh and lok lok – with the lok lok in Mount Austin being my favourite. Venues in JB also tend to be a lot less crowded, as there’s just more space. I can easily book a badminton court or a karaoke room with free-flow food and drinks. Securing the same facilities in Singapore is far more competitive, often requiring a ballot just to get a badminton court. As I manage my chronic sinusitis with long-term medication, which is far more affordable in Malaysia, my husband and I regularly pick up supplies for ourselves and his family whenever we visit JB. I’ve also been able to attend a variety of craft workshops in JB that would typically be far too expensive to try here. But cost savings aren’t always my only concern. I once went for a perm in JB. While it cost only $200, the curls lasted a grand total of one week – and I was left with damaged hair. In comparison, the same perm in Singapore usually costs me a whopping $500, but my hair is undamaged and the results stay intact for at least half a year. My visits to JB usually take up an entire weekend, so I can’t schedule anything else over those two days. During our most recent trip, my husband and I headed over on a Saturday morning and returned on Sunday afternoon. By the time we got home, there was barely any time left before dinner, ruling out any possibility of scheduling other plans. Even our cat ended up with a late tuna dinner that night. For all its cost savings and fun, trips to JB failed to give me what I valued most: time. There are many things I want to do every weekend. As a broke university student, I loved heading to JB to have a good time on a budget. As a working adult with a steady income, however, I’ve realised that chasing the cheapest deal usually means giving up something that’s not money. When I spend time in JB, I give up spending time with my family, my friends and my cat. Because I’m busy on weekdays, weekends are the only time I have to catch up with the people I love. Choosing to go to JB on the weekend means I won’t be able to go for my regular barre session with my friends. I also can’t eat lunch with them afterwards or have dinner with my parents. And catching up on sleep is out of the question. Even with the new RTS, it will still take a couple of hours just to travel to the Singapore terminus station in Woodlands North, take the train and book a private-hire vehicle out of Bukit Chagar. That doesn’t even include the time needed to reach your actual destinations in the city. As a time-starved Singaporean, it has become important for me to prioritise what matters most – scoring a cheaper manicure is simply not as important as time I could spend with family and friends. A couple of years ago, a lorry collided with the side of my dad’s taxi. Luckily, he survived with a few fractures, but it left him with a permanent leg injury. It made me realise that time with him is finite. The cost of living has risen significantly in recent years, making it natural to try and get the best bang for our buck. But while money can always be earned back, lost time with our loved ones is gone forever. In my pursuit of financial security and the next great money-saving hack, I hope I never lose sight of what makes life truly meaningful. And maybe I’ll finally get enough sleep, too.

events.title: OpenAI models hacked a crypto wallet and breached more websites
events.summary: OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Trump says White House didn't order Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump denied that the White House had ordered restrictions on SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet services in Ukraine this week. Ukrainian officials complained on Tuesday and Wednesday that SpaceX had limited internet connectivity via Starshield without advance notice. Musk said any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine would have come from decisions by the president or White House. President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield , a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test Blue Origin plans $330 million Florida expansion to ramp New Glenn launches SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday , citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order. On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far." Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. events.title: Iran-backed militias sending money back to cash-starved IRGC, U.S. says
events.summary: Iran-backed militias in the region have been sending money back to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to relieve the economic pressure it's under after nine months of war , U.S. CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said Friday. Why it matters: While the U.S. military has been preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran, the Trump administration continues to put immense pressure on the regime with its naval blockade and severe sanctions. U.S. officials say the economic chokehold is causing serious difficulties for Iran and its security forces, while making the regime frustrated and aggressive. The White House hopes the pressure will induce Iran to make a deal that includes nuclear concessions. But so far, that hasn't happened. Driving the news: Cooper said the naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in lost oil revenue. Additionally, CENTCOM and the Treasury Department have managed in recent weeks to freeze $350 million that Iran had in cryptocurrency. Behind the scenes: In a video message released Friday, Cooper revealed that Iran-backed groups such as Hezbollah, Hamas and Shia militias in Iraq — which have been funded by the IRGC for years — now have to give the money back. "The financial strain on Iran's military has become so significant that there are reports about Iran-aligned militia groups across the region withholding payments for their soldiers in order to funnel money back to the IRGC, which also isn't paying its troops," he said. Cooper said the Iranian government is withholding salaries, pensions and benefits from public sector workers, including the internal security forces and the IRGC. State of play: Cooper attributed the significant increase in Iranian attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz to "desperation" within the IRGC. Despite those attacks, he said that the Strait of Hormuz is still open — with 400 ships and 100 million barrels of oil moving through it over the last week. Yes, but: In recent weeks, CENTCOM has almost completely stopped conducting strikes against Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers in the area of the strait. The pause in strikes, which was ordered by the White House to avoid escalating the war ahead of the midterm elections, made Iran more confident about launching attacks, a U.S. official said. Consequently, CENTCOM is concerned that the increase in ship attacks will cause shipping companies to think twice about transiting the strait — resulting in less oil coming out and a spike in oil prices. U.S. officials say Iran is also attacking more ships to try to raise oil prices and ratchet up pressure on Trump ahead of the midterms. What to watch: The White House and Qatari mediators are still waiting to hear back from Iran about a U.S. counterproposal to end the war. "It's still in internal deliberations in Tehran," a U.S. official said. Regional mediators told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in recent days that Iran shouldn't wait until after the midterms to give its response, a regional source with direct knowledge said. The regional mediators told Iran there's no guarantee that Trump will be more conciliatory after the midterms — on the contrary, he might be more aggressive.

events.title: Thune enjoys surprisingly clear path back to GOP leader despite Trump's attacks
events.summary: The News John Thune took criticism from President Donald Trump, agitated online conservatives, and occasionally frustrated some of his own members this year. Yet his next leadership election is looking smooth compared with the past couple of bouts to lead the Senate GOP. In fact, Thune may actually run unopposed this year, regardless of how the midterms go. “I’m not aware of anyone who wants the job. I certainly don’t,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., told Semafor. “I don’t envy the leader’s task.” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who challenged Thune in 2024 and Mitch McConnell in 2022, told Semafor there’s “no wiggle room; I am not running for leader” this cycle. He said Thune is “probably the only person that’s going to run. But I always want to say if other people run and someone comes up with better ideas, you’ve got to listen to them. But I’m not running.” Know More The biggest headache for Thune was the Save America Act, a voter ID bill that lacked a strategy to become law in the Senate. Trump repeatedly leaned on Thune to kill the filibuster in order to pass it, and other senators wanted Thune to try to force Democrats to pull off a talking filibuster to block the bill. Eventually, though, the effort and outrage over its stalled status faded away. With Democrats favored to win the House and potentially even take the Senate, the fight over killing the filibuster is back on ice. That’s all good news for Thune, who says he’ll likely run for another term regardless of whether Republicans lose the Senate. If no one challenges him, it would be the first unanimous GOP leadership election since 2020. Notably, Johnson had backed Scott in previous leadership races. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told reporters on Thursday that Thune “will get elected pretty resoundingly.” “Do I think he’s got broad support? Yes. I don’t think there’s an insurgent movement that’s against him,” Moreno said. “There’s not a single Republican running nationally that’s saying, ‘Hey, if you elect me, I’ll vote against John Thune as leader.’” Several Democratic candidates say they won’t support Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for another term as leader of their caucus. But no one is indicating they are looking to challenge Schumer, either, which means those could just be protest votes. Former Democratic leader Harry Reid received a handful of “no” votes in his leadership race after losing control of the Senate in 2014. Republicans will have their leadership election on Nov. 10; Senate Democrats are likely to have theirs in early December, although the date isn’t set yet. The midterm results remain an X factor for both Thune and Schumer’s futures. Notable Thune told us in June he’d probably run again. Scott said in September he wasn’t committed to supporting Thune.

events.title: FAA equity talks raise questions about the agency's legal authority
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration’s pursuit of an equity stake in a private company that uses AI to manage air traffic is raising questions about whether it has clear legal authority to strike such a deal. The Trump administration has negotiated stakes in dozens of other companies, but none through the FAA. The agency’s interest in owning part of Air Space Intelligence, first reported by Politico , is too “premature” for there to be specifics, a person familiar with the matter told Semafor. Talks so far have been limited to a handful of internal conversations, the person added. One possible statutory underpinning for a deal: Existing law authorizes Transportation Department financial help for state or local governments to “acquire an interest” in some public transportation companies. That argument, like other agencies’ , would be a stretch. “It’s further proof that the administration doesn’t have a ‘plan’ or ‘strategy,’” said Tad DeHaven, who tracks the stakes for the Cato Institute . — Eleanor Mueller and Shelby Talcott

events.title: Copper thefts leave Perth roads in darkness and cost taxpayers millions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This section of Tonkin Highway en route to Ellenbrook has been without working street lighting for years. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) Major roads and paths across Perth remain dark because widespread copper theft has left street lighting out. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, and police are increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget to replace stolen street lighting cable and upgrade security. More than 100 kilometres of major roads and paths across Perth remain unlit, some for years, because of widespread copper theft. This week, police charged three people with stealing copper wire, which is lucrative on the black market. Police said they arrested and charged a 31-year-old man who allegedly stole more than 190 metres of telecommunication cable from Gidgegannup, before selling the recovered copper to a scrap metal recycler. That theft allegedly occurred over the King's Birthday long weekend in September from a Telstra site, where about 500 kilograms of copper was pulled out of the ground. Roads across Perth's metro area are in darkness at night due to the theft. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "This had a significant impact on the Gidgegannup and surrounding areas," Mundaring sergeant Tony Signal told 102.5 ABC Perth. Sergeant Signal said police were increasingly scrutinising scrap metal recyclers. "They're obliged by law to record any second-hand dealing of copper at the moment and we find that that's slipping through the cracks," he said. Col Blanch says organised crime groups would find illegal ways to get away with breaking the rules. ( ABC News: Kenith Png ) Police Commissioner Col Blanch previously told the ABC organised crime sought to circumvent those rules when offloading stolen metal. "We know that some scrap metal dealers are doing the wrong thing and doing a lot of business under the table … that's what [the] police's job is to stamp out," he said. "However, when they can't sell it to a second-hand dealer, scrap dealer here, they will put it in a container and they will send large amounts of scrap metal overseas." It's far from an isolated incident involving telecommunications infrastructure , with detectives charging a man with stealing around 50 metres of copper cabling from an exchange site in Wattleup last month. A Telstra spokesperson said copper theft widely impacted service companies and that the telco's copper theft prevention team works closely with police agencies across Australia. Streetlights don't work when the underground copper wiring is removed. ( ABC News: Samantha Goerling ) "We encourage anyone seeing any suspicious activity near our facilities to contact police immediately," the spokesperson said. Street lighting also continues to be targeted, with police arresting a 41-year-old man and a 50-year-old woman this week, after a member of the public reported suspicious activity along Tonkin Highway in Ellenbrook. Police stopped a vehicle in the vicinity a short time later and allege they found a significant amount of stolen insulated copper wiring. Copper thieves taking exceptional risks Demolition sites are being stripped for copper at an escalating rate, according to a Perth demolition contractor, risking electrocution and asbestos exposure to sell the scrap metal on the black market. Main Roads WA said as of October 2, more than 1,400km of cable had been stolen from its network, taking more than 100km of street lighting and nearly 30km of pedestrian/cycle paths lighting offline. "Since cable theft became a widespread issue, Main Roads have replaced 480km of copper roadway and PSP lighting cable as well as re-cabling and re-energising over 500 individual poles," a spokesperson said. "Currently, Kwinana Freeway, Tonkin Highway and Reid Highway are the three priority routes that Main Roads is focusing on for cable replacement and anti-theft treatments. "Works are also planned in key locations along Forrest Highway, Great Northern Highway, Mitchell Freeway, Roe Highway, Albany Highway, Ennis Avenue, Mandurah Road and Armadale Road." The WA government has allocated nearly $12 million in the 2026-27 state budget for street lighting cable theft replacement and security upgrades but still faces an uphill battle. Main Roads director of metropolitan operations James Pinnington said he expected the program to take several years.

events.title: Tariffs pose a risk to US-India relationship
events.summary: President Donald Trump faces a deadline Sunday to decide whether to impose certain penalties on other countries under a bipartisan sanctions law he signed last month. Any move by him to waive sanctions on Russian individuals or entities will be met with criticism, as would a decision not to impose tariffs on China for buying Russian gas. But Washington is hoping he’ll spare at least one country: India. “Both the United States and India should not buy Russian oil and gas, but I don’t think simply imposing big tariffs on India is the way to get them to” reduce their purchases, said Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security. Punishing India for its reliance on Russian energy “would deal a body blow to the US-India relationship,” argued Sadanand Dhume, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations. The US and India are currently locked in trade negotiations, which more tariffs would surely disrupt. Fontaine said it is “100%” possible that the Trump administration uses the sanctions law to pressure India to give in to its demands in those discussions. Trump had previously hiked tariffs on India over its Russian energy purchases, but later removed them as trade talks progressed. Asked whether Trump had made a decision on which sanctions, if any, to impose at the deadline, a White House official said that he “signed the act and the administration will comply with the act’s requirements.” The bill gives the president broad power to waive penalties if he deems it in the US interest. — Morgan Chalfant
