events.title: Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA Expand Strategic Partnership to Advance Safe Highly Automated Driving in the Next Decade
events.summary: Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA will extend their partnership to jointly develop the next generation of driver assistance and automated driving systems. The collaboration combines Mercedes-Benz automotive engineering and MB.OS with the NVIDIA Hyperion compute and sensor architecture, Alpamayo Stack software and Halos safety system to accelerate the development of automated vehicles. Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA today announced that they will extend their strategic partnership to advance the next generation of automated driving systems. The collaboration brings together Mercedes-Benz’s automotive engineering and safety expertise and its MB.OS operating system with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI technologies. “NVIDIA is our most important strategic partner in automated driving. Together, we developed the first Mercedes-Benz assistance system for urban point-to-point driving for the western world,” Jörg Burzer, member of the board of management of Mercedes‑Benz Group AG and chief technology officer, development and procurement. “The expansion of our partnership marks a significant milestone and reflects the mutual trust we have built over the years. Together, we aim to bring further pioneering innovations to the road, offering our customers the best automated driving experience while upholding the high safety standards they expect from a Mercedes-Benz.” “Accelerated computing is giving vehicles the intelligence to understand the world and reason through complex driving situations,” said Ali Kani, vice president of automotive at NVIDIA. “Mercedes-Benz brings the engineering excellence and commitment to safety this transformation demands. Together, we’re building on NVIDIA Hyperion to bring that intelligence and full-stack safety to the road and make autonomous driving an everyday reality.” Mercedes-Benz’s MB.OS operating system supports new driving functions and over-the-air updates, working with NVIDIA Hyperion’s in-vehicle computing and sensor architecture. NVIDIA Alpamayo Stack provides full-stack driving software with AI reasoning capabilities, supporting point-to-point urban assistance, active safety and automated parking. NVIDIA Halos adds to the Mercedes-Benz safety foundation, including a parallel safety stack that adds redundancy and guardrails. Together, these technologies support advanced driver assistance and the development of future SAE-Level 4 applications, including robolimousines. Beyond automated driving, Mercedes-Benz also relies on NVIDIA technologies for vehicle engineering simulation and within MO360, its digital production ecosystem — from virtual planning to AI-based applications. The two partners are working to further enhance efficiency, flexibility and quality across the global production network. About NVIDIA NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is the world leader in AI and accelerated computing. Mercedes‑Benz AG at a Glance Mercedes‑Benz AG is part of the Mercedes‑Benz Group AG with a total of around 164,000 employees worldwide and is responsible for the global business of Mercedes‑Benz Cars and Mercedes‑Benz Vans. Ola Källenius is Chairman of the Board of Management of Mercedes‑Benz AG. The company focuses on the development, production and sales of passenger cars, vans and vehicle-related services. Furthermore, the company aspires to be the leader in the fields of electric mobility and vehicle software. The brand portfolio of Mercedes‑Benz Cars includes the Mercedes‑Benz brand, as well as Mercedes‑AMG, Mercedes‑Maybach, and the G‑Class product brand. events.title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
events.summary: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair.  Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. It also degrades privacy and security for everyone by forcing people to submit sensitive personal information to prove their age. In our work , we’ve found that parents and kids both want smarter, more nuanced policies that protect children, families, and their rights. That can take the form of mandating stronger limits on data collection by companies, or giving families flexible tools to control content and access on their own terms.  Age gates won’t bring about the desired change, nor will they simplify parenting in the digital world. At best, they will only raise thornier questions and postpone the conversation to a child’s 16th birthday. At worst, they’ll leave kids with no guidance as they make their way through the online world. A less safe internet for kids When young people circumvent restrictions, they are often doing what we want developing minds to do and what we celebrate in other contexts: lean into curiosity, problem-solve, and exercise independence. It’s important for kids to do this online, an arena where they often develop social skills and refine their identities . Bans sweep these motivations under the rug, taking a paternalistic approach that doesn’t consider young people’s needs or the realities of what they do online.  It also ignores what some parents want. When we examined social media safety interventions last year, parents told us that they often join their kids in lies that help them gain access to needed but gated services. This isn’t a new phenomenon; research all the way back in 2011 showed that parents taught their children how to evade Facebook age restrictions. Some may say these parents are oblivious to the harms posed by the web or just don’t care. But parents are not a monolithic group. Many simply see offering their children responsible access to social media as a way to help them connect with like-minded peers, find informational content, and learn digital safety skills early on. Many parents believe the benefits outweigh the risks.  When parents don’t help provide access and kids are not able to get into the platforms they desire, they will likely move toward alternative online spaces, often ones with fewer guardrails. Sometimes kids wind up on fairly innocuous, if unconventional , platforms, communicating with each other in Google Docs or podcast comment sections . Other times they move to more dangerous platforms that can leave them vulnerable to abuse and predation. In the aftermath of the Australian social media ban, preliminary research shows that kids’ screen time has not meaningfully decreased but has sometimes been redirected, with some young users going to spaces that are unmonitored and unknown to parents. Just as cities are sketchiest when they are not bustling, the most risky platforms for young people are those with the fewest eyes on the digital street . Outdated, dying, and under-resourced platforms tend to attract both vulnerable youth and those who prey on them. A less safe internet for all Age gates come with dangers of their own. Some platforms automatically track users’ online activities to confirm their age. In doing so, they profile users—collecting and analyzing their data to make inferences about them, which can increase the risk that data will be misused or leaked.  Companies may also ask for personal documents like driver’s licenses to verify age, which can lead to mishandling of sensitive documents or even identity theft. Data breaches happen: Last year, for example, Discord reported that one of its third-party services, 5CA, which is used to confirm age, had been compromised, exposing at least 70,000 images of users’ government IDs. It can take little effort to find ways to use that kind of information for malicious purposes by, say, connecting driver’s licenses to specific accounts and private online activity, which could reveal anything from users’ political opinions to their sexual preferences.  Efforts to make it harder for kids to get around age gates have also led policymakers to clamp down on kids’ access to VPNs. State age verification bills in Michigan and Utah have tried to interfere with the privacy protections offered by these tools (the Utah bill is now blocked by a federal court ), and Australia’s eSafety Commissioner is nudging social media platforms to detect and block their use. But requiring adult users to prove their age to gain access to a VPN fundamentally defeats the purpose of that privacy-focused technology. It can put many users, particularly journalists and human rights defenders working on sensitive issues, in danger of government surveillance and even retaliation. What could work instead? Rather than attempting to block young people from online services that allow them to access information and engage in age-essential communication, policymakers should focus on the incentives that drive companies to engage in behavior that creates risks for kids in the first place.  For example, platforms should decrease what experts call unhealthy engagement or addictive activity by limiting the collection and use of data that companies use to target content and features to all users, including children. Nearly all parents and teens we spoke with want policymakers to impose such restrictions, knowing full well that the companies’ use of data is at the core of features such as targeted advertisements. events.title: Buyer still wanted for Spirit of Tasmania ferries
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Spirit of Tasmania I and II sale details unclear days before final Bass Strait voyages The Spirit of Tasmania I is set to sail its final journey between Devonport and Geelong at the end of next week. ( ABC News: Morgan Timms ) There are questions over where the Spirit of Tasmania I and II will be moored, and at what cost, after they are replaced. The Tasmanian government says talks to sell the vessels are "progressing well", but the state opposition has doubts. The ferries will be replaced by the new Spirit IV and V by the end of this month. Just one week out from their final voyage between Devonport and Geelong, it is still not known what exactly will be happening to the two current Spirit of Tasmania vessels. TT-Line, the state-owned company which runs the ferries, has said a sale process is underway for Spirit I and II, which were launched nearly 25 years ago. But it would not say where the ferries would be moored, and what this would cost if they were not sold by the time Spirit IV and V began operating. One of the newer, larger Spirit of Tasmania ships passes one of the old fleet in Devonport earlier this year. ( Supplied: TT-Line ) The two new ferries have been moored in Geelong, and the Tasmanian government has expressed confidence in a deal being secured to sell the soon-to-be decommissioned ships soon. Earlier this year, a parliamentary inquiry heard the total cost of the new ferries was more than $700 million above forecast , which did not include the cost of berthing them in Scotland and Victoria while a new Devonport deeper water berth was constructed. 'No berths' in Tasmania for old ships TT-Line chief executive Chris Carbone confirmed Spirit I and II would stop sailing from October 24 and said a sale process has been underway for some time, with "interest in the ships". He ruled out the vessels being moored in the state. "Depending on when the ships are sold will determine where they are stored — there are no berths in Tasmania," Mr Carbone said. Chris Carbone says there is "interest in the ships". ( ABC News ) Labor infrastructure spokesperson Anita Dow expressed doubt that a sale was progressing. "They've said they've got interest from buyers in acquiring those old vessels, but they've gone quiet for some time now about whether there's actually been a successful follow-through," she said. "The government should be providing regular updates to the community about this process, about what these plans are for the old ships. Anita Dow is questioning why the Tasmanian government has "gone quiet" on the sale of the current ferries. ( ABC News ) During a public accounts committee earlier this year, TT-Line said the cost of mooring the new ships ranged from $600,000 a month in Scotland to $900,000 a month in Geelong, but the company did not provide the total cost incurred. The same committee heard the company was expected to remain in debt until 2052. "Every month that they're being stored [is] a cost endured by the company that's going to eventually eat into the price that's paid for these vessels into the future," Ms Dow said. Minister declines to answer 'hypotheticals' When asked where Spirit I and II would be docked when Spirit IV and V came into service at the end of the month, government minister Jo Palmer declined to answer. "I'm not going to be getting into hypotheticals," Ms Palmer said. "As I say, the process is underway. There's been a great response to that, and we look forward to making that announcement when that process has gone through." Kerry Vincent says the state government is "confident" the current ferries will be sold soon. ( ABC News: Jake Grant ) The state's infrastructure and transport minister, Kerry Vincent, said the sale talks were going well. "The Tasmanian government is confident TT-Line will secure a deal to sell Spirits I and II as soon as possible," Mr Vincent said. "TT-Line are working hard with their brokers and negotiations are progressing well. [They] have discussed the sale process and provided updates." The minister said due to negotiations being underway, he would not comment further.

events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Manufacturing and process technology GlobalFoundries will operate two new fabs in Malta, New York , under a U.S.-Japan initiative involving up to $21B in investment. The first fab is expected to come online in 2029. GF also unveiled an FD-SOI roadmap for physical AI. Applied Materials unveiled its $5B EPIC Center , a 600,000-s.f. semiconductor process and equipment R&D facility in Silicon Valley. Infineon and Wolfspeed inked a new multi-year supply agreement for 200mm SiC wafers . Nikon introduced a new lithography system for advanced packaging, offering 1.5 µm line-and-space resolution and 40% higher throughput than its predecessor, at 72 panels per hour. The maskless system supports large substrates and RDL patterning, with availability planned for April 2027. Packaging and test FormFactor and Teradyne will co-develop semiconductor test technologies for HBM, advanced packaging, silicon photonics, and HPC. Teradyne also agreed to invest $300M in FormFactor. Teradyne also introduced a semiconductor test platform for edge-AI chips. ASE expanded its PowerSiP platform with a vertically integrated 3D packaging solution that places voltage regulation closer to AI processors, reducing parasitic routing losses by 50% or more to improve power efficiency in data centers and HPC systems. China narrows the gap CXMT reportedly plans to introduce a DDR5 server RDIMM using 4F² DRAM cells by year-end, potentially improving density and manufacturing costs. The development could help narrow China’s memory gap, although CXMT has not disclosed production yields, manufacturing volumes or evidence of cost competitiveness. China-based Langdao Silex unveiled a prototype EUV light source with 90% localized components, reports SCMP. TrendForce says the source exceeds 15W output but remains far below commercial EUV power levels, with mass production still estimated to be three to five years away. Nvidia ’s AI-accelerator shipments in China fell 44% year over year in the first half of 2026, leaving it with 34% of the data-center AI-accelerator market by units shipped, compared with Huawei’s 28%, according to IDC data reported by Reuters. Around the Valley This week’s SEMICON West conference: Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi said in a keynote address that autonomous chip design can already take some customer specifications to verified RTL, while physical implementation, verification and final sign-off still require human involvement. Nvidia expanded its AI tools for semiconductor manufacturing , including the new cuPotential CUDA-X library for atomic-scale simulation. Lam Research plans to integrate Nvidia NanoVDB into SEMulator3D, which is expected to speed select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x. Siemens and Nvidia integrated cuLitho with Calibre to speed computational lithography , saying it’s up to 12x faster for full-chip OPC workloads. It supports High-NA EUV and curvilinear inverse lithography. Fig. 1: Synopsys President/CEO Sassine Ghazi and Semiconductor Engineering’s Ed Sperling at SEMICON West this week. Source: G. Haley/Semiconductor Engineering The OCP Global Summit was also held this week in San Jose. Find all the highlights in our New Technologies section below. Earnings season heating up TSMC reported Q3 revenue of roughly US$46.7B , up 41.2% year over year in U.S. dollar terms, with 2nm accounting for 8% of wafer revenue. CEO C.C. Wei said the company has seen “no sign of slowdown” in AI demand. But rising prices and macroeconomic uncertainty are weighing on consumer and other price-sensitive markets, prompting more cautious planning for 2027. TSMC also said it has discussed participating in Musk’s Terafab, but any fab collaboration would need to be operated by TSMC. ASML reported record Q3 sales of €11.7B, up about 55% from a year earlier, and said planned supply for the next two years will not fully meet customer demand. The company is evaluating additional capacity beyond its previously planned expansion. Market and investment More than $8.5B in Q3 chip industry startup funding was tracked across 80 companies, with AI inference, memory alternatives, photonics, networking, and other data-movement technologies drawing some of the quarter’s biggest rounds. SEMI projects global 300mm front-end fab equipment spending will rise 31% to $149B in 2026 and reach $227B by 2029, driven by AI, HPC, and leading-edge semiconductor demand. Equipment investment in the Americas is expected to more than double from $18.1B in 2026 to $40.6B in 2029. Fig. 2: SEMI 300mm Fab Outlook, Q326 update. Big hauls Salience Labs raised $125M to accelerate deployment of its optical circuit switching technology for AI infrastructure. Mueon raised $65M to scale up its stackable, modular 3D platform that integrates compute, memory, interconnect, power delivery, and thermal management. events.title: UBS exploring options abroad in case Swiss rules prove intolerable, sources say
events.summary: Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse. UBS is weighing overseas options, including moving its headquarters or merging, if Swiss banking rules become too strict after the Credit Suisse collapse. The bank is studying possible US bank purchases and even a takeover of UBS, but sources say there are no active talks. Swiss plans could force UBS to hold up to 100% CET1 capital for foreign units, which UBS says would trap more than US$20 billion and hurt competitiveness. ZURICH – UBS is working on possible scenarios including shifting its headquarters, or a merger with another bank , if Switzerland introduces new banking rules it deems excessively strict, according to three sources familiar with the matter. Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse , and a Lower House committee will later in October begin debating rules passed in September by the Upper House that UBS hinted were intolerable. A group inside the bank is considering the various options, which include drawing up a list of smaller banks in the United States that UBS could potentially buy, and the prospect of the bank being taken over itself, according to the sources. There are no active talks under way, the sources said. UBS, which is closely following how events play out in Parliament, said: “We don’t comment on speculation or views expressed on such matters.” The British government and UBS discussed in 2026 the possibility of a move to London if the bank were to redomicile, the Financial Times said on Oct 16. The city emerged as one of the best options in the bank’s 2025 contingency planning, a source told Reuters at the time. In March, UBS obtained a US banking licence and is eager to expand its business in the United States. But the rules drafted by the Swiss government are partly designed to reduce the risk taxpayers could face if the bank suffered losses in the United States. Sources familiar with the bank’s thinking say US investment bank Morgan Stanley would be the best theoretical match for UBS. The Swiss bank has repeatedly stated that it is not planning to move and sees great value in its Swiss base. There are notable ties between the leadership of the two banks, as UBS chairman Colm Kelleher spent many years at Morgan Stanley, eventually rising to one of the top jobs there. Kelleher said in September that UBS might need to consider its future in Switzerland if the incoming rules were too harsh. Under its overhaul, the Swiss government wants ⁠UBS to back its foreign units with 100% Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital, which could tie up in excess of US$20 billion (S$25.6 billion). UBS views this as excessive and harmful to its international competitiveness. The Upper House in September trimmed that requirement to 90% CET1 capital, but UBS also regards that as excessively high. At present, the bank needs to 60% capitalise its foreign units, but that can be partly met with cheaper capital. Since 2025, speculation has swirled around the possibility that UBS could move its base abroad to avoid the tougher regulation, and sources familiar with the bank’s thinking say it has a duty to shareholders to consider all options. Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who has led the charge to introduce tougher banking rules, said in September she felt it was unlikely that UBS would leave its homeland, arguing this would be costly and legally complicated. events.title: Warsh boosts market expectations of Fed rate hold in October
events.summary: At the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok, US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh reiterated that the Fed will deliver price stability. Warsh did not signal any policy change, which lifted bets that the Fed will hold rates at its Oct 27-28 meeting. Market odds of a hike fell from about 27% to below 15%. He repeated that the Fed will deliver “price stability” and said he does not “prejudge meetings”. Stocks rose and the US dollar slipped after his remarks, said Derek Tang of Monetary Policy Analytics. Warsh also backed artificial intelligence as a major innovation, but warned it is boosting demand now and could overheat the economy. His AI task force will hold a field hearing in San Francisco Bay Area on Nov 16. US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the US central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of October . In a moderated discussion on Oct 16 morning in Bangkok at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, he made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, apart from reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. “We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” Warsh said. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.” Investors pared their bets for a rate hike at the US central bank’s Oct 27-28 policy gathering. The odds, which were hovering around 27% before Warsh spoke, dropped below 15% following his remarks. Stocks extended gains and the US dollar edged lower, with futures for the S&P 500 Index erasing losses of as much as 0.6% to climb 0.2%. “It was clear that he wasn’t going to deliver anything that the market could latch on to as hawkish,” Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, wrote in a note to clients. The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in September , the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely in 2026 . A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasised they have time to gather economic data before acting again. Warsh repeated his bullish views on artificial intelligence, calling it the most important innovation in the global economy during his lifetime. But he also warned that it may be driving demand in the near term. The Fed chief said that as a central banker, he is taking the new technology seriously but also “soberly, responsibly”. “It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s going to hit the supply side of the economy,” Warsh said. “If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognise this as a shock.” While it is a positive supply shock in the medium term, Warsh argued, it is driving increases in aggregate demand now and the impact on employment is uncertain. Some of Warsh’s colleagues have expressed similar concerns, even questioning whether the surge in investment that is buoying the AI build-out could lead to an overheating of the economy. Warsh also announced that his task force on productivity and jobs – which is grappling with the implications of AI – will hold a field hearing in the San Francisco Bay Area on Nov 16. It is one of five task forces he convened that will present recommendations to the Federal Open Market Committee in late 2026 or early in 2027. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Stocks, futures rise as Fed bets ease after Warsh: Markets wrap
events.summary: Stock markets were already rising on Oct 16 before US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh’s comments as a selloff in chip stocks eased. Stocks rose after Fed chairman Kevin Warsh gave no signal of urgency for more rate hikes, and traders cut October hike bets to 15%. Asian shares gained as chip stocks recovered, with Samsung and SK Hynix up more than 4%, while South Korea’s Kospi rebounded 4%. Indonesia’s stocks fell sharply after MSCI removed its emerging-market status, and investors warned the rally may stay fragile if gains remain focused on AI shares. Stocks extended gains as traders pared bets on an interest-rate hike after United States Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signalling greater urgency to tighten policy despite this week’s hotter-than-expected inflation data. The dollar edged lower. MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 1.4% , while US equity-index futures climbed 0.2%. European shares were set to gain 0.8% at the open. The modest uptick in sentiment – stocks were already higher as a rout in chip stocks eased – came after Warsh’s comments about the benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) to the US economy. He made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, save for reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. “Warsh’s refusal to commit to another rate hike is resulting in some Fed-rate-hike bets being unwound,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets. “His comment that ‘I don’t prejudge meetings’ after strong inflation prints is not helping the dollar.” Traders reduced bets on a Fed rate hike in October to 15% after Warsh’s speech, from more than 25% on Oct 15. A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar fell 0.1%, after dropping 0.3% the prior session, which was the biggest decline in more than a month. Gold was little changed at US$4,172 an ounce . Treasuries stayed lower on the day as Warsh spoke, after rallying across the curve in US trading. Global crude oil benchmark Brent dropped 0.7% to US$105.20 a barrel. Investors looked to Warsh’s speech in Bangkok for clearer signals on the policy path after the fastest US inflation in five months boosted expectations for further Fed tightening . US inflation has remained stubborn, fuelled by elevated oil prices since the Middle East war broke out. “We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” Warsh said in Bangkok. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.” The Fed raised rates by a quarter percentage point in September, the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely in 2026. A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasised they have time to gather economic data before acting again. “Markets are reassured to hear Warsh reiterating his belief that AI will uplift productivity in the medium term, which could help moderate inflation expectations and temper fears of back-to-back Fed rate hikes,” said Chang Wei Liang, a macro strategist at DBS Bank. Stock markets were already rising on Oct 16 before Warsh’s comments as a selloff in chip stocks eased. In Asia, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both advanced more than 4%. That helped South Korea’s Kospi Index rise 4% rebounding from the slump on Oct 15 that sent the gauge to its lowest close since April. Indonesian stocks slumped as much as 11%, the most since January 1998, after MSCI said the country no longer merits emerging-market status. The rupiah also edged lower. The durability of the equity rebound may depend on whether gains spread beyond the technology heavyweights that have driven much of the advance in 2026. Broader participation across sectors would help reduce the market’s reliance on AI-linked stocks after this week’s volatility exposed the risks of that concentration. “It seems like we are seeing a technical rebound, with the overall market settling down somewhat,” said Ryuta Otsuka, a strategist at Toyo Securities. Volatility could remain relatively high next week as traders monitor earnings “while searching for a bottom”, he said.

events.title: Keeping the haze out: Malls shut automated doors, suspend outdoor activities
events.summary: A sign at VivoCity on Oct 16 stating that an automated door is closed to keep the haze out. Singapore malls are closing automated doors and outdoor areas to protect shoppers and staff as haze stays unhealthy for a 12th day. Lendlease, Far East Organization and CapitaLand Investment are cleaning filters, checking air systems and giving N95 masks to workers with outdoor exposure. Malls are following NEA advice and may change access or suspend events; past haze cost Singapore $1.83 billion in 2015, according to NTU researchers. SINGAPORE – Major retail landlords told The Straits Times they were taking steps to reduce haze exposure for shoppers, tenants and staff. Lendlease, Far East Organization and CapitaLand Investment have stepped up air filter cleaning and monitoring for their air-conditioning and mechanical ventilation (ACMV) systems. To protect people indoors, they are keeping automated mall entrances shut, with landlords such as Lendlease and CapitaLand Investment distributing N95 masks to employees and contractors facing prolonged outdoor exposure. At noon on Oct 16, the hourly PM2.5 readings across the island hit the “high” range, which is above 150, while the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in western, central and eastern Singapore remained in the “very unhealthy” range above 200. Singapore’s PSI has five bands – good (0-50), moderate (51-100), unhealthy (101-200), very unhealthy (201-300) and hazardous (more than 300). A CapitaLand Investment spokesman said management may reduce inflow of outdoor air into its malls – including ION Orchard, Plaza Singapura, Tampines Mall, Junction 8, Funan and Kallang Wave Mall – by closing windows and automatic sliding doors where possible and directing shoppers to alternative entrances. Outdoor facilities at the malls may also be closed when air quality reaches unhealthy levels, the spokesperson added. A sign on the sliding entrance doors at Junction 8 stated that they were disabled to maintain indoor air quality as pollutant levels hit the unhealthy range , directing shoppers to use the side entrances instead. Deborah Tan, director for operations and marketing at Far East Organization’s commercial group, said mall tenants with exterior exits have also been advised to keep their entrances closed. Far East Organization’s portfolio of malls includes Orchard Central, Clarke Quay Central, Square 2 and One Holland Village. Tenants at One Holland Village, which has a more open layout, have been advised to keep their shop doors closed where feasible , while outdoor events have been rescheduled to November. Tan added that they are monitoring updates from the National Environment Agency (NEA) closely and will adjust their safety approach as conditions develop. Jenny Khoo, head of retail and workspace management at Lendlease, said staff are encouraged to prioritise their well-being and discuss any concerns with their supervisors, and that flexible work arrangements “may be considered where appropriate”. She added that under normal conditions, the malls’ ACMV air filters are cleaned and replaced on a stringent maintenance schedule. When haze conditions worsen, management steps up active monitoring of indoor air quality and filter performance, and carries out additional replacements. Khoo added that management has also enhanced the malls’ air quality with bipolar ionisation systems, which release positive and negative ions to eliminate dust, odours and pathogens such as bacteria and viruses. Retail malls in Lendlease’s portfolio include Parkway Parade, 313@somerset, Jem and PLQ Mall. Khoo said outdoor play areas at Lendlease malls, such as Jem, may close temporarily when the 24-hour PSI reading exceeds 200. “Lendlease takes precautionary measures guided by prevailing NEA advisories, including suspending outdoor facilities and activities,” she added. Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust, which manages VivoCity, declined to comment, although one of its entrances featured a sign stating it was closed to keep the haze out. VivoCity’s level-three rooftop features an open, shallow wading pool, while level two has free-to-access outdoor playgrounds alongside children’s ride operator ZooMoov. A spokesperson for City Square Mall said its outdoor playgrounds have been temporarily closed, while mall personnel’s non-essential outdoor duties have been reduced. “Non-essential” auto-doors have also been closed to limit outdoor pollutants entering the mall. The mall will also offer 100 complimentary honey lemon drinks, while stocks last, at the mall’s customer service counter at B2 from Oct 19 to Nov 1, from 10am to 10pm daily. The Singapore Institute of International Affairs had in June issued a rare “red” warning in its Haze Outlook 2026 report, and said there was a high risk of severe transboundary haze affecting Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

events.title: Drone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO
events.summary: Drone attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea this month have raised concerns among NATO members SOFIA, Bulgaria -- A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow's full-scale invasion. The attacks in the two countries' exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine. Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube river ports, leaving Kyiv increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine's Danube ports. In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones Wednesday and Thursday, one in Romania's territorial waters. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Thursday in Brussels that “two drones” had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. “There will be a reaction from the Romanian state,” he warned. Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia. “There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia — and indeed, the logic points in that direction,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament. “The problem is that we cannot prove it.” The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader , a chemical tanker traveling from Tunisia to Romania, was struck by a drone Thursday and caught fire. Five crew members were rescued but another seven are missing. On Wednesday, a drone strike and fire were reported on the Comoros-flagged Yara J, a chemical and oil tanker traveling from Turkey to Romania. Romania’s acting Defense Minister Radu Miruta said an investigation was underway. On Tuesday, two ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria's coast. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from the Ukraine-operated Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, but 11 crew from the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity are still missing . The crew of the Chelsea 3 reported the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. Earlier this month, sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. A Togo-flagged ship sank with no sign of the 12 sailors reported on board, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated 18 crew members from a Palau-flagged vessel that was damaged. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters. Russia's ambassador in Sofia, Bulgaria, said she didn't have any information from the Russian defense ministry. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Thursday that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and “the latest attacks on commercial shipping.” “NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” he said. “NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.” Article 5 of the NATO charter has a mutual defense guarantee — an attack on one is an attack on all — but Romanian defense analyst Radu Tudor said it was uncertain as to whether it covers many of the Black Sea drone strikes because they occurred in the alliance members’ exclusive economic zones. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Iran live updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded “It’s a matter of discussion whether the exclusive economic zone is included in the Article 5-type reaction or not,” he said. “And it seems that until now, it isn’t — which raised a lot of questions.” NATO has been too slow to respond in the Black Sea, he argued. “Tens of incidents are happening and Russia is getting closer to NATO borders. … Words are not enough,” Tudor said. The Black Sea drone incidents in October are just the latest in a long string of drone airspace incursions to rock Romania and other NATO members since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. While most have come from Russia, Ukrainian drones have also crossed borders.

events.title: World Bank sets fivefold minerals goal as Fed chairman Warsh flags financial stability risks
events.summary: The World Bank aims to increase its critical minerals business fivefold over the next five years, while US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh expressed surprise at the resilience of major economies amid geopolitical shocks and tighter monetary policy. "In critical minerals, we ⁠plan to quintuple our business in five years … this ​week, ⁠we launched our ‌first country compacts with MDB partners, to build local industries and keep ​more jobs and value at home," World Bank president Ajay Banga said at the 2026 IMF -World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, as the multilateral lender seeks to support mining, processing and local industries. He also outlined plans to expand partnerships with countries developing critical minerals industries. The World Bank's new metals and minerals implementation plan is aimed at securing $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the 2026-2030 fiscal period, up from $3.6 billion in the 2021-2025 fiscal period. The lender has identified 20 countries with which it could partner on critical minerals development projects. It also launched its first country compacts with its partners this week, aiming to build local industries and retain more jobs and economic value in producing countries. Mr Banga also laid out a vision on Friday for how the World Bank should operate, focusing primarily on creating jobs, expanding economic opportunity and connecting private capital to developing nations that need investment. Addressing the plenary session at the annual meetings, Mr Banga said the current economic climate of tightening fiscal space, rising debt and global conflicts had made the work challenging – but not impossible. “Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address: making scarce resources go further, while helping countries create jobs at scale. They must be addressed together,” he said in prepared remarks. “The future of development will depend on bringing public finance , private investment, philanthropy and technology together around what each country needs. The partnership – and mix – should evolve as countries do.” He also spoke of the World Bank’s new initiative to focus on “small AI” – bespoke artificial intelligence-enabled applications that do not rely on the most advanced and expensive version of the technology, but can provide solutions for people in the developing world. “Practical, or ‘small’, AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers,” Mr Banga added. Separately, Mr Warsh said the Fed needed to consider financial stability risks as it assesses the outlook for the US economy , while declining to offer indications about its next interest-rate decision. ⁠Speaking at the annual meetings, heh said he did not “prejudge” policy decisions before the Fed’s meetings from October 27 to 28, when markets expect interest rates to remain unchanged. The Fed raised rates in September and made it clear that it intended to deliver price stability and withdraw some monetary policy accommodation, he said. “I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Mr Warsh said. He said ⁠the Fed must ​continually bolster its credibility to get ⁠monetary policy right, adding that that includes the supervision and operations side ⁠of the central bank. He also expressed optimism about AI and its potential to transform the real economy, although he said the technology’s near-term impact on employment remained uncertain. Mr Warsh also said he was surprised by the global resilience and how many G20 member ⁠states are “hanging in there” amid the geopolitical shocks of recent months, ​as ⁠most ‌central banks tightened monetary ​policy to deal with inflation. “We're seeing common things and we're taking action and I view that as a positive development,” Mr Warsh said. “I believe, optimistically, ​you ‌might think ⁠naively, at least ​in the US, we're ​going ‌to come out of ⁠this stronger with a ⁠more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.” With reporting from Reuters and AFP

events.title: Commercial goods are no longer entering Gaza, raising fears
events.summary: No commercial goods are entering the Gaza Strip, Israeli authorities said, attributing the suspension to local vendors they said are fed up with Hamas raising taxes on them JERUSALEM -- No commercial goods have entered the Gaza Strip for two days, Israeli authorities said Thursday, blaming the suspension on merchants angered by taxes imposed by Hamas — a claim that Palestinian importers deny. The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of food and other critical supplies as fears grow about procuring supplies needed to get through winter in the territory. The move stands to immediately reduce Gaza's supplies, because the closed-off territory is completely reliant on whatever goods Israel allows in through border crossings. Aid groups generally bring in staples such as flour, while merchants import more perishable foods like fruits and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza. The suspension is raising fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control. “The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council, an aid group. “The markets need to be functioning.” COGAT announced the suspension of commercial shipments Wednesday. Its deputy spokesperson, Lt. Daniel Kantorovich, said the agency was acting on a decision made by Palestinian merchants a day earlier and could reverse it at their behest. “We were prepared to coordinate the entry of their trucks as usual, but the vendors informed us that they were cancelling the coordination due to Hamas’s taxation mechanism and threats against them,” Kantorovich said. “The merchants don’t want to bring goods into Gaza.” The world’s leading authority on food insecurity reported earlier this year that conditions in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but were still at crisis levels. Most families in the war-battered enclave weren’t getting nearly enough to eat, said the report, adding that “even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains.” Merchants in Gaza coordinate directly with vendors outside the territory, whose shipments are examined by Israel's military before entering Gaza. In announcing the measure, COGAT claimed to be communicating a decision made by local merchants in Gaza who had grown tired of Hamas taxing their trucks and threatening them. Israel has long accused the militant group of levying fees on imports to fund its operations. COGAT said no private-sector vendors had attempted to import goods to Gaza since the merchants alerted Israel on Tuesday. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia But the head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, disputed Israel's account, saying they were the ones who had made the decision. “The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments,” he said. “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.” Following COGAT's announcement, Sheheiber's union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods. The ministry had been asking merchants to pay 10,000 shekels (about $3,226) per truck entering Gaza, Sheheiber said. At the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab told the union that the amount was not a tax, but rather a donation sought by the ministry to help pay civil servants in the strip. It was not clear from the COGAT announcement if aid agencies would be allowed to increase shipments into Gaza to compensate for the loss in commercial goods. The agency claimed that Gaza's population — of roughly 2 million people — required approximately 250 truckloads of goods each day. That's far below the minimum of 600 trucks a day stipulated by a ceasefire brokered by the U.S. a year ago. The war started when Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people on Oct. 7, 2023, and took 251 hostages . Israel responded with a massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. That includes over 1,400 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire took effect, the ministry says. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts.

events.title: Yields on S’pore Government Securities climb higher: Should investors buy in or stick to stocks?
events.summary: The interest rate on the one-year T-bill rose to its 2026 high of 1.92% on Oct 15. T-bill yields in Singapore have risen to about 1.9%, and experts expect more gains as US Federal Reserve hikes push up short-term rates. Nov's Singapore Savings Bonds hit a 2026 peak of 2.45%, though early redemption cuts year-one yields to 1.67% Some investors still prefer dividend stocks, as their yields can beat T-bills and SSBs, while keeping more cash ready for market opportunities. SINGAPORE – The returns that retail investors are getting for Treasury bills (T-bills), a type of short-term Singapore Government Securities, are climbing after dipping to around 1.3% to 1.4% in 2025 and the first half of 2026. With yields now hovering near 1.9%, fixed-income experts believe there is more upside in the coming months. Another form of Singapore Government Securities, Singapore Savings Bonds (SSBs), will pay the highest rates so far in 2026 for its November issue. If investors hold the SSBs for the full duration of 10 years, they will earn an average return of 2.45% a year. T-bills are short-term securities with maturities of either six months or a year. Investors buy the bills at a discount upfront and receive the full face value at maturity, earning the difference as interest. In contrast, SSBs are longer-term instruments that can be held for up to 10 years, though investors have the flexibility to exit their investment in any given month without penalty. Both T-bills and SSBs are deemed risk-free investments backed by Singapore’s triple-A credit rating. The appeal of T-bills grew in 2022 as yields climbed steadily from sub-1% levels. The six-month T-bill subsequently hit a peak of 4.4% on Dec 8, 2022, and the one-year T-bill went as high as 3.87% on Jan 26, 2023. Drawn by their safe nature and rising yields, investors from all walks of life piled in. Senior lab technician Dallas Goh was one of them. He accumulated as much as $100,000 in T-bills at one point. Interest in these short-term government securities waned in 2024 as equity markets became more attractive. Investors – including Goh, who stopped buying T-bills in the middle of 2024 – looked elsewhere for higher returns. However, the yields on T-bills are climbing again. The interest rate on the one-year T-bill rose to its 2026 high of 1.92% on Oct 15, from 1.68% on July 23. There will be no more one-year T-bill auctions in 2026. Meanwhile, the cut-off yield for the six-month T-bill dipped slightly to 1.9% on Oct 8, remaining just shy of its Sept 24 peak of 1.92%. There are five more six-month T-bill auctions – on Oct 22, Nov 4, Nov 19, Dec 3 and Dec 17. Goh said the yields are “still too low” and that he will wait until they cross 2.5% before he considers investing in T-bills again. His wish may just come true. Market watchers anticipate higher yields in the upcoming auctions as the US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates at least once by December 2026 and a total of twice within the next six months. Eugene Leow, head of fixed-income research at DBS Bank, said: “As long as Fed hike bets are in play, we would reasonably expect six-month T-bill rates to continue climbing.” He noted that the interest rates on a six-month T-bill reflect where investors expect the Fed to move rates over the next half a year. “We think the six-month and one-year T-Bill rates would still grind higher in the coming months as Fed hikes get delivered,” he added. Wesley Hoon, research analyst with the global fixed-income team at digital wealth platform FSM Global, noted that the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the economy through the exchange rate rather than by setting interest rates. As a result, Singapore’s short-term rates largely take their cue from US interest rates. To illustrate his point, Hoon noted that following the Federal Reserve’s rate hike on Sept 16, the cut-off yield for the six-month T-bill auction on Sept 24 climbed from 1.7% to 1.92%. “If the Fed pauses in October and hikes in December, as markets expect, that adds upward pressure into year-end, though some of it is already reflected in today’s yields,” he said. Hoon expects six-month yields to keep climbing over the remaining auctions in 2026. FSM Global is also positive on the one-year T-bills. However, since there are no more one-year bills in 2026, investors must wait until January 2027 to participate. To avoid sitting on idle cash, Hoon suggested that investors consider building a T-bill ladder with staggered maturity dates by spreading their cash across multiple upcoming auctions. Because six-month bills are auctioned every two weeks, investors can allocate a portion into each of the next few issues, making January 2027’s one-year T-bill just another rung in their ladder rather than the final destination, he added. “With a ladder, you don’t have to call the peak to earn a decent yield,” Hoon said. “Part of your money matures every couple of weeks.

events.title: Fuel costs squeezing margins for some businesses
events.summary: Diesel prices in Jersey have reached more than £2 per litre in recent weeks Some businesses in Jersey have expressed concern about the impact of rising global fuel prices. Locally, and in the UK, diesel prices recently topped £2 a litre , and global leaders have since made efforts to ease the strain on supply. The Government of Jersey has proposed to freeze fuel duty in 2027 in a bid to "help ease cost-of-living pressures". A&A Scaffolding Solutions said it welcomed that move, but said it would provide "limited relief if global prices continue to rise". Listen to the latest news for Jersey Fuel duty was frozen in Jersey from 2023-2025, before rising in line with inflation in 2026. In the proposed budget for 2027 , external , the government has suggested freezing it once again. It said "maintaining fuel duty at its current rate will help avoid additional costs for households and businesses that rely on transport, providing continued support at a time when many islanders remain under financial pressure". However, some businesses on the island worry that it will not be enough to offset global prices. Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine? Published 4 days ago Kelly Keating, from A&A Scaffolding Solutions, said "rising diesel prices are a real concern for us, particularly when they come on top of so many other costs that seem to be increasing across Jersey". "Construction is taking a hard hit. We rely on diesel for machinery, vehicles and deliveries, so increases put direct pressure on the cost of carrying out work. "Alongside rising material, freight and operating costs, this is squeezing margins and making it harder to price projects with confidence". "A freeze in fuel duty would be welcome, but our concern is that it would offer limited relief if global fuel prices continue to rise. "The wider issue is the cumulative impact. Businesses can only absorb so many increases before they affect investment, project viability and ultimately the prices customers pay". Businesses said it was becoming more difficult to absorb price rises Fuel costs are also having a "noticeable impact" for tree surgeons, Jonathan Le Maistre Ltd. Darren Hopkins, from the firm, said "we depend on our vans, trucks, chippers, stump grinders, and other machinery that consume significant amounts of fuel". "Increased diesel prices will raise our operating costs, reducing margins on jobs and making it more difficult to absorb costs without passing some of them on to our customers". Hopkins said continued increases would be a "concern for their business, and the wider industry". However, some businesses are managing through the disruption. Jeremy Phillips, from Barette Plant Hire, said it "hasn't been too much of an issue so far, but that fuel surcharges are being added to hourly rates". However, he said that "if the prices keep going up, customers aren't going to be carrying on with their projects". Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said support was being targeted directly at consumers rather than expecting businesses to absorb costs In the run-up to the unveiling of the 2027 budget, Deputy Lucy Stephenson called for a reduction in fuel duty , but those plans were withdrawn following assurances from ministers that support was coming. Speaking at the time, Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said the government "didn't like the idea of reducing fuel duty because it wasn't targeted". Instead, ministers opted for a freeze on duty for 2027, prioritising targeted support for families and those "struggling the most". Responding to the fresh concerns from businesses, Maclean said: "Rather than expecting businesses to absorb increased costs such as higher fuel prices, the budget provides support directly to consumers to help them manage those pressures and spend in the local economy". "Fuel prices are largely driven by global markets and geopolitical events outside Jersey's control. "What the government can do is avoid adding further pressure where it can. "The proposed freeze in fuel duty will help mitigate the impact of prices rises by reducing the level of duty in real terms". events.title: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule. It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies. Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10- to 15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference. “The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.” Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.” Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.” He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said. Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added. Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid. events.title: 'TV and cheap booze' blamed for landlord quitting
events.summary: Landlord Patrick Hughes says fewer people are going to the pub Former pub landlord Patrick Hughes is blunt when explaining why he has called time on his tenure behind the bar. "I thought there was a gap in the market but there was no market for the gap", he said. The 66-year-old took over The Royal Mail Cart pub in Spalding, in August 2025, hoping to attract customers with live music nights and "a sense of community". Just over a year on he is packing boxes and looking around the empty rooms after he quit his tenancy with the pub's owner, Stonegate Group. The government said it was supporting pubs with business rates discounts. Patrick has given up his tenancy of The Royal Mail Cart in Spalding Patrick told BBC Politics North that he blames a perfect storm of rising utility and wage prices, people's changing habits and major roadworks directly outside the pub, which began in the summer. "These days people are used to staying at home, watching TV, having cheap drink from the supermarket or off licence and getting food deliveries," he said. "To make a pub like this work you need to turn over £12,000 a week, some weeks we were doing quite well, around £8,000, but once the road works began outside that went down quite dramatically." Figures from the Office for National Statistics , external show that 27% of pubs and bars in Lincolnshire closed between 2009 and 2025. That is a drop from 710 to 515. In South Holland, of which Spalding is a part, the rate is almost double that, at 53%, a drop from 75 to 35. That is also way above the England average of 19%. "The government needs to look at the low cost of alcohol in supermarkets primarily," said Patrick. "Certainly the taxation in supermarkets needs to be looked at to bring about some kind of equilibrium." Duty paid on draught alcohol in pubs and bars is up to 11 pence cheaper than that sold in supermarkets. But other costs associated with running a business still makes supermarket alcohol cheaper overall. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced a 20% cut in business rates for qualifying pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, effective from April 2027. Emma McClarkin OBE, chief executive of the British Beer and Pub Association, says they want that to be made permanent at the Budget this month, "alongside a freeze in beer duty and a widening of the draft discount". "We're set to lose one pub a day by the end of the year and 295 have closed already," she said. "When a pub does close, it's not just the front door that's closing, it's the heritage, the culture, the economic contribution to society and the social value." Mark Newlands believes that people still want to visit their local pub Just outside Spalding, The Ship Inn pub stands by the River Welland in the small hamlet of Surfleet Seas End. "There used to be tables and chairs with people eating food and drinking by the river," said Mark Newlands, who lives a few doors down. The pub closed last year but now some locals, led by Mark, have formed The Shipmates group to try to raise £600,000 to buy and run it. So far they have managed to get the pub listed as An Asset of Community Value under the Localism Act 2011. That gives them the right to bid for the property, if it goes up for sale. "People have become fed up of the Covid way of living and they want to see their pub open," said Mark. "The indications from smaller and larger investors is that it's worth doing and we've proven to our own satisfaction that it is a viable business." An HM Treasury spokesperson said: "The Chancellor prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues - saving thousands of locals over £1,000 a year." Stonegate has been approached by the BBC for comment. Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds , watch the latest episode of Look North .

events.title: The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win | Frances Ryan
events.summary: The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment Back in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”. The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even provided an interactive map (in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”. events.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
events.summary: The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows. Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks. Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks. As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests. BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported. Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes. Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts. The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners". Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby. The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard. Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said. Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route". Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen. About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day. The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August. Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman. These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore. So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships. Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day". "The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added. The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media. Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman. A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard. Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said. Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship. events.title: ASEAN companies keen on AI for business benefits, despite its energy costs
events.summary: Firms should assess not just the token prices before building an AI application, but also its carbon footprint, says an expert. SINGAPORE – Almost four in five South-east Asian businesses expect the benefits from artificial intelligence to outweigh its energy burden – even as they brace themselves for rising costs and infrastructure pressure. Out of 514 regional business leaders polled by The Business Times and market research firm Kantar, 78% see AI’s benefits outweighing its energy requirements. Released on Oct 12, The Business Times Insights: Powering ASEAN’s Future 2026 – the second regional survey by BT and Kantar – showed Singapore, Vietnam and Thailand as having the highest levels of optimism. This comes as AI adoption is accelerating across South-east Asia – 62% of respondents have increased their investments in AI or data-driven technologies over the past 12 months. Growth is particularly pronounced in Indonesia, where 85% of businesses reported moderate-to-significant increases in AI investment over the last year. The regional optimism around AI is “no surprise” to Sunil Veetil, whose Singapore advisory Perdura helps companies with green finance and the energy transition. He noted that AI returns materialise quickly when applied to the right use cases. For instance, it can enable multilingual customer service, providing distinct advantages in a region as diverse as ASEAN. In addition, said Manik Bhandari, ASEAN data and AI leader at EY, energy costs are currently “a very small fraction” of the overall AI token pricing, and thus “quite minimal” when building AI applications in an enterprise setting. Bracing for costs, infrastructure pressure That said, there is awareness of energy pressures – 41% of ASEAN businesses expect a moderate increase in energy demand as AI adoption scales, while another 40% are bracing themselves for a significant increase. Businesses expect energy demand to manifest in operational challenges: Rising electricity or operating costs, as cited by 46% of respondents; Pressure to upgrade existing infrastructure (39%); and Increased competition for energy resources (37%). While businesses may not currently be bearing the energy costs of AI, Veetil noted that this “changes when AI becomes captive or domestic, when companies run their own models or countries build sovereign (models) on local power”. “Then, the energy bill lands on the business.” Some markets are less optimistic about AI. In the Philippines, just 64% of respondents see AI’s benefits outweighing energy requirements, below the regional average. One explanation could be that “the trade-off looks different in markets where electricity costs, grid reliability and energy security are already significant business concerns”, said Zayana Zaikariah from the Institute of Strategic and International Studies in Malaysia. Climate exposure may be another reason. “In countries facing frequent typhoons, flooding and other disruptions, businesses may place a higher premium on the resilience of electricity and digital infrastructure before adding new sources of demand,” she said. It is thus critical for businesses to use AI judiciously. Lawrence Loh from the National University of Singapore said FOMO – the “fear of missing out” – is leading many businesses to step up AI adoption, and that their staff and management “may be experiencing severe AI fatigue now”. “The wrong metric for business is how much AI is being used,” said Loh, who is director of the university’s Centre for Governance and Sustainability. “The right one should be how much measurable economic and other benefits are being derived.” EY’s Bhandari said that before building an AI application, companies should assess not only the token prices, but also the application’s carbon footprint. Businesses can use smaller, task-specific models that reduce memory usage and can be run on standard hardware or edge devices, with a vastly reduced carbon footprint. “Not only is it cheaper for me as an enterprise, it’s also better for the environment,” he said. Zayana echoed that businesses should “match the level of compute to the value of the task”. A compute-intensive AI system “should not be the default if a smaller, task-specific model can achieve the same business outcome”, she said. AI-driven hunger for energy has implications not just for businesses, but also for countries’ energy resilience and decarbonisation goals. If not managed well, greater energy demand from AI could translate to more dependence on fossil fuels, said Dinita Setyawati, external affairs and strategic impact lead for Asia at energy think-tank Ember. Conversely, AI facilities “can actually become part of the solution if they help mobilise investment in renewable energy, storage and the grid infrastructure needed to support that demand”, she noted.
