events.title: Proposed Dalby data centre to harvest rainwater from roof
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Proposed Dalby data centre to 'air-cool' operations and harvest rainwater from roof The concept model of a large-scale data centre project that has been proposed for the Western Downs. ( Supplied: Urbis ) The proposed Western Downs Digital Park says it will air-cool operations and not draw from bores or town water. Its developer says artificial intelligence customers would be responsible for paying for the power supply. The development application remains in its early stages and public consultation is ongoing. The international developer that has proposed Australia's largest data centre says it would be able to operate during even the worst droughts. The proposed $32 billion Western Downs Digital Park in regional Queensland would consist of four data centres, the first of which has been leased by Anthropic for use as early as 2027. Zerra DC is holding community consultation session in Dalby on the Western Downs. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Planning documents by Singapore-based developer Zerra DC said each of the four buildings planned for the Western Downs Digital Park would require 21,000 litres of water a day, equivalent to the water usage of a small shopping centre. The company's chief data centre officer Matt Ward said modelling showed that even in 2019, when Dalby received less than 200 millimetres of rain, it would catch enough rainwater to operate. Matt Ward says the developer is committed to being a "good neighbour". ( Supplied: Zerra DC ) Mr Ward said the buildings housing the data centres were "large sheds" with "35,000-odd square metres of roof space" and the facility would be entirely air-cooled and would not draw from bores or town water. Mr Ward said supplying new power to the grid would be the responsibility of its artificial intelligence customers such as Anthropic, which the company has signed an agreement with. He said Zerra DC would act like the "landlord of any commercial building", where the tenant, Anthropic, would be responsible for paying for power supply. The data centre is proposed on the site of a feedlot outside of Dalby. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) It comes as the federal government works to establish a framework that would require data centres to bring as much power into the electricity grid as they take. Australia's largest proposed data centre could draw a quarter of Queensland's energy use The proposed $30 billion data centre in Queensland has a peak capacity comparable to the average power requirements of 1.5 million households. But who pays for that power production was a dilemma, according to Climate Energy Finance director Tim Buckley. He said both sides needed to be "collectively held to account" to commit to new renewable energy generation. "If they aren't held to account in substance over the life of the project, we will inevitably see higher power prices for everyone across Queensland as a result," Mr Buckley said. Some in the Western Downs have questioned how the region would benefit from the multi-billion-dollar investment. Zerra DC began community consultation sessions during the day last week, but recently announced the "drop-in" sessions would run in the afternoons from midday to 8pm. Robyn Sheehan attended an information session in Dalby about the proposed data centre. Zerra DC has committed to 1,500 jobs per year during construction and 1,400 ongoing operational jobs at full capacity, which would transform the local economy. "To keep this thing running, we'll need a team of skilled people across mechanical, electrical, security, engineering at a 24-7 basis," Mr Ward said.

( AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts ) RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26. RBA workers are demanding an 11 per cent pay increase over three years, but the RBA is offering 9.5 per cent. The latest data show Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, but economists say the RBA may not have finished lifting rates. The Reserve Bank's senior officials are among the highest paid people in Australia. RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26, with a base salary of $1.01 million. Deputy governor Andrew Hauser received total remuneration of $955,033, with a base salary of $903,217. Half of young adults living with parents Half of all young Australians are still living with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001, a survey reveals. The RBA's four assistant governors received total remuneration between $743,000 and $868,000 each, and its chief operating officer received total remuneration of $905,543. The figures can be found in the RBA's 2026 annual report , which was released on Thursday afternoon. The median annual earnings for all employees in Australia is $74,672 . In March this year, Ms Bullock received unwanted media attention when she and her husband bought a $2 million home in Yamba, in northern NSW, on the same day that the RBA lifted interest rates on February 3. It was her third investment property. Her property purchase was recorded in her declaration of material personal interests on the RBA's website. Michele Bullock says she sympathises with the plight of Australian workers. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The RBA governor's pay is slightly above most federal departmental or agency heads, which are mostly clustered around $900,000-$1,000,000. However, the chief executives of some publicly owned corporations are paid far more. Ellie Sweeney, the NBN Co chief executive, received $3.4 million in total remuneration in 2025-26, up from $1.9 million a year earlier, making her Australia's highest-paid public servant . Paul Graham, the chief executive of Australia Post, received $3.3 million in 2024-25. Dennis Barns, the chief executive of Snowy Hydro Limited, received $2.1 million in 2024-25. RBA workers don't want a real wage cut The RBA is currently arguing with junior RBA staff about pay and conditions. Lower-ranked RBA staff have been asking for a pay increase of 11 per cent over three years and an inflation-protection mechanism that triggers additional pay rises if inflation outpaces wages, to avoid real wage cuts in coming years. Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth, research suggests But last month, hours after the RBA lifted rates for the fourth time this year, Ms Bullock emailed RBA staff and asked them to vote for a pay offer of 9.5 per cent over three years. A majority of RBA staff had rejected a similar proposal in July. The Finance Sector Union says enterprise agreement negotiations have been dragging on since late last year and the RBA has refused to move on its original pay offer. The latest round of voting for the RBA's proposed enterprise agreement will close on Monday at 5pm . After lifting interest rates last month, Ms Bullock said she sympathised with the plight of Australian workers. But she said the only way workers could keep receiving sustainable increases in real wages was from productivity growth, and Australia's economy was struggling to deliver it. "People are feeling, quite rightly, very annoyed and very upset about the fact that the costs of everything are rising, that their wages are not keeping pace with that, they’re seeing real wage cuts," she said . "If we don't get productivity growth, there's not going to be real wage rises coming down the pipeline." According to the RBA's annual report, the bank has 2,201 employees, equating to 2,082 full-time equivalent employees. It has 76 senior executives, and another 222 highly paid staff. The RBA's workforce has increased by 8 per cent over the past 12 months. The RBA says that reflects the additional resources it needs to implement its transformation and change agendas. The additional staff are concentrated in technology and corporate support functions. RBA staff numbers increased by 8 per cent in the past year. ( Source: RBA annual report 2026 ) Higher unemployment will help to control inflation Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, in seasonally adjusted terms.

events.title: Malaysia’s growth tops forecasts as AI boom drives export surge
events.summary: The government expects Malaysia’s economy to grow at 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity. Malaysia’s GDP rose 5.3% in the third quarter, beating the 5.1% forecast, but growth slowed from 6% as mining fell and most sectors still stayed positive. AI demand lifted exports, especially electronics, while strong domestic spending and household support kept the trade-dependent economy resilient. The government expects about 5% growth in 2026 and 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, with full third-quarter GDP details due on Nov 18. KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia’s economic growth slowed but still exceeded expectations as the artificial intelligence boom continued to bolster exports and domestic demand remained resilient. Gross domestic product (GDP) rose 5.3% in the three months through September from a year earlier, according to advance estimates from the Department of Statistics Malaysia on Oct 16, beating the 5.1% median prediction in a Bloomberg survey. Third-quarter growth, however, slowed from the 6% expansion in the previous three-month period. Third-quarter growth was underpinned by positive performance across most economic sectors, the department said in a statement. Only the mining and quarrying sector contracted, it added. The better-than-expected reading underscores the resilience of Malaysia’s economy, even as growth moderates from a strong first half. Robust domestic consumption and demand for electronics used in AI have helped cushion the trade-dependent economy from disruptions caused by the US war against Iran . “The out-turn is broadly in line with our forecast and suggests the growth momentum remains robust, albeit moderating from strong growth in the first half of 2026,” said Lavanya Venkateswaran, economist at OCBC Bank. “This very much leaves the door open for Bank Negara Malaysia to normalise its policy rate by 25 basis points. Our baseline for the adjustment is in January but it is a close call for the November meeting.” The ringgit was steady at 4.08 to the US dollar after the GDP print, while local stocks held losses. The services sector rose 5.4%, bolstered by wholesale and retail trade, information and communication as well as finance, the statistics department said. Manufacturing strengthened by 7.5%, backed in part by export-oriented industries, particularly electrical and electronic products. Bank Negara Malaysia governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said in an interview this week that the economy is likely to grow about 5% in 2026, with the nation’s diverse sources of growth helping to cushion it against any slowdown in the AI boom. Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5% during the first three quarters of 2026, the department said, above the government’s revised growth forecast of 4.8% to 5.3% for the year. The government in October raised the forecast from 4% to 5%. Household spending remains firm as fuel subsidies helped shield consumers from elevated energy costs. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim earlier in October also announced more cash aid and a higher minimum wage for 2027 to ease cost-of-living pressures. The Malaysian government expects the economy to grow at 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity. Preliminary GDP data, which will provide a detailed analysis of the third quarter, will be released on Nov 18. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Palm oil stocks slide after Singapore begins looking into which firms responsible for haze
events.summary: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. Singapore is investigating which firms may be behind haze-causing fires, and may act under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, PM Lawrence Wong said. Palm oil shares fell after a report named First Resources and Bumitama Agri in areas with haze source points; First Resources blamed outside fires and a severe El Nino drought. Singapore’s air quality worsened sharply, with the central PSI at 227 and “very unhealthy”; Indonesia blamed peatland damage and said it will restore its peat ecosystem. SINGAPORE – Shares of palm oil producers fell on Oct 16, a day after Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that Singapore is looking into which companies may be responsible for haze-causing fires. Where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries, said PM Wong in a Facebook post on Oct 15 . Bumitama Agri retreated 7.5% to an intraday low of $1.73, then rebounded somewhat to close 4.8% lower at $1.78. Golden Agri-Resources shares dropped one cent to 28 cents. A report by The Straits Times on Oct 15 cited a recent Greenpeace investigation which named First Resources and Bumitama Agri among entities with concession areas registering haze source points. First Resources on Oct 15 defended itself, stating that fires detected within its Indonesian palm oil concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. The company attributed the elevated fire risk in West Kalimantan to a “severe” El Nino-induced drought. Indonesia on Oct 15 blamed peatland degradation by past food estates for its worst wildfire season in 11 years, and said it will work to restore its peat ecosystem. Air quality deteriorated across all areas of Singapore overnight. The 24-hour PSI reading for the central region hit the “very unhealthy” level at midnight on Oct 16 and stood at 227 at 9am – a new high for 2026. Readings for the rest of the country were at the “unhealthy” level. On whether Singapore will take action against errant companies under the Act, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said on Oct 14 that the country was “keeping its options open”. That followed a National Environment Agency spokesperson stating that the agency “has been closely monitoring the haze situation, gathering information on fire hot spots, their sources and impact on Singapore’s air quality”. events.title: Nationals say Liberals oppose EU trade deal, Liberals beg to differ
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Liberals insist EU free trade position not settled, despite Canavan's assertion Some Liberals are frustrated by Matt Canavan's suggestion that both Liberals and Nationals oppose the free trade deal with the EU. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Liberals insist they have not agreed to oppose the proposed Australia-EU trade deal, despite Nationals leader Matt Canavan claiming both parties are against it. Some Liberals believe Trade Minister Don Farrell could renegotiate aspects of the deal, an idea strongly rebuffed by those on both sides of the negotiations. A joint parliamentary committee is expected to scrutinise the deal early next year. Nationals leader Matt Canavan's claim that both Nationals and Liberals are against a slated European Union trade deal has angered some Liberals who privately insist the issue has not been settled. In an opinion piece published in The Australian today, Senator Canavan said the deal landed by Trade Minister Don Farrell would "weaken Australia's sovereignty on climate change policy" and was bad for the steel industry and some farmers. He said the deal, which parliament must approve, was opposed by both Coalition parties. That assertion was backed by his colleague, Bridget McKenzie. "Don Farrell can try all he likes to find a Coalition senator willing to vote for it. He won't because we are absolutely united," she told ABC Radio National today. But two Liberal senators subsequently told the ABC the proposed deal was better than the status quo and should be adopted. One cited the diplomatic importance of the deal at a time when the US was waging trade wars. "As long as it's not a really bad free trade agreement, and I don't think it is, we should support it," the senator said. "It goes to what the Liberal Party stands for. "There is a lot of internal disquiet about this." 'Opposed … subject to proper process' Multiple senior Liberals told the ABC the matter had not been considered by shadow cabinet or discussed in the Coalition party room, and that could only happen after scrutiny by the parliament's joint standing committee on trade. Farmers rubbish 'worst ever' EU free trade agreement The National Farmers' Federation says the deal will leave farmers without meaningful access to the EU market. "You can't short-circuit that by [writing] an op-ed," one said, framing Senator Canavan's intervention as a clear attempt to strongarm Liberals, reigniting tensions between the parties that plagued the leadership of Angus Taylor's predecessor, Sussan Ley. The joint standing committee process is still some time away. While the deal's text was agreed between leaders this year, it will not be signed until Australia and each EU member country complete the requisite legal checks, most likely early next year. Some Liberals believe this leaves time to renegotiate aspects of the deal. Two Liberals seeking to downplay any disagreement said the agreed position was "opposed to the deal as it stands, subject to the proper parliamentary and Coalition process". Senator Canavan used more cautious language in a press conference today, saying the opposition was "opposed to the deal in its current form". Farrell says veto would be 'vandalism' The government has rubbished the idea that renegotiation would be possible. "There is no room … the deal is done," Senator Farrell said today. The minister has projected confidence that the Senate, where the government does not have the numbers in its own right, will not stand in the way of the deal, telling the ABC on Wednesday he believed "enough senators … understand how important this is". One interpretation of that comment is that Senator Farrell believes enough Liberals might cross the floor to vote for the deal, although none of those who spoke to the ABC suggested they would. Don Farrell (right) led negotiations with the European Union and says the deal is no longer up for negotiation. ( Supplied: Supplied: Minister for Trade and Tourism ) Another is that Senator Farrell is confident that the Coalition – or at least the Liberals – will eventually land in favour of the deal, a view shared among some European diplomats, who have directly lobbied Mr Taylor and other Liberals in recent weeks. One diplomat from an EU nation told the ABC it would be "very damaging" if Australia did not ratify the deal and echoed Senator Farrell's comments: "There is no appetite [in Europe] to revisit this … the deal is done." The deal broadens access to the European market for Australian beef and sheep meat exporters, although not by as much as those industries had hoped.

events.title: Indonesia gets a ‘wake-up call’ as MSCI prepares to remove it from global indexes
events.summary: MSCI said on Oct 16 it would put Indonesia on a path to “standalone” status. MSCI said Indonesia is no longer fit for ‘emerging market’ status and plans to move it to ‘standalone’ status, which could force major fund outflows and cut it from global indexes. The announcement shocked investors, sent Jakarta shares down 11.57% in their worst fall since 1998, and pushed the rupiah to its weakest since late July. Indonesia rejected the move, said it has improved transparency, and the regulator fined market participants over alleged manipulation in three listed firms; MSCI will consult until April 2027. JAKARTA – Indonesia’s stock market is no longer worthy of “emerging market” status, MSCI said on Oct 16 , laying out a plan to expel it from a suite of indexes tracked by funds, a shock move that sparked the steepest one-day drop in Jakarta shares since 1998. Coming a month ahead of a scheduled review, MSCI’s change of tack stunned investors and irked Jakarta officials, with the Indonesian regulator unveiling sanctions against those linked to alleged trading manipulation in shares of three firms. The benchmark stock index, already the world’s worst performers in 2026, closed down 11.57%, in its biggest single-day drop since January 1998 . The rupiah currency slid as much as 0.8% to 18,070 per US dollar, its weakest since late July, but recovered some ground . Equities in South-east Asia’s biggest economy have struggled since January, when MSCI froze Indonesia in its indexes and threatened a downgrade to “frontier” status because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour. The market has lost more than US$350 billion (S$447.77 billion) in capitalisation since, with about US$60 billion wiped out on Oct 16 alone. MSCI cited insufficient reforms to tackle the problems and said even a downgrade to “frontier” status would not reflect the severity of the issues, but proposed instead to move further beyond that, to “standalone” status. “Significant concerns remain around market dysfunction,” MSCI said in a statement on Oct 16. “Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an emerging market no longer appropriate.” The lower “standalone” status it proposed would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by billions of dollars in passive investment, forcing funds that follow, or are ranked against, the indexes, to sell. UBS estimated a removal by MSCI could trigger about US$4 billion of passive outflows from Indonesia, with active investors potentially adding a further US$15 billion in outflow. Foreign investors have already net sold US$4.7 billion worth of Indonesian stocks in 2026. Indonesia’s senior economic minister Airlangga Hartarto said there was “a big question mark” over why MSCI did not discuss downgrading the country to “standalone” status during a meeting this week in Bangkok. He made the comment ahead of a meeting of the country’s top officials, including the finance minister, the governor of the central bank and other related officials to discuss MSCI’s announcement. The Indonesia Stock Exchange said it has taken concrete steps to enhance transparency and integrity in the country’s capital market, and chief executive Jeffrey Hendrik said in a statement he would request further clarification on the basis for the announcement. Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, said the move does not reflect the health of the vast majority of listed companies or indeed the Indonesian economy, and “grouping Indonesia with Lebanon, Palestine and Argentina does not make sense”. “This is a wake-up call for Indonesia,” he said. Indonesia would be the largest economy in the group if it was downgraded to “standalone” status. MSCI scrutiny raises more questions MSCI’s announcement piles pressure on the government under President Prabowo Subianto. It is the latest of a series of setbacks in 2026, with Moody’s and Fitch cutting their sovereign rating outlooks to negative, citing reduced policymaking credibility. “The proposal highlights MSCI’s dissatisfaction with the pace of reforms and raises further questions about the investability of the market,” said Tan Altundag, investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management. “ The investment implications could be significant,” said Altundag, who has no holdings in Indonesia. The office of Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara, who chairs the country’s financial stability board, did not reply to a request for comment. In a sign of investor anxiety over the index provider’s move, there was a rush for the exits when the market opened, triggering a 30-minute trading halt on the Jakarta exchange. “It’s the first time this has ever happened in my 20 years in the stock market,” said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at stockbroker Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia.

events.title: 3M lays out 'attack' on Commonwealth's $2 billion PFAS lawsuit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 3M sheds light on defence to Commonwealth lawsuit over PFAS contamination 3M is being sued by the Australian government for PFAS contamination. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) The Australian government is suing 3M, the manufacturer of a firefighting foam it claims contaminated 28 Defence Force bases across the nation. The US chemical giant has detailed its planned defence to the $2 billion lawsuit. 3M must file its defence by December 11. US chemical giant 3M has shed light on its planned "attack" on the federal government's $2 billion lawsuit, which alleges the company withheld evidence that its firefighting products were toxic to humans and the environment. The Commonwealth is seeking damages arising from per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination at 28 Defence Force bases across Australia and the areas surrounding them. The largest-ever court claim brought by the Australian government alleges the company continued to make and sell aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) until 2003, despite knowing the dangers of its chemical make-up since 1979. The 1,600-page statement of claim says the use of 3M's AFFF "resulted in significant contamination" of land and water, including drinking water, that posed risks to human and animal health and the environment. Citing 310 internal company documents, the federal government's lawyers allege 3M falsely made assurances the product was safe despite having studies that proved variants of PFAS were toxic to animals, could cause birth defects and harmed the environment. During a case management hearing in the Federal Court today, King's Counsel for 3M Phillip Solomon outlined what the defence's case would entail when it was filed to the court on December 11. Mr Solomon KC said a "large team is working hard" and that it would "attack" the case. He told the court that there were three courses of action it would plead to; public nuisance, a Victorian Environment Protection Authority claim, and a misleading and deceptive conduct claim. Mr Solomon said the latter would need to be "delineated" between the overseas manufacturer and the local distributor of 3M products. In its statement of claim, the Commonwealth alleges the company caused a public nuisance by interfering with the use and enjoyment of the environment and by hindering access to contaminant-free water. Justice Catherine Button was told by the defence that the issue of public nuisance was not available in the matter. "We will plead and ultimately contend that it doesn't contend a nuisance claim," Mr Solomon said. "The allegation [is] that we had the means to abate the nuisance, that we caused the nuisance, that we were responsible for the special loss associated with the nuisance … and broadly had the ability to control the nuisance." Williamtown residents in NSW have been exposed to PFAS chemicals from firefighting foam used at the RAAF base. ( Four Corners ) The 28 bases have been split into three categories, including steady state, expanding, and in exceedence of Australian Drinking Water Guidelines and Australian Recreational Guidelines. The Commonwealth has proposed that 3M plead to six "representative bases" that have features across those categories, including Wagga (NSW), Tindal (NT), Townsville (Qld), Oakey (Qld), Edinburgh (SA) and East Sale (Vic). Mr Solomon told Justice Button the defence would be seeking to focus on one of the 28 bases in question, rather than six. In reply, counsel for the Commonwealth Fiona McLeod AO SC said the Crown was "seeking representative bases" that covered issues such as cross-contamination, topography and soil type. Questions over liability and toxicity 3M's AFFF firefighting foam was used by the Australian Defence Force for training and operational activities. ( Supplied: CRC CARE, file ) The Commonwealth is seeking $2 billion to cover "substantial costs" incurred from contaminated land and water. That includes $214 million for investigations, remediation and ongoing monitoring, and $367 million in settlements from five class actions brought against the government. Mr Solomon told the court the case raised questions about allegations of toxicity and whether there was subsequent liability, particularly in instances where remediation had been carried out. The court also heard discussion about the definition of the term "potentially toxic". "[The phrase] "potentially toxic" isn't a legal concept," Mr Solomon told the court. "If [the Crown] mean to tell us that their reliance isn't really on a collection of words but a particular concentration [or] type, they can tell us.

events.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney says US is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has campaigned for national unity as advance voting is underway in oil-rich Alberta in a referendum that could set the province on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada CALGARY, Alberta -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned Thursday that the United States is trying to break Canada so it can “own us” as he urged oil-rich Alberta not to begin a process toward separation in Monday’s referendum. The vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, which has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. “This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” Carney told a large pro-Canada rally in Calgary. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.” He did not directly mention the U.S. or its President Donald Trump in that passage, but has done so in similar past speeches. Carney’s warning came as U.S. President Donald Trump wages a trade war with Canada and after his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney has argued that Canada needs to become more economically resilient and less dependent on the United States. Carney urged Albertans not to use the vote simply to send Ottawa a message, saying a decisive result could settle the separation question. “Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” Carney said. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.” Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent Thursday campaigning in Calgary before addressing the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre. His office estimated about 5,000 people attended, with some waiting more than two hours to get through security. Organizers were also holding a second rally with Carney in Edmonton on Friday. Earlier Thursday, he pointed to the many Albertans who were born or educated elsewhere in Canada and to firefighters who come from across the country to help Alberta during wildfires as examples of the ties binding the province to the rest of Canada. At the rally, Carney also acknowledged the grievances that have fueled alienation in Alberta. “The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” he said. Carney said that while growing up, Ottawa made Albertans feel “like our resources weren’t our own” and that more recently the province was made to feel its energy contributions were “against the tides of history.” The setting is striking for a Liberal prime minister. Alberta has spent decades feuding with Liberal governments in Ottawa, particularly over energy and federal power. But Carney has broken with some of the policies associated with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, fast-tracked a proposed new oil pipeline to the Pacific and called Canada an energy superpower. Carney pointed to the Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of a changed relationship, saying it would create more than 140,000 jobs and generate revenue for social programs. His biggest cheer came when he said the pipeline would reduce Canada’s dependence on the United States. “Careful, they might think that’s election interference. A little touchy,” Carney joked, drawing laughter. He was referring to U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra’s warning to Canadian politicians not to interfere in the U.S. midterm elections. Tanya Clemens, co-chair of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, acknowledged Carney presents a challenge. “He’s formidable for sure,” Clemens told The Associated Press. Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Iran live updates: Trump admin prepares options, including 'mother of all bombs' Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Clemens argued, however, that Carney’s agreements with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith amount to “pinky promises” that do not resolve long-standing grievances with Ottawa. Keith Wilson, another leader of Let Alberta Decide, rejected Carney’s argument that global instability made this the wrong time for the vote. “The worst timing for this, why? I don’t understand what’s the logic,” Wilson said. “Then it’s the best time for him to get back to Ottawa.” Wilson said Carney should ask Parliament to repeal federal measures that separatists say have hurt Alberta, including authority he says could be used to tax oil exports in retaliation against the United States. He predicted Carney would eventually impose such a tax despite Carney saying he sees no value in using Canadian energy exports as leverage against the U.S. “It’s one cabinet meeting away,” Wilson said. “He’s gonna do it. He has to do it.” Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, cast her ballot Wednesday and said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada.

events.title: Crypto operator Solana abruptly cancels Shanghai event after office plan raises eyebrows
events.summary: Company pulls plug after splashy marketing campaign that raised questions given Beijing’s ban on crypto activities Solana, which operates one of the world’s largest cryptocurrencies, has cancelled a high-profile event in Shanghai at the last minute as local police appeared on site, according to social media posts, just a day after the firm touted the opening of a fancy new office in the city. Solana was slated to host its Solana Accelerate China event in Shanghai on Friday morning, part of a week-long event across major cities in mainland China. Shortly before the event kicked off, however, the company said in an email update to attendees that the programme had to be “postponed” due to “last-minute logistical considerations”, according to screenshots circulating on social media. Social media posts also indicated that a few local police officers showed up at the event venue. Solana did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The abrupt suspension of the event followed a splashy marketing campaign in the city earlier this week, which raised questions about how the company was able to do so amid Beijing’s strict ban on crypto-related business activities.

events.title: Leaving portfolio decisions to the professionals
events.summary: Investors have more information at their fingertips than ever, but deciding what to do with it can still take time and judgement. HSBC Portfolio+ gives retail banking customers access to professionally managed portfolios, an approach traditionally more closely associated with wealthier investors, through its mobile app. [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] For anyone with a smartphone, market information is rarely far away. Market prices, company news, economic data and analysis can all be pulled up in just seconds. But access to information does not necessarily make the next investment decision any easier. It is a dilemma many investors will recognise. Research may be readily available, but deciding how much to invest, where to allocate it, when to make changes and whether market movements warrant action still requires judgement. The challenge does not end once investments have been selected. Portfolios need to be monitored over time. A strong run in one market can leave an investor more exposed to that market than originally intended, while changes in interest rates, valuations or economic conditions may also affect how different assets are allocated. For a keen investor, following those movements may be part of the appeal. But for someone juggling work, family and other commitments, managing a portfolio can start to feel like another item on an already crowded to-do list. Recently launched in Hong Kong, the digital discretionary portfolio management service allows retail banking customers to have a portfolio managed by HSBC investment professionals according to their investment objectives and risk tolerance. HSBC is also the first retail bank in Hong Kong to offer a discretionary portfolio management service to retail banking customers. Under discretionary portfolio management, the investor sets parameters such as objectives and risk appetite, while investment professionals make ongoing portfolio decisions within those parameters. With Portfolio+, HSBC portfolio managers construct the portfolios, monitor them and rebalance allocations when required, including executing transactions where necessary to keep the portfolio broadly aligned with its intended strategy and risk profile. This means investors do not have to decide for themselves whether every market movement calls for a change. Starting with what the money is for Investors may have very different reasons for putting their money to work. Some may be investing mainly for longer-term capital growth. Others may be seeking income, while sustainability considerations may influence how some investors want their money allocated. HSBC Portfolio+ offers three core strategies: Growth, Enhanced Income and Sustainable. Investors can also select Future Trends as an optional add-on for exposure to opportunities in innovation-led sectors. Different strategies can be combined into separate portfolios according to an investor’s preferences and objectives, while personalised names can be assigned to make individual portfolios easier to distinguish. Delegating decisions without losing visibility Handing over day-to-day portfolio management can make visibility just as important as professional oversight. HSCB Portfolio+ provides a look-through of holdings within individual portfolios as well as across all of an investor’s portfolios, with allocations available by region, sector and company. Market commentary from HSBC portfolio managers and shorter market insights can also be accessed through the app. That distinction is important for investors who want professional management but still want to understand where their money has been allocated. The service therefore separates two activities that are often treated as the same thing: keeping informed and making every investment decision personally. An investor can still follow markets, read commentary and see what is held in the portfolio without having to decide whether each development calls for a trade or a change in asset allocation. Professional management through an app Discretionary portfolio management has traditionally been more closely associated with wealthier investors receiving personalised investment services, partly because the cost and complexity of ongoing portfolio management made it difficult to offer at retail scale. Digital wealth infrastructure is making that model accessible to retail investors. Capabilities such as digital onboarding, data-driven investor profiling, automatic portfolio rebalancing and fractional ETF investing can make professionally managed portfolios available to a larger group of customers. HSBC Portfolio+ applies those capabilities through HSBC’s mobile app, enabling retail banking customers to access professionally managed portfolios. HSBC is currently offering a HK$0 platform fee for Portfolio+ until 1 January 2027.

events.title: El-Sayed pushes back at Republicans who judge him because he ‘might pray differently’
events.summary: The News MARQUETTE, Mich. — Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Thursday night accused President Donald Trump and Republican rival Mike Rogers of using his Muslim faith as a political cudgel. “Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who’s ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution,” El-Sayed said in response to a question from Semafor. Republicans have recently amplified claims that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Trump posted a video Thursday night that directly called El-Sayed a member of the group, which was founded in Egypt; his administration has designated chapters as terrorist organizations. El-Sayed, an American of Egyptian descent who would be the first Muslim senator if elected, has rankled at the GOP accusations, including in a recent TV interview . His comments on Thursday are as close as he has come on the campaign trail to alleging Islamophobia by his opponents. “They don’t want to talk about any of the other issues that people are actually experiencing in their lives. They want to talk about me or point to my mom or my sister,” El-Sayed said. “My mom and my sister are not running for office. I’m running for office.” El-Sayed called it “an insane thing to assume” that members of his family were part of the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he didn’t “know what my mother was doing in Egypt in the 1970s.” Republicans have cited social media posts from his half-sister that appear to refer to his mother’s engagement with the group. “My parents got divorced when I was very young — 3,” El-Sayed said. “I didn’t see my mom for years after I was raised by my dad and my stepmom, and when I asked, [to] the best of my knowledge, nobody in my family’s been a member of this organization.” Know More El-Sayed said insinuating he might not be loyal to the Constitution because of his faith was “the same thing that was done to JFK when they tried to say that, ‘Oh, well, he’s going to answer to the Pope because he’s Catholic.’ Same thing they tried to do to President Obama.” John F. Kennedy, the first Roman Catholic president, faced some false accusations of “dual loyalties” because of his faith. And the hard right pushed conspiracy theories about the religious practices of Obama, who is a Christian and was the first Black president. El-Sayed was campaigning in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula this week as part of a swing with progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. El-Sayed and Democrats are hoping they can grow the electorate in what has traditionally been redder territory in the state. Notable A Washington Post analysis found that rhetoric about El-Sayed from right-wing social media users has increasingly focused on his faith since his Michigan primary win this summer.

events.title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.” Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion. “This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.” Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph acceleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car. All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour. Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.” Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels. Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket. Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster. “If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year . Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said. “This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’” Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in “The Spy Who Loved Me” — a car Musk owns , which was on display at the event. In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet. “Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote. Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions. Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …” But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan.

events.title: White House’s AI task force gets to work
events.summary: The White House’s AI task force has formally adopted its charter, kicking off the short 120-day window it’s been given to answer some extremely thorny questions about how the government should handle the rapid development of AI technology. According to an announcement shared first with Semafor, the task force agreed after its first official meeting Thursday to commission a report from the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology to evaluate AI risk in three areas: cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and model control and accountability. “Throughout its work, the [task force] will engage with frontier model developers and other SI companies, consumer protection groups, and civil liberties advocates, industry stakeholders, and federal and state law enforcement agencies to inform and implement its efforts,” a White House official said in a statement. “The [Super Intelligence Force] stands ready to ensure implementation of the Accord and continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people.” It also agreed to make a working group tasked with implementing the White House Accord on Super Intelligence that major AI CEOs signed this month, a process led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the task force’s chair, along with National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. Defense Undersecretary Emil Michael, a task force vice chair, will lead an effort to develop protocols for labs to tell the government about breaches, hacks and other cyber issues. Michael is also in charge of interfacing with frontier AI labs and figuring out long-term coordination on AI across the government. The task force also agreed to create a “law enforcement and consumer protection coordination committee” including the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, led by FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, also a vice chair. The last vice chair, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, will work with the public and private sector on critical infrastructure protection, and will work with the Department of Labor on studying the impact of AI on the American workforce and economy. Members of the task force beyond the chairs include: Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, plus Cairncross, Chris Klomp, the nominee to be the No. 2 at the Department of Health and Human Services, Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano, and National Security Agency Director Joshua Rudd, along with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her deputy, Richard Walters. It’s not yet entirely clear how compliance with the task force will be enforced or how current law may apply to companies who don’t adhere to the new protocols. A White House official told Semafor one stick could be export controls, which the Commerce Department at one point temporarily imposed on Anthropic after the company refused to grant the government unfettered access to its models.

events.title: 'Canary in the coalmine' for a major Wall Street collapse, analysts warn
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Investors brace for big tech collapse as debt levels soar Investors are increasingly concerned the cost of the debt is growing too much for the big tech firms to service. ( Reuters: Brendan McDermid ) The cost of insuring against a debt default by Wall Street's tech titans has hit record levels. Neocloud company CoreWeave is among the most expensive to insure against. Analysts view the firm as the "canary in the coalmine" for the artificial intelligence boom more broadly. The cost of insuring against a big technology firm defaulting on its debt has soared to record highs. These contracts are known as credit default swaps. Heavily indebted data centre operator CoreWeave has been among the hardest hit. Investors who lent the company money are now paying a lot to buy these credit default swaps to insure against losing their investments if the company defaults. The so-called neocloud company has taken on more than $US50 billion ($72 billion) in debt. The yield on CoreWeave bonds maturing in 2031 has hit 15.78 per cent. This week, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps soared 16 per cent to a record 1.14 per cent, before easing slightly to 1.03 per cent. Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu said the record highs in tech credit default swaps were an extension of CoreWeave's spreads blowing past 1 per cent. "[It] has revived worries about how the AI build-out is being financed," Ms Wu said. Wall Street's big tech firms are increasingly turning to debt and private credit financing, having exhausted options to raise money in the share market. But elevated global inflation is putting upward pressure on interest rates, which is increasing the cost of this debt. Competition for debt from governments and other big tech firms is also increasing interest rates, and the cost of servicing this debt. Investors are increasingly concerned that debt costs are rising too much for big tech firms to service, and they are buying insurance to prevent harmful financial losses. Ms Wu conceded financial markets were growing more anxious about these mammoth companies' financial health. "Nvidia's Jensen Huang defended CoreWeave in Stockholm yesterday, saying its cost of capital is falling and it needs no Nvidia backstop, but I think investor sentiment on tech is fragile after the chip sell-off, so this is more sentiment than fundamentals for now," she said. Elsewhere in the market cloud ⁠computing giant Oracle has seen its credit default swaps rise 0.3 per cent this week, while costs to insure against debt defaults for Nvidia, STMicroelectronics and SpaceX also rose sharply. Credit default swap ⁠spreads for Amazon, Alphabet and Meta also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave. Jensen Huang has defended CoreWeave's debt levels, saying its cost of capital is falling. ( Reuters: Evan Vucci ) "This is not the first time we've had a sizeable market wobble on the back of AI fears, ⁠but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said. "AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges." The US is experiencing a 'boomcession'. Is Australia, too? Wall Street risk signal flashing red Credit default swaps for US big tech companies are soaring to record highs. It means investors are fearful of a major Wall Street company collapse. events.title: Trump names scapegoats as Republicans sweat in Texas
events.summary: President Trump is preemptively blaming Sen. John Cornyn and Karl Rove for "doing everything possible to make it hard for Ken Paxton " to win the Texas Senate race. Why it matters: The president is publicly spinning what would be a disaster for Republicans on election night. Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. "If Ken Paxton loses , it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove," Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump won Texas by 14 points just two years ago. What to watch: Trump's post comes the same day FEC campaign finance reports confirmed Elon Musk's efforts to help Paxton across the finish line. Musk gave $158 million to the Senate GOP's main super PAC in September over two transactions, as Axios reported Thursday morning . The day after each Musk donation , SLF made an equal-sized transfer to a Texas PAC— a pop-up super PAC dedicated to electing Paxton. The big picture: A new poll this week in Texas showed Democrat James Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton, 50% to 47%. Republican leaders warned Trump for months that if Paxton won the primary against Cornyn it would be cost the party far more to keep the seat. Those predictions are proving true, with more than $500 million in ad spending already flowing into the Texas Senate race, according to AdImpact. "Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs," Cornyn told Semafor earlier in October after audio leaked from a Paxton event in D.C. The other side: Talarico is getting pummeled with some of that money, but he's far from defenseless. He was already on the air in August, when Paxton and Republicans were still figuring out their game plan — and who would foot the bill. Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter off an army of small donors. His campaign said 97% of contributions were under $100. Talarico's fundraising prowess allowed him to raise hard dollars, which command lower ad rates. "Oh my god, holy crap, I saw Talarico," Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said on Thursday. "I don't even know how you raised $64 million in a quarter. I mean, that's a number that's mind-blowing." Paxton brought in $18 million.

events.title: Basel Committee finalises measures to address window-dressing in the G-SIB framework and consults on G-SIB methodology review
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) The Basel Committee has published amendments to address window-dressing behaviour in the framework for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). Banks will be required to report and disclose indicators used to calculate G-SIB scores based on average values over the reporting year, rather than year-end values, by January 2030. The Committee consults on whether to incorporate its previously agreed treatment of cross-border exposures within the European Banking Union (EBU) into the methodology. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision today published final amendments to address window dressing in the G-SIB framework and a consultation on the G-SIB methodology review. "Window dressing" seeks to temporarily reduce banks' perceived systemic footprint around the reference dates used for the reporting and public disclosure of G-SIB scores . As noted previously by the Committee, window-dressing by banks is unacceptable. Such behaviour undermines the intended policy objectives of the Committee's standards and risks disrupting the operations of financial markets. The amendments aim at constraining banks' ability to lower their G-SIB scores through window-dressing. This will be achieved by requiring banks participating in the G-SIB assessment exercise to report and disclose all stock G-SIB indicators based on an average of values over the reporting year, rather than year-end values. To provide sufficient time for banks to develop a robust and comprehensive reporting process, the revised standard will be implemented by 1 January 2030. In addition, the Committee has agreed to increase the G-SIB reporting and disclosure threshold from EUR 200 billion to EUR 350 billion in leverage ratio exposure measure, to be implemented from 2027. Separately, as part of the Committee's periodic review of the G-SIB assessment methodology , the Committee is consulting on whether to incorporate the treatment of cross-border exposures within the EBU in the G-SIB framework. The Committee welcomes comments on all aspects of the consultation from stakeholders. Comments should be submitted here by 14 January 2027 .

events.title: GOP senator: Cancel Thanksgiving recess if we lose
events.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno wants his fellow Republicans to cancel their holiday plans and jam through "everything that we could possibly get" if they lose the majorities in November's midterms. Why it matters: Republicans couldn't muster the votes for a megabill this summer, and leadership is not confident they can now. But Moreno (R-Ohio) is calling for the GOP to make a bigger push in the event of losing power. "We will do a reconciliation bill, one way or the other," Moreno — who said it is "more likely" the GOP holds the Senate — told reporters outside the Capitol on Thursday. But if Republicans lose: "It'll be the 'Last Supper.' So it'll be a giant reconciliation bill where we take all the Republican priorities that we can get done." "If we lose the House and the Senate, we should be here from Nov. 9 until Dec. 31 with no break at all," he said. "Like, we'll have turkeys here for Thanksgiving." Zoom in: Conversations have been ongoing in congressional offices about what a reconciliation package might look like in the lame-duck session between the election and the new Congress next year, a source familiar with the matter tells Axios. "We are working with the House and White House to develop what all is included to be able to sell to the public and our Republican colleagues when we return," Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), chair of the Budget Committee, told Axios. Election outcomes won't substantively change much for frequent holdouts like Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) who are on their way out. That's not to mention Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), who are appropriators and known to break from the party. What to watch: Republicans face a long to-do list in the lame-duck, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and raising the debt ceiling. Those could all be considered part of a massive reconciliation package that requires just a majority vote to pass. But not everything qualifies for the reconciliation process — and big bills can cause big headaches. Other to-do items include: Passing the National Defense Authorization Act Reauthorizing FISA Section 702, the warrantless wiretap authority Passing the farm bill Passing permitting reform Confirming nominations Between the lines : Some of the administration's top priorities are banking on the partisan-led funding maneuver of reconciliation, including Trump's sprawling Golden Dome missile defense system, autonomous weapon advancement efforts and upgrades to the F-35 fighter jet. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told attendees at an Army conference on Wednesday the Pentagon needs "a minimum" of $350 billion to "rebuild the military." The intrigue: If Republicans lose their Senate majority, it will almost certainly be Moreno's job to try to win it back. He is running for National Republican Senatorial Committee chair — so far, unopposed. Axios Defense reporter Thomas Novelly contributed to this story.

Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence. Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March. Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days. “From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.” The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.” Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said. Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much. “I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter. Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million . Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
events.summary: The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered to take action over odours Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem. For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill. "When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump. While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day". Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology. The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells. Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts." The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality. Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory. When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells. In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue. Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance. This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks. "You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world. Bad smells from waste sites are among the most difficult to resolve The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away. Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells. But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers. Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner. Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says. In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city. A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits. "Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume." The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus. The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns. This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?

events.title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
events.summary: Jess says returning online purchases is less hassle than shopping in person Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online. As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says. "The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough. Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on". And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection". Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22. But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain . Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases. The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes. Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein. Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic. Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019. Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town." 'I basically never go into clothes shops' Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online. "I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says. "I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important." Julia does most of her shopping online, but likes going into book stores Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted. The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces." Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically. "I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed." The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule. Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale". However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete. "Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks. "When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time." But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns. This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor". "Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."
