events.title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
events.summary: Challenge now is to safeguard UK economy's resilience, says chancellor The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey. Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction. It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week. Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time. Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will". But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending". The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August. "It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said. The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain". Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply. The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted. Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period. But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period. August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%. Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought". He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs". PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance. "The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added. What's happening to the UK economy and how does it affect you? Published 2 days ago What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 1 day ago Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register". He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents. The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations. Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks." The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget". Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing." He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate". "The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet." Healey went on to say the Budget would be tough and not include inflation top-ups for public sector pay. Some experts and unions have called for extra cash for some departmental budgets, to account for the rising costs of providing public services and pay.

events.title: The AI boom's next bottleneck is money, not chips
events.summary: Liz’s view The bottleneck in the AI boom was chips, then power, then memory. It’s about to become money. That might sound strange as Anthropic prepares for a $1 trillion-plus IPO and data centers keep sprouting like big-box poppies. But the fear and exasperation among the lenders whose money fuels this game sharpened noticeably over the past week. It’s not just the days-long chip selloff that’s messing with global markets. “There’s shortages in chips. There’s shortages in power. And soon, there will be shortages of capital,” the CEO of Singapore’s biggest bank, DBS, warned Semafor’s Shelly Banjo in Bangkok this week. “We’re not an ATM for your dystopian future,” a major financier of data centers told me yesterday. Rest assured, he would happily play the part if the risk-return math made sense, but it doesn’t. Good luck enforcing Potemkin guarantees from hyperscalers or arguing that local protests excuse a construction delay that blew a hole in the financing. Investors get scared the same way moguls go bankrupt, gradually, then quickly. You see it in deals like Volta’s $5 billion Norwegian data center, which months ago would have been waved through by investors now demanding tougher terms . You see it in CoreWeave’s tanking bonds. You see it in the cost of a policy to protect against SpaceX defaulting on its debt, which goes for 80% more than it did three months ago. And in the early price talk for the rocket company’s $40 billion loan being marketed this week, which I’m told is around 1 percentage point higher than its existing bonds. To quote Elon Musk himself: Yikes. Yes, OpenAI will have no trouble raising the $30 billion it’s looking for and equity markets will probably recover from this week’s chip selloff. But it’s worth remembering that telecom bonds began cracking six months before the dot-com crash. In 2007, subprime mortgage bonds peaked eight months before the S&P 500 did. Equity investors get paid to be dreamers. Lenders get paid not to lose money. Notable For now, spending on the AI remains strong: Goldman Sachs expects AI infrastructure investment to drive a $7.6 trillion boom through 2031 .

events.title: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Starlink satellite services are restored
events.summary: Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield satellite services — critical tools in its war against Russia that were unexpectedly throttled this week — have been restored to full capacity, a Ukrainian official tells Axios. The official also said that Ukraine conducted a strike overnight against a Russian oil refinery — defying President Trump's demand that it stop hitting those facilities. Why it matters: The twin developments further strained the U.S.-Ukraine relationship, as the war with Russia drags on and the Trump administration sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week by lifting sanctions on Russian oil sales. State of play: The move angered Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelensky responded by calling it "a weak decision" and a "gift to Putin." Trump then called for Ukraine to elect a new president. The crisis intensified this week when Elon Musk's SpaceX restricted service of Starlink — a satellite service used for defensive purposes in battle — while Starshield, a tool used for offensive war operations that is controlled by the U.S. government, was also slowed. After more than a day, the services were restored. Ukraine, meanwhile, fired on a Russian oil refinery, which U.S. officials are unlikely to look kindly upon. The Ukrainian official said the country resumed strikes because Russia continued to hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure, despite Trump announcing that the two sides had agreed to a ceasefire. That ceasefire declaration came as a surprise to Zelensky. The bottom line: It's still unclear to many inside the Trump administration and the Ukrainian government whether Trump ordered the satellite restrictions.

events.title: The EU's methane rule pause may not help energy prices
events.summary: The EU’s decision to delay the implementation of its methane regulations won’t help consumers much, environmental groups argued. European officials decided this week to delay the regulation — which was meant to come into effect in January 2027 to introduce stronger reporting requirements for energy companies’ methane emissions — after facing pressure from industry stakeholders and French leadership , who argued it would further drive up energy prices. However, a Carbon Limits report found that compliance would cost between 0.03-0.6% of production value. “We’re not saying [the regulation] has no impact [on prices]. We’re saying that it is not driving any of these massive [cost] burdens you’re seeing, and therefore can’t solve [them] either,” Léa Pilsner, the Environmental Defense Fund’s energy policy director, told Semafor. The legislation also shifts the deadline for setting intensity standards for methane emissions from imported fuel, “which is really where you start seeing the benefits when it comes to the climate,” she added. — Eugenia Perozo

events.title: Fossilflation is a permanent risk to the US
events.summary: Tim’s view Fossil fuels are an economic liability, and not just because of the war in Iran. Rising energy costs were a major driver of the hotter-than-expected US inflation figures reported yesterday. This fact won’t surprise anyone reading this newsletter. Still, the numbers are pretty astonishing: Behind an overall gain of 3.7% across all goods and services in the past 12 months, gasoline prices are up 34.2%, and fuel oil prices (relevant mostly for home heating) are up 74.2%. The proximal cause is the war, of course, and the figures cement that US President Donald Trump has by now run out of time to change the picture ahead of the midterm election. But the broader takeaway here is that the inherent volatility of oil and gas prices is a persistent vulnerability in the US economy that can only be solved by limiting exposure to these energy sources. Many politicians before Trump have seen their domestic economic agenda undermined by global fossil fuel price dynamics largely outside their control — an effect European Central Bank official Isabel Schnabel dubbed “fossilflation.” The best evidence of the benefits of a less oil-reliant economy is that inflation isn’t even higher now; during the US oil crises of the 1970s, when cars were less efficient and oil was far more widely used in power and other sectors, Consumer Price Index inflation surged well above 10% . Domestic drilling has put more of the supply-demand balance under US control, but can’t shield American consumers from global price turmoil. The transition to non-fossil energy has its own inflationary impacts, from the costs to heavy industry of adopting new technologies to the production costs of critical minerals. If the Fed chooses to raise interest rates to tamp today’s inflation down, capital-intensive renewables will suffer. But from an economic standpoint, the best thing about replacing oil and gas with non-fossil electric alternatives is that the energy they produce, in addition to being cheap (although not always to consumers’ benefit, as we discuss below), can be predictably priced. A world with very boring energy prices would be one in which inflation is significantly more divorced from geopolitics. Notable The US is considering lifting sanctions on shadow fleet vessels — which have commonly been used to transport sanctioned oil from producers such as Iran, Russia and Venezuela— to ease record high freight rates , a US official said yesterday.

events.title: As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
events.summary: If AI systems have been humming along nicely for weeks or months at a stretch, will the human overseeing them be able to take over when things go wrong? Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome. But does the employee know how to do the task? I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise. AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening. The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not. What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed. Human in the loop explained. The success paradox The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does. This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work. More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ ironies of automation ”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem. This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization. What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult. The accountability problem Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control. This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility and capability can begin to separate. Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem. The measurement problem Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity . Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps. But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment. The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them. The governance problem Organizational governance – defining roles and responsibilities – is also under pressure from AI. Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time . There is nothing inherently wrong with that change. The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today? In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic. Maintaining the human backstop Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained. Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed. As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. events.title: India becomes increasingly vital to Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala amid global fragmentation
events.summary: Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala sees India as increasingly vital in the emerging world order. Global fragmentation is “a new normal for the next five, 10, or 15 years,” Deputy Group CEO Waleed Al Muhairi said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi this week. That conviction is guiding the $385 billion Abu Dhabi fund on its investment decisions. India is “increasingly important for our capital,” Al Muhairi said, citing its market size and “massive infrastructure program” that is driving tens of billions of dollars of investment into the world’s most populous country. Asia-Pacific is still a small share of Mubadala’s portfolio, making up 13% of its holdings, against 44% for North America. But Abu Dhabi’s ties with New Delhi are already deep: UAE-India trade topped $100 billion for a second straight year in the 12 months to March and the two countries are looking to double that figure by 2032. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Is the world pricing the risk of a US diesel export ban?
events.summary: One driver of higher U.S. diesel prices is a major drop in supply from Russia and the Middle East. AP Photo/David Zalubowski) A spike in diesel prices is hammering broad sectors of the U.S. economy – especially agriculture and shipping – and becoming a flash point ahead of the November 2026 midterm elections . This squeeze has prompted Republicans from hard-hit farm states to call for a ban on U.S. diesel exports, with President Donald Trump reportedly weighing the idea as well. He also announced a deal on Oct. 9 to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets. Meanwhile, the G7 countries have agreed to release an additional 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from their emergency reserves . What would happen if the U.S. did enact an export ban? It’s a net exporter of petroleum products, so such a move would split the U.S. and world markets for diesel. The resulting mismatch between domestic demand and supply could depress U.S. diesel prices in the short term. This would give some relief to American consumers, at least temporarily. But as a professor of finance who studies commodities and market volatility, I also see a big adverse shock hitting the rest of the world under that scenario. The current political response to pricey diesel, however, shouldn’t be a surprise. A recent paper of mine, co-authored with two other economists, asks more broadly when governments are more inclined to restrict commodity exports. We found that export bans are more likely when prices are high and when politicians start weighing the preferences of commodity users , like consumers, over those of commodity producers, like the oil industry. This could be what’s happening right now, amid record energy prices and just a few weeks from Election Day. A global supply squeeze Diesel prices are hovering near all-time highs. The Energy Information Administration reports that the average price of the U.S. benchmark, known as ultra-low sulfur diesel, has topped US$7 per gallon in some regions like the West Coast. Soaring energy prices are also continuing to push U.S. inflation up more broadly. Consumer prices in September jumped year-on-year by a higher-than-expected 3.7% , with gas prices responsible for more than half of the most recent monthly increase. How did this happen? Before the conflict with Iran erupted in February 2026, key diesel exporters included Russia, Middle Eastern producers, the United States and China. Since then, those first two export sources have withered . Russia, now in the fifth year of its war against Ukraine, banned diesel exports in July 2026 after Ukraine launched an effective air campaign that has knocked out more than half of Russia’s oil refinery capacity and destroyed many diesel storage-tank farms. That retaliatory campaign has pushed Russia from being a top diesel exporter to importing refined oil products , including diesel. The price of transporting oil has more than quintupled, as tanker owners charge record fees to travel through the Strait of Hormuz, hiking up the price of diesel. Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA via AP Meanwhile, in the Middle East, crude oil prices surged following missile attacks against Iran at the end of February . The Strait of Hormuz, which was the transit route for more than one-fifth of the global crude oil and natural gas output, essentially shut down amid fears over Iran targeting commercial ships sailing through. Since then, increased shipments through Saudi and Emirati pipelines and actions by the U.S. Navy in the strait have helped restart petroleum flows. But the threat to Hormuz shipping remains real, as seen by recent strikes by Iranian forces on multiple tankers in early October. These shocks have changed the economics of petroleum shipments in two ways. First, the price of transporting oil has more than quintupled , as tanker owners charge record fees to travel through the strait. Those fees, of course, bleed into the price that diesel buyers pay. Second, in the strait, the content of tanker cargo has changed. Many ships are now loaded with crude oil, rather than diesel , after Iranian strikes on Gulf countries earlier this year knocked out a substantial share of the Middle Eastern refining capacity. Insofar as there isn’t much additional refinery capacity elsewhere in the world, even these restored crude oil flows can’t bring diesel prices down to prewar levels. What an export ban would look like The effects of removing Russian and Middle Eastern diesel from the market are being felt worldwide. One result is that U.S. diesel exports to the rest of the world have surged due to heightened foreign demand for the product and the high prices it can fetch abroad. Those export flows have been accompanied by the diesel price spike at home. That jump in domestic prices is what’s driving discussions of a possible ban on U.S. diesel exports, and it reflects a dynamic that my co-authors and I laid out in our study of commodity export restrictions and bans. While we focused on agricultural markets, our findings also apply to the current diesel crunch. Governments of commodity-exporting countries typically balance the interests of commodity producers and exporters, who prefer high prices, against those of domestic consumers, who like lower prices. When consumers’ wishes matter relatively more – for example, as elections approach – the likelihood of a ban rises. American consumers never like high energy prices. Nowadays, after years of elevated inflation, they seem especially unhappy about them. Until the Iran war, Trump had been able to tout a substantial fall in petroleum product prices after he returned to office in January 2025. That’s no longer the case. Higher diesel prices are being felt across the economy . The fuel is used to heat homes, especially in the Northeast, and to power machinery, tractors, trucks, boats and trains. This is why farmers and transportation operators are especially hard hit. Furthermore, these businesses typically try to pass their cost increases on to their customers. So shoppers are shelling out more for groceries and any other goods that must be transported. Under the scenario of an export ban, the cost of U.S. diesel might fall in the short run, but world prices would spike. Soaring prices, however, would not be the only issue for the rest of the world. Our research shows that a major exporting country’s ban would also increase market uncertainty and volatility . This is because restricting exports would effectively concentrate the rest of the world’s production, making the remaining supply base more fragile and increasing the rest of the world’s exposure to any subsequent output shocks. If other countries think that their diesel situation is already bad, it would be much worse under a U.S. export ban. And the G7 move to release more diesel into the global market indicates that the rest of the world might understand how U.S. politics could lead to that outcome. Michel Robe does not work for, consu

Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists.  The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. The results are a big milestone. But the team still needs to establish whether the approach could work for humans. Dissect what the breakthrough means for organ transplantation . —Jessica Hamzelou How much more can nuclear power plants give? In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about the nuclear industry trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. On October 5, the Department of Energy awarded Vistra a $4.2 billion loan to upgrade three plants. Pushing existing reactors to produce more could quickly provide more clean power for data centers. events.title: Taiwan chipmaker TSMC explores Texas investment to expand production in the US
events.summary: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. is exploring potential investments in Texas to expand chip production in the U.S. The company says it is open to collaborating with Elon Musk’s planned “Terafab” chip manufacturing complex in Texas HONG KONG -- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. is exploring potential investments in Texas to expand its chip production in the United States, the advanced chipmaker said after posting another record profit on strong artificial intelligence demand. TSMC said during an earnings conference Thursday that it is open to collaborating with Elon Musk’s planned “Terafab” chip manufacturing complex in Texas. TSMC, which produces over 90% of the world's most cutting-edge chips, supplies to U.S. technology giants include Nvidia and Apple and has pledged $265 billion of investments in building plants in Arizona, including $100 billion the company committed in July. The company's earnings results are seen as a barometer for the world's AI development during a global scale-up in AI computing power. For the July-September quarter, the chipmaker reported a record 763.1 billion new Taiwan dollars (nearly $24 billion) in net profit, which was better than expected and up 69% from the year before. Revenue for the quarter was at 1.49 trillion new Taiwan dollars ($46 billion), up 51% year-on-year. “The AI market continues to be very strong,” C.C. Wei, chairman and CEO of TSMC, said during Thursday's conference. “The demand, actually, is still far above our capability today to supply, and we’re working very hard to narrow the gap.” TSMC is working hard to expand in response to requests from most of its large U.S. customers to increase capacity, Wei said. The chipmaker based in Hsinchu, Taiwan, recently has explored expanding its capacity outside of Arizona and Texas is among the options under consideration, he said, confirming earlier media reports. “We sent the teams to Texas to do all the evaluation,” Wei said, adding that the plan is still under deliberation. Musk confirmed on X earlier this month that there have been discussions with TSMC over its potential role in Terafab, but he also said “we will build and run the fab,” referring to chip fabrication facilities, and TSMC at most would be subleasing part of the Terafab. TSMC has said it has an annual capital expenditure budget of $60 billion to $64 billion for this year, up from its previous estimate earlier this year of $52 billion to $56 billion. Spending between 2026 and 2028 will be significantly higher than the past three years, TSMC Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang said during the earnings call. But TSMC, one of the world’s most valuable public companies, also cautioned there will be macroeconomic challenges. “Looking ahead, we continue to observe consumer and price-sensitive end market segments are being challenged due to the impact of rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainties,” Wei said. “As such, we have been prudent in our business planning going into 2027.” Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
events.summary: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic has been drumming up support for its expected stock market listing as it seeks to reassure investors of its profit-making potential. Anthropic revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands. In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on tech. It also emphasised safety at its event after warnings by current and former researchers of serious and even existential risks to humanity posed by AI. Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period. The company also told investors during the event at its headquarters in San Francisco that it had made a third quarter profit on an adjusted basis, an accounting method which ignores non-recurring costs. Investors reportedly left the Anthropic investor event optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability. Alongside concerns about profit generation, there have also been fears about the safety of AI models. Anthropic has been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down . In September one of its researchers warned of a greater than 10% chance that AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade , and a former researcher said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity . The firm itself said in September it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons . However, US President Donald Trump has said researchers have been " bringing up things that won't happen " and that in a race between the US and China to develop the technology, "whoever wins AI, wins". Rival tech firm OpenAI has also warned about safety, with its chief executive Sam Altman saying in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns. The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn. Stocks in some US technology companies dropped on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI. In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank were down by more than 9% on Thursday. South Korean semiconductor giants also dropped, with Samsung falling by 9.5% and SK Hynix 11% lower. Tan said at a conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino". The falls deepened after US inflation data released on Wednesday showed price rises accelerated by more than expected in September. events.title: Heavy rain shuts down Istanbul, causing flooding and 3 deaths
events.summary: A heavy downpour has shut down Istanbul, flooded homes and roads and killed at least three people ISTANBUL -- A heavy downpour has shut down Istanbul, flooded homes and roads and killed at least three people, officials said Thursday, as rescuers worked overnight to save hundreds of people stranded at their workplaces. The downpour Wednesday night flooded homes and businesses and inundated roads and underpasses, stranding vehicles and causing traffic chaos in Turkey’s largest city. The Istanbul governor's office on Thursday reported three deaths in the city and said four other people were reported missing. A 14-year-old was electrocuted after stepping in a puddle at a park in the Fatih district, and a 34-year-old slipped on a sidewalk in the Sariyer district and hit their head, local media reports said. The governor's office said the body of a third victim was discovered near another park in the Kagithane district. Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci said that more than 2,700 people who were stranded by the floods were safely evacuated throughout the city. The Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality said that some areas had the highest amount of rain since 1985. events.title: Traders sour on AI stocks despite bumper third-quarter revenues
events.summary: Bumper earnings from bellwether tech giants Anthropic and TSMC did little to assuage a market that has turned bearish on the AI trade, sending stocks plummeting. events.title: US venture firm picks Doha for first office outside Bay Area
events.summary: The News US venture capital firm Activate Capital will open its first office outside the US in Doha as Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund expands its effort to make the country a hub for tech and startup investors through its $3 billion Fund of Funds platform. Qatar Investment Authority (QIA) put in an undisclosed sum to become a limited partner in Activate as part of the deal, and will help the San Francisco-based growth equity firm bring some of its portfolio companies into the region. Those businesses work in areas like energy, space, supply chain resilience, and climate adaptation. Activate is the 13th venture firm to become part of QIA’s program in Doha joining other venture investors including B Capital, Founders Circle, and Liberty City Ventures. Qatar has also used partnerships with QIA as a way to attract firms including JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs to build up operations in the country. Know More QIA’s move to back venture firms taking risks on startups represents a small fraction of the $580 billion fund, but is part of a broader strategy to develop the local economy, and get access to emerging managers with the potential to deliver outsize returns. Its long-term goal is to build up a venture capital and entrepreneurial scene in Doha that helps the country generate more value from research and innovation. “It’s a commercially driven program. We’re in the business of making money here,” QIA’s head of funds Mohsin Pirzada told Semafor. Managers are also held to development goals tied to Qatar’s national strategy, he added. The program’s aim is to bring venture firms, their portfolio companies, and their know-how to Doha. Managers must staff a local office with senior investment professionals. QIA encourages them to relocate the startups they back, offering those companies incentives like compute power once they open shop in Qatar. Pirzada also pitched Doha as a gateway market: “a four-hour flight that captures a population of 2 billion.” Talks with QIA began about a year ago, said Anup Jacob, Activate’s co-founder and managing partner. Despite the breakout of the Iran war, decision-making stayed on schedule. “In any normal massive disruption that we’ve had in our lifetimes … business as usual just stops, and we did not find that here,” Jacob said. Activate’s backers requested the Doha office invest from the same pool of capital rather than a separate regional vehicle, according to Jacob. Its Doha team will look for deals in Qatar and across the Global South, and will steer portfolio companies toward the region’s “much cheaper energy and much better access to compute,” Jacob said. Being backed by QIA also helps Activate access competitive deals, he said. Jacob described a CEO with an oversubscribed round who asked, “Why should I let you into my round?” Without backers like QIA, “our capital is just capital.” There’s still a learning curve for fund managers coming from abroad, according to Haya Al Ghanim, Qatar funds director at QIA. The most frequently asked question, she said, is about the dress code. Once they are on the ground in Doha, though, many are investing more in the country than they originally planned to, she said. “Across all the fund managers, they come in with a plan of what they are committing to do in Qatar, but what I see from all of them is they are going beyond that.” Notable Like most of its peers in the Gulf, Qatar Investment Authority is maintaining its appetite for investment during the war , Semafor reported. The UAE and Saudi Arabia dominate venture funding, accounting for almost 90% of the $3 billion raised by startups in the region, according to venture capital tracker MAGNiTT.

events.title: Hormuz matters but UAE has more than one gateway, economy minister says
events.summary: The gateway to the Gulf is more than one port and certainly more than one road. That is the message from Abdulla bin Touq, Minister of Economy and Tourism. “ Hormuz really matters and it will keep on mattering,” he said in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Rise Summit in Dubai . “It's really important to really focus on Hormuz as well, to have it as a gate.” It is a direct rebuttal to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks last month, who said the strait would be “a worthless piece of water” within two years. Before the Iran war , roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited the Strait of Hormuz. However, traffic flows through the waterway have dropped sharply since the war began on February 28. But while the strait matters, it is not the only way in, Mr bin Touq said. “The UAE doesn't have only one road. It has many roads to come to it,” he said. The UAE has revealed plans to reduce its reliance on the strait as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to diversify trade routes and supply chains. It has established regional logistics corridors linking the Arabian Gulf to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman. Development of east-coast ports at Khor Fakkan and Fujairah , outside the strait, has been accelerated. The UAE is also building a new pipeline to provide additional capacity for exporting Abu Dhabi oil via the Gulf of Oman. If Hormuz is the front gate, the east coast is the side door and business is already walking through it, Mr bin Touq said. Asked where the next boom would be, he pointed to company registrations on the east coast. “Redundancy means dollar signs. It means investments,” he said. Resilience does not mean retreat, though. The UAE is not making the economy safer by “closing and shrinking it”, he added. However, Mr bin Touq resisted the idea of a dramatic pivot from west to east. He said the UAE continues to function as one connected economy. With Etihad Rail now linking Abu Dhabi to Fujairah in under four hours, “we can have breakfast in Khor Fakkan, lunch in Sharjah or Dubai and dinner in Abu Dhabi”, he said. The rail line binds “these seven economies that [are] very knitted together”. Tourism rebound anticipated In terms of crises like the Iran war, tourism is the first sector to be hit and the last to recover “anywhere in the world”, with its return heavily dependant on airline capacity. The UAE is working with other countries to secure removal from their travel advisory lists, as tourism figures show signs of recovery after months of disruption because of the conflict. With Lufthansa and Air France committed to resuming UAE flights by the end of this month, “this shows you there is confidence”, Mr bin Touq said. That makes November and December a critical final window for tourism this year. The early signs are encouraging. Hotel occupancy reached about 68 per cent at the end of August. September's figures have not yet been published but the minister described the trend as “really, really nice”. Economic football The International Monetary Fund expects the UAE economy to shrink 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding 7.7 per cent in 2027. “It is 3.9 per cent, and there is decimal points, so it's not 4 per cent,” Mr bin Touq noted. The UAE's real gross domestic product also grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war . The minister discussed his plan for the economy as a football formation. “In front, I have attackers: my tourism. My midfielder is the businesses … and my defence is when it comes to IP and innovation capacity,” he said. “What happened is I lost my attacker and my midfielders are scoring goals.” For 2027, tourism must lead from the front again. Meanwhile, the midfield needs reform and access to capital. On reform, he meant legislation and “the things that we tolerated through the crisis”. On capital, he pointed to the Dh1 billion Emirates Growth Fund, where he sits on the board. The fund aims to take companies with revenue of Dh1 million to Dh10 million up to Dh50 million to Dh60 million. “We're already investing,” he said. The government also wants more venture capital in the region and artificial intelligence “embedded within the systems of these companies, of these factories”. As for the interviewer's place in his squad, the minister offered a trial. “Play a winger,” he said.

events.title: CEO confidence drops into negative territory
events.summary: Data: The Conference Board and The Business Council; Chart: Axios/Emily Peck CEO confidence in the U.S. economy sank into negative territory earlier this month, finds a survey out Thursday morning from the Conference Board . Why it matters: Business leaders are mind-melding with most consumers, whose opinions on the economy are now lower than during the pandemic . Such sour sentiment is shaping up as a key issue in the midterms just weeks away. Where it stands: The CEO Confidence Index fell to 46 in the most recent period, down from 52 just three months ago — any number below 50 connotes negative sentiment. The nonprofit Conference Board and the Business Council surveyed 131 Fortune 500 CEOs from Sept. 21-Oct. 5. The survey measures how chief executives at major public companies feel about current economic conditions and their expectations for the economy and their own industries over the next six months. By the numbers: 41% of CEOs expected economic conditions to worsen — up from 19% in the previous quarter. Executives' concerns over cybersecurity, AI and geopolitics rose significantly from three months ago. 94% of CEOs cited cybersecurity threats among their top AI-related concerns. The surge in energy prices — particularly diesel, which is crucial to companies' energy costs — also contributed to the fall in sentiment, Dana Peterson, chief economist at the Conference Board, tells Axios. "All these inflationary shocks, one after the the other, is weighing down on the confidence of both CEOs and consumers," she says. Between the lines: The key worry when CEO moods darken is the spillover into the economy, as they pull back on spending and hiring. Reality check: Despite their dimming views, CEOs have for the most part maintained their spending plans, per the survey. Case in point: A separate survey also out Thursday morning found that 89% of U.S. CEOs said they expected to increase headcount over the next three years as AI creates more business opportunities. "As we put more AI into our processes and platforms, the capacity opens up," Tim Walsh, the CEO of KPMG, which conducted the survey, told Axios' Nathan Bomey. "What you're seeing there is CEOs being really optimistic that they can actually expand their business, which is going to result in a bigger workforce for them." The bottom line: CEOs are gloomy about the economy, but their dark mood hasn't yet translated into a meaningful pullback in investment plans.

events.title: NVIDIA Expands Advanced Technology Access for Europe’s Scientific Community Through Open Learning Resources, Collaborations and Compute
events.summary: Much of today’s scientific progress begins with computation. But turning accelerated computing’s potential into scientific progress — modeling climate systems, designing molecules, simulating materials and more — depends on more than breakthrough technology. Especially for smaller labs, early-career scientists or science-based startups, the hardest part of research can be everything that comes before the science: assembling tools, finding compute and building the expertise to use both. At the AI in Science Summit in Dublin today, the European Commission launched the AI in Science Enablers Initiative, a shared framework connected to RAISE — the Resource for AI Science in Europe — that brings private-sector support closer to Europe’s research community. NVIDIA is joining the campaign , providing: Access to accelerated tools, models and platforms Compute, cloud resources, data and scientific resources Skills, training and technical support Collaborative projects and pilots along with support for researchers and talent Support for startups and ecosystem development “Europe’s ambition in AI in science can only become reality if we bring together the strengths of our research community, industry and other partners,” Ekaterina Zaharieva, European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation. “Through the AI in Science Enablers campaign, we are turning this ambition into concrete commitments that give researchers access to the tools, expertise and resources they need to innovate.” NVIDIA’s pledge begins with open source technology. NVIDIA has released more than 250 open models, 250 open datasets and over 1,400 open source software projects spanning large language models, healthcare, robotics, climate science, physical AI, autonomous vehicles and scientific research. The models and datasets are available on Hugging Face and GitHub. Building on this open ecosystem, researchers can build agentic reasoning capabilities with NVIDIA Nemotron — a family of architectures, open weights, open source models, training data and recipes — and scientific software including NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit , NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo libraries, NVIDIA Earth-2 models and NVIDIA ALCHEMI NIM microservices to accelerate research across biology, chemistry, molecular design, weather and climate, energy, engineering, physics and material sciences. Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute. The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline. Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs . NVIDIA is collaborating with cloud infrastructure partners and European national AI factories — including in France , Spain and Sweden — to open new routes for startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to access sovereign European compute and services. The NVIDIA Inception program for startups provides access to compute resources and technical support, lowering the barrier to entry for startups seeking high-performance infrastructure and technological education. AI2F in France is the first AI factory to have collaborated with the Inception program for four months, demonstrating strong results. The BSC AI Factory ran a pilot initiative and is now rolling out its first full accelerator program, with growing interest from other European national AI factories in replicating the model in 2027. Beyond startup support, this program is designed to contribute to a broader strategic objective: building self-sustaining AI ventures in Spain and Europe. Sweden AI Factory , one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and SMEs enterprises across sectors including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Finally, EuroHPC supercomputing centers such as CINECA and JSC provide academia and startups with free access to NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and services for open research. NVIDIA complements this access with office hours, bootcamps and hackathons that help researchers fine-tune models on their own datasets. As an example, NVIDIA is co-organizing an European AI hackathon this month alongside Austrian Scientific Computing , the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre , the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart and The Cyprus Institute, for Pharos-CY . To top it all off, NVIDIA is powering Europe’s most ambitious expansion of AI infrastructure to date, with 35 supercomputers currently in development across the continent — the largest single-year buildout of supercomputing capacity Europe has ever seen. Together, these systems will equip over 3 million researchers with next-generation infrastructure, accelerating discovery across domains from climate science and drug development to materials research and beyond. Explore NVIDIA technologies for science and open source courseware , and find hands-on training through the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute . Follow the European Commission’s RAISE Pledging Initiative . events.title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
events.summary: In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants. Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on? Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33. But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen. And existing plants are looking to uprate again. Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant. But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment. Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor. That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity. To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded. The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama. A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019. Things could pick up soon, though. Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors. The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes. Behind it all? Big Tech money. Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen. As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO, told the New York Times : “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.” Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio. Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has already signed on to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal. A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant. Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand. Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity. Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere between three and eight additional gigawatts on the table from uprates. A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032. It’s crucial to put these plans (and the total potential for uprates in the US) in perspective, though. PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast, expects about 30 gigawatts of additional peak demand because of AI by 2030. All the possible nationwide nuclear uprates would cover just a fraction of that. Making the most of existing nuclear reactors is a relatively easy win at a time when we need all the zero-emissions power we can get. But there’s still a lot of demand, and if we want more nuclear power to meet it, eventually that will require actually building new reactors. This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

events.title: Trump Says the Border Is Secure. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott Keeps Declaring an Emergency.
events.summary: Emily Scherer for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune. Source images: The Texas Tribune and documents obtained by ProPublica. Last month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott repeated a claim he’s made for the past five years. He stated that the number of people crossing the Texas-Mexico border illegally “posed an ongoing and imminent threat” across the state. In doing so, he renewed a border security disaster proclamation that has greatly expanded his powers without going through the state Legislature. Abbott’s declaration stands in sharp contrast to the numbers reported by the Trump administration, which says the drop in the flow of migrants crossing the border has been unprecedented and has reached historic lows since it took over in January 2025.  Yet, since Abbott first declared an emergency at the border during the Biden administration in 2021, he’s renewed or amended the proclamation at least 69 times — 21 of those during Trump’s tenure.  The Republican governor, who is running for his fourth term next month, has consolidated power like no Texas governor before him, building on his predecessors’ efforts to strengthen what by design is supposed to be a “weak governor” state as the constitution limits what can be done without legislative approval, ProPublica and The Texas Tribune have reported. One of the methods he’s used to do that is issuing executive orders and disaster declarations that allow him to shift funds, suspend regulations and award no-bid contracts at times of emergency.  Since January 2025, two of the top agencies involved with border enforcement — the Department of Public Safety and the Texas Military Department — have awarded more than $5 million in noncompetitive contracts citing the emergency for items like a Ford F-150, rifles and apartments, state records show. “I think it’s unprecedented,” said Cal Jillson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University in Dallas. “I don’t think that there is a similar example, certainly not as to the length of the emergency, and certainly not after the emergency has seemed to pass.”  Abbott’s office did not respond to specific questions for this story, including about the noncompetitive contracts, but Deputy Press Secretary Madeline Waschak said in a written statement that the governor has been clear that border security is an ongoing priority. “The damage caused by four years of failed border policies under Democrat rule did not disappear overnight, and the progress we have made will not sustain itself without continued vigilance,” she wrote. “Securing the border requires constant, deliberate action to combat illegal crossings, cartel smuggling, fentanyl trafficking, and other criminal activity that threatens public safety in Texas. Governor Abbott will ensure the tools remain in place to safeguard our state as we work alongside the Trump Administration to deter, arrest, detain, and deport illegal immigrants,” she added. At the time of Abbott’s first border declaration, four months into President Joe Biden’s term, Border Patrol was making more than 180,000 apprehensions along the southwest border in a single month. According to Abbott, the federal government’s inability or unwillingness to enforce immigration laws had created a humanitarian crisis in many communities in Texas.  “The Biden Administration’s open-border policies have enabled escalating violence from the cartels, dramatically increased the risk of human trafficking, and created a severe crisis of illegal drugs crossing into the United States,” the order stated . Since then, apprehensions along the southwest border have dropped on average to about 8,000 a month this year.  The border security declaration remains Abbott’s longest continuously running emergency proclamation. Abbott similarly renewed his 2020 COVID-19 disaster declaration for three years, even as he downplayed the severity of the pandemic.  “This is the quiet power of the governor,” said Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston. “It’s not something often that they brag about because the more that it becomes a political issue, the more that there might be some contestation of it.” Other than border security, the governor’s second longest-running emergency declaration is related to droughts. He declared a state disaster in July 2022 and within days amended it bringing the total of counties to 189. He’s continued to renew it, but now it applies to about a third of the counties originally identified. State lawmakers have repeatedly tried — and failed — to curb the governor’s powers under the state’s disaster act. Last year, legislators from both parties filed at least a handful of measures that would mandate Abbott get approval from the Legislature if he wanted to extend a disaster declaration, but none passed.  Abbott’s emergency declarations have been accompanied by record spending on border security efforts. Texas budgeted over $11 billion during the Biden administration and allotted an additional $3 billion last year, after Trump took office.  It’s all part of Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, an initiative he launched in March 2021 contending it was needed to stem the smuggling of drugs and people into the country through Texas. Because of the emergency declaration, police could charge immigrants with criminal trespassing for crossing the border through private property, and the governor was able to shift money from other agencies to fund the operation and build border barriers, deploy the National Guard and get help from other states.  Much of the funding for Operation Lone Star is funneled through the Texas Military Department and DPS, two of the agencies responsible for major enforcement efforts. But the governor’s share of border spending has also ballooned since Abbott took office over a decade ago. State lawmakers allotted his office nearly $230 million last year to distribute through grants, largely to local prosecutors and government agencies helping the state with Operation Lone Star. Though the situation on the ground has changed, one aspect of the emergency declaration has remained constant: the ability of state agencies to award noncompetitive contracts.  DPS and the Texas Military Department have awarded at least six noncompetitive contracts so far during the second Trump administration for work related to the operation where they cite an emergency. This includes a more than $2 million contract to Texas-based CTC Gunworks LLC for rifles and pistols for active-duty personnel. CTC Gunworks officials could not be reached for comment.  Officials with the Texas Military Department referred questions about its procurement process to the governor’s office. events.title: Trump doubling down on Russian diesel deal as Republicans run from it
events.summary: The News President Donald Trump is pushing ahead with his deal to import Russian diesel, blowing past his party’s growing complaints about taking help from Vladimir Putin. “The president’s main priority and commitment is to the American people and to help lower costs for the American people, and he’s doing that,” a White House official said after days of withering complaints by Republicans. “The president has not shifted his stance on it.” The Trump administration caused an intraparty furor earlier this month by announcing that Russia will “immediately” export more than 300,000 tons of its diesel in an effort to ease fuel price spikes that have hurt Republican candidates on the midterm campaign trail. It’s unclear exactly when the imports will officially arrive, but the economic boost from Moscow is sparking discontent as Republicans in tight races scramble to message around the surprise announcement. Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, who is running for the Senate, said on Tuesday in a debate that she vastly preferred other options to bring down fuel prices — among them, suspending the gas tax, creating a diesel rebate program, and using more biofuels. “We need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to be making a deal with Russia to do it,” Hinson said. The Russia deal completes a trio of Trump economic moves that are politically toxic to swing-state Republicans, joining his bid to encourage beef imports and his Canadian trade war. All three are unpopular enough among members of Trump’s own party to create significant discord about the GOP plan to tackle rising prices. Republicans are signing onto letters bashing the Russia diesel agreement and distancing themselves on the campaign trail: Former New Hampshire Sen. John Sununu, seeking the Senate again, said this week that the move would do little to lower prices in the US and “provides an advantage to Russia” In Michigan, former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers similarly broke with Trump. But other Republicans defended Trump’s policy change. “The president’s got energy security and economic security front of mind right now. He’s focused on Americans first,” Sen. Bill Hagerty, R-Tenn., a top Trump ally, said this week. Hagerty dismissed the prospect that US diesel purchases would unfairly aid Russia in its war against Ukraine: “We’ve got a number of sanctions in place and a number of efforts to bring Putin into alignment.” For the White House, the argument is simple: Diesel prices are too high, and even a smaller-scale import plan helps ease the burden. Others in the administration privately acknowledge, however, that there’s a clear reason for the recent rise in prices: Trump’s ongoing war with Iran. His administration also has long entertained ways to unwind certain sanctions on Russia in a bid to secure a peace deal with Ukraine — one that would also help ease inflation. “Having to do this is yet another inevitable consequence of the Iran war,” said a second Trump administration official, who added a hope that the diesel deal becomes part of “a broader diplomatic strategy.” Know More Already, two bipartisan groups of senators have pushed back on the decision, including seven Republicans. One House Republican has said he’ll introduce legislation to block it. “Trump and his team have misread the room on the Republican caucuses in the House and the Senate on this issue,” Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy told Semafor. “They’re trying to respond to concerns from congressional Republicans in farm states about diesel prices … and it doesn’t seem to be landing very well.” Fueling that discontent is Republicans’ dimming faith that Trump will choose to impose recently enacted Russian sanctions that were passed in honor of his longtime ally, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said earlier this month that the administration planned to “name names” — but whether to use that sanctions power would be “for the president to decide.” Asked this week about GOP skeptics of his diesel purchases from Russia, Trump dismissed them as “Republicans that can’t really be serious,” adding that it’s “a deal for the rest of the world.” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers praised Trump’s “great deal to supply the global market with massive amounts of diesel.” “Lowering prices for America’s great farmers, truckers, and families remains a top priority as the President simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers,” Rogers said in a statement. “We didn’t think [the bill] would change anything on the sanctions front … and I think that this decision just reinforces that view,” said Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations. Room for Disagreement A handful of GOP lawmakers, including Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker of Mississippi, are taking a different tack by predicting the diesel imports never materialize.Some Republicans posit that Trump’s new import deal violates a 2022 law that bans the US from purchasing Russian energy products. Others point to hurdles like European sanctions and Russian shortages . Even if it does become real, it won’t do much to lower prices. Investors are already pricing in “little near-term impact,” Kennedy said, since the world uses far more diesel than Russia will export. Wicker said he’s pitched the administration on alternative ideas. It’s unclear what those could be. Shelby, Eleanor, and Burgess’ View Whether it’s red-dye diesel or Russian diesel, the Trump administration is pulling out all the stops to convince voters that it’s bringing prices down … even as it maintains an Iran war that is driving costs up. So far, the president’s advisers have little to show for it beyond making life harder for the rest of their party. Notable Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan it’s “painful” to watch Trump’s deal-making with Russia.

events.title: YOLO Chuck: Schumer's final fight
events.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is on the cusp of leading his party to midterm victory and reclaiming his title as Senate majority leader. Winning the majority isn't guaranteed. But this son of Brooklyn, who has been in public life for 52 years, is more than favored to win a secret ballot to remain Democratic leader. Why it matters: At age 75 (76 by the time the new Congress convenes in January), Charles Ellis Schumer, an old-school pol who visits all 62 of New York's counties every year, looks poised to do what very few people do in life — go out on top. Behind the scenes: For starters, Democratic senators aren't quietly maneuvering — or publicly positioning themselves — to take the top job, according to senior aides. You can't beat someone with no one . A handful of Democratic Senate candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, haven't committed to supporting Schumer for leader. But they likely don't have the votes to stage a coup. And Schumer's super PAC is spending heavily to get them across the line. That calculus could change if Republicans overperform expectations with a massive win, potentially triggering a serious leadership challenge. Otherwise, the job is Schumer's for the asking — and he's asking. "I am running for re-election for leader. Period," he said two weeks ago. The intrigue: The bigger question surrounding Schumer involves 2028 and whether he'd retire at the top of his game or risk an embarrassing primary loss to, perhaps, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was born in the Bronx and represents parts of the Bronx and Queens. If Schumer decided to retire, he could spend his final two years in leadership, freed from the political pressures that have defined his career. That would give Senate Republicans and President Trump an entirely new political animal to contend with: YOLO Chuck. Republican YOLO senators (with nothing left to lose, since You Only Live Once) have been playing hardball with President Trump. But it's unclear how a YOLO Chuck would behave as Senate majority leader. Schumer, first elected to Congress when Carter was president, has spent nearly 46 years plotting what's next. Not even his closest allies know what he'll be like if he's freed from the political pressures that have defined his leadership. Zoom out: Schumer finds himself in a position remarkably similar to that of the man he'd replace: Senate Majority Leader John Thune . Both are distrusted by their parties' most vocal activists. The insults hurled at them — weak, coward, sellout — are almost interchangeable. But most of the criticism comes from outside the chamber . Behind closed doors, their caucuses are expected to close ranks . What we're watching: If Schumer takes the majority, he'd have to weigh when to confront, and when to cooperate with, a president he says is synonymous with "costs, chaos and corruption." Schumer has known Trump for decades, and they have a "complicated" relationship . But he'd be facing him as the co-head of a coequal branch of government. Funding the government and passing the National Defense Authorization Act are must-do pieces of legislation. Schumer would have to navigate those politics with up to eight Democratic senators running for president. Between the lines: The Senate Democratic leader would also have to coordinate with a potential House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, who has struggled to maintain discipline within his ranks. In the minority, the two New York Democrats have clashed over how to confront Trump . They split over Schumer's decision to help Republicans avert a government shutdown in March 2025. Progressives were furious with Schumer . House Democrats held venting sessions. Tensions resurfaced this year when Schumer negotiated a short-term DHS funding deal that Jeffries refused to embrace . The bottom line: If Schumer announces early in the next Congress that he won't seek another term as leader in 2028, Washington could find itself in an unusual position — with a term-limited president negotiating with a Senate majority leader who has nothing left to lose politically.

events.title: Gen Z and millennials are running for Congress in record numbers, but few reach November
events.summary: Gen Z and millennials have launched their biggest bid yet to remake Congress, but roughly seven in 10 were out by early September, a new report finds. Why it matters: These two generations are struggling to clear the first hurdles of a political system that rewards experience, fundraising and established party support. State of play: A new report from Future Caucus , a nonpartisan nonprofit that works with younger elected officials, found that a record share of this cycle's congressional candidates came from the nation's two youngest political generations. The group identified 3,918 candidates who filed for Congress this cycle, 31% more than in 2024. Of candidates with known or estimated ages, 36.4% were millennials or Gen Z, up from 23.4% in 2024. The report counts everyone who filed and doesn't track how many were first-time candidates. Between the lines : Many young candidates are trying to reach Congress without the political experience that helps candidates advance. Just 1.7% of Gen Z candidates and 9% of millennials have served in a state legislature. Among congressional challengers with age data, nearly 40% of those with state legislative experience reached the general-election stage, compared with 26.2% without it. By the numbers: Only 21.2% of Gen Z congressional candidates remained in the race at the report's September cutoff. That figure rose to 30.2% for millennials, 41.1% for Gen X and 44.5% for Baby Boomers. Nearly 33% of Gen Z candidates failed to qualify for a primary ballot, compared with 18.3% of millennials and 9.4% of Gen X. Incumbents averaged 59 years old, nearly nine years older than challengers. What they're saying: "They're done waiting for somebody else to fix the problems," Future Caucus President and CEO Layla Zaidane tells Axios. Zaidane said Gen Z candidates running outside the two major parties face steep hurdles: raising money, recruiting volunteers and building name recognition without party infrastructure. Zoom in: Women make up just 17.1% of Gen Z congressional candidates, compared with 26.6% of millennials and 30.7% of Gen X. Younger men withdrew or failed to qualify for the primary ballot at higher rates than women in their generations. Younger candidates are disproportionately Democrats, even as President Trump's GOP competes for young voters. Yes, but: Young candidates are scoring some wins. In Colorado, 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros ousted 15-term Democratic Rep. Diana DeGette in the primary for a heavily Democratic Denver seat. In Iowa, 29-year-old Republican Joe Mitchell , a former state lawmaker, captured his party's nomination for an open House seat.
