events.title: As Christmas rush looms, how do China-made toys find their way to the US?
events.summary: China is the world's largest toymaker, producing the majority of toys on sale in the US On the underside of most children's toys on sale in the US you'll find the same three words – "Made in China". Nearly eight in 10 toys (78.3%) imported into the country in 2024 came from China, according to US government figures. , external Last year, toys imported from China were worth $9.8bn (£7.4bn), trade figures show. , external With Christmas on the horizon, the toy industry in the US and elsewhere is about to have its busiest time of the year by far. As retailers prepare their stocks for the festive rush, be they online giants or "mom-and-pop" physical stores, the BBC World Service's Follow the Money series traces how a toy gets from a factory in China to the US. And where the money goes. Guangdong province, which neighbours Hong Kong in southern China, is the heart of the country's toy manufacturing industry. In the city of Dongguan workers on the floor of the Mihox factory pop plastic toys out of steel moulds, and pile them into crates ready for painting. The company says it employs more than 800 people and makes around 55 million toys a year for the American market, which represents half of its business. Follow the money: The journey of a $30 toy from China to America Every toy starts with a design from a customer, such as an American toy company. The factory then makes a prototype, and builds moulds from which plastic parts and other components are formed. Going from the first idea to finished toy takes one to two years, says Melanie Wang from the Mihox sales team. Much of that is the customer going back to the drawing board. "They modified the design again, again, and again to improve it." Once the design is signed off, things move more quickly. A mould takes about a month to make, and the production run lasts about three months. The Mihox factory in Dongguan employs more than 800 people So, how much of the US retail price does the factory get? "About 20%," says Wang. On a $30 toy, that's $6, which has to cover the price of the plastic and other materials, production costs including wages, and what profit the factory makes. Chinese factories typically make a profit of between 3% and 10%, according to Jay Foreman, chief executive of US toy firm Basic Fun. So for a $30 toy that's between 60 and 18 cents of the $6 the factory charges to make it. Samson Ko is president of the Toys Manufacturers' Association of Hong Kong. Many of his members moved their factories across the border into mainland China in the 1980s, attracted by cheaper land and labour. He says the way toys are made has barely changed since then. "Automation now takes place mostly in the moulding and the packaging process. But for soft toys, or even some of the electronics nowadays, it's still very labour intensive." And Chinese labour isn't cheap anymore, he adds, after recent rises. Melanie Wang explains that Mihox gets 20% of a toy's retail price Average pay in Vietnam is about half of that in China, said one report , external at the start of this year. Yet fewer than 10% of Ko's members have moved any production outside China, and in those cases mostly only because customers asked them to do so. The Chinese factories remain busy, he says, because a single toy can undergo more than one manufacturing process, from moulding the parts, to adding electronics, sewing materials, and final assembly. This often requires it travelling to different factories. Ko adds that in Guangdong these separate facilities are located close to each other, and used to "working in harmony". He says this makes the whole manufacturing process run more smoothly than in other countries. From the factory, the toy goes by truck to a port, such as Shenzhen, the biggest in Guangdong. Ivy Tse is co-founder of FreightAmigo, a Hong Kong logistics company that runs an online platform for both Hong Kong and mainland China exporters. These businesses can book a cargo container, sea passage to an overseas destination, arrange insurance cover, and secure finance. Tse says it takes about 15 days for a cargo ship to get from Shenzhen to the US west coast, and 25 to 30 days to the east coast. This year's Christmas toys left China in August and September. Freight, from factory to the US, usually adds about 10% to the manufacturing cost of a toy, adds Tse. So if we stick to a toy that retails for $30 in the US, and therefore costs $6 to make in China, the cost of getting it to the states is 60 cents. Once the toy reaches the US there is currently a tariff on Chinese toys that has to be paid to the US Customs and Border Protection (CBP). Following talks between President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, the two governments have recommended toys for lower tariffs. But no new rate or start date has been set, and the US must first hold a public consultation. For now the basic rate is 12.5%, and some toys pay more.

events.title: How much is the minimum wage?
events.summary: The official minimum rates of pay rose for 2.7 million workers on 1 April. The rate for workers aged 21 and over is called the National Living Wage, while those aged 18 to 20 are paid the National Minimum Wage. What is the National Living Wage, and how much is it worth? From 1 April 2026, workers over 21 on the National Living Wage are paid £12.71 an hour, 50p more than in 2025. For someone working full time (37.5 hours a week), that amounts to £24,784.50 a year - an increase of £900. What is the National Minimum Wage and how much is it worth? The rate for 18 to 20-year-olds has gone up to £10.85 an hour. That's an increase of 85p per hour. It amounts to an increase of £1,500 a year for a full-time worker. The government said its goal is to eventually scrap this separate rate for 18 to 20-year-olds, and have one rate for all adults. The minimum wage for 16 and 17-year-olds has also risen to £8 an hour. What is the apprentice rate and how much is it worth? There are different rates of pay for apprentices , external depending on their age and what stage of apprenticeship they are in. Apprentices aged 16 to 18 are entitled to the National Minimum Wage rate for that age group which is currently £8. Those aged 19, or in the first year of their apprenticeship, are paid the same amount. But those over 19 - or who have already completed their first year - are entitled to the appropriate National Minimum Wage or National Living Wage rate for their age. What is an apprenticeship and how much is the pay? Published 20 August Who doesn't qualify for the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage? Some workers do not qualify for either the National Minimum Wage or the National Living Wage. This includes the self-employed, company directors, volunteers, members of the armed forces and prisoners. People with disabilities or in long-term unemployment who take part in government work programmes are paid fixed amounts at different stages of the scheme. These are less than the equivalent National Minimum or Living rate. Do employers have to pay the National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage? Yes. It is a criminal offence for employers not to pay the correct National Minimum and Living Wages to eligible employees. The rates apply even if workers are not paid by the hour. Calculator: Am I getting the right wage? , external If you think you are being paid the wrong amount, you can complain via the HMRC website , external . You can also get advice from workplace experts Acas , external . What happens if employers don't pay the right wage? Any employer not paying the correct amount can be penalised by HMRC. In March 2026, the government said that 389 employers had been fined around £12.6m for failing to pay staff properly , external . They must also repay the missing £7.3m to the around 60,000 workers who were underpaid. Firm named included the Nursery chain Busy Bees , Norwich City Football Club, Hays Travel and Costa Coffee. What is the Real Living Wage and how much is it? The Real Living Wage , external is an unofficial hourly rate of pay which is overseen by the Living Wage Foundation charity, who say it is set at a rate to meet the cost of living. Some firms choose to pay the Real Living Wage, but it is not mandatory. According to the charity almost 500,000 employees working for nearly 17,000 firms receive the voluntary rate of pay. In October 2026, the foundation said the UK rate would increase by 4.8% to £14.10 an hour, while the London Living Wage for workers in the capital would go up by 4.4% to £15.45. The Living Wage Foundation says the rate is worth over £2,700 more per year than the legal minimum wage in the UK, and over £5,300 more in London. events.title: Apple gears up for AI product push in China
events.summary: Apple’s first foldable smartphone will feature Alibaba’s AI when it launches in China next week, as Apple Intelligence — the company’s generative suite — gears up for its mainland appearance after years of regulatory delays. Apple sees AI features as critical to competing with Huawei , the only firm it lags in China. The world’s largest smartphone market has slumped amid weak consumer spending and rising hardware costs. Still, China’s cutthroat industry is seeing new entrants: AI lab StepFun launched a $600 AI agent smartphone Tuesday. An analyst described the move as “ quite bold ” under present conditions, but one that might be explained by the smartphone’s unparalleled ability to continually gather user data , allowing AI assistants to become ever-more personalized. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Iran ramps up ship strikes in Hormuz ahead of US midterms
events.summary: Iran’s increasing attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz have made October one of the most violent months in the waterway since the war began, as Tehran looks to exploit US President Donald Trump’s political vulnerability ahead of midterm elections. Two Emirati cargo vessels sank in the past 24 hours after being struck; Iranian officials told Reuters that Tehran was deliberately ramping up strikes to keep oil prices elevated before Nov. 3. Washington’s lack of response is “remarkable,” a Eurasia Group analyst said: “ Trump continues to promise action , but only after [midterms].” That’s also when Washington could be more amenable to joining Saudi Arabia’s strikes against the Houthis, another analyst suggested: “Trump’s preference is for it to happen afterwards .” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: White House played central role in antitrust probe of TV networks
events.summary: The Scoop The White House played a central role in the Justice Department’s antitrust investigation into major TV networks’ temporary suspension of pooled coverage of the president, three people familiar with the matter told Semafor. While the probe is progressing, some inside the DOJ are concerned about its legal merits. Two former DOJ officials said that the networks suspending their pool participation after three news outlets got barred from the White House are likely protected by the First Amendment — one cited a 1982 Supreme Court ruling that afforded those constitutional protections to group boycotts for political purposes. Two of the people familiar with the matter suggested that the idea of an antitrust inquiry was first discussed inside the White House, which ultimately pushed for it from the DOJ. A third described the White House-DOJ interplay as a “distinction [without] a difference,” given how closely the two are intertwined under President Donald Trump’s administration. A DOJ official disputed that the White House first raised the idea of a probe, saying that “seasoned attorneys within the Justice Department, including the antitrust division, first discussed this.” The official added that any requests for information from networks which may have been sent were written “because there is sound legal footing to investigate.” In addition to the longstanding Trump-era blur between the DOJ and White House, the department’s antitrust division has close ties to presidential priorities. Sara Matar, formerly the division’s chief of staff, joined the White House counsel’s office in August as an associate. The White House initially referred comment to DOJ. After this story’s publication, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis responded in a statement: “Your sources have it wrong. As the Department of Justice said, this investigation did not initiate with the White House.” Notably, Laura Loomer — a staunch MAGA ally whose outside influence has occasionally resulted in changes within the White House — tweeted last month wondering why the DOJ hadn’t “filed an antitrust lawsuit” against outlets that “colluded to refuse to cover” Trump. Loomer attacked Woodward in her post; the following week, she traveled with Trump to Alabama, though it’s unclear whether she raised the issue with the president personally during that trip. Know More The Trump administration has long argued that the Justice Department is not wholly separate from the White House, counter to the norms that took root after the Nixon era. At Semafor’s World Economy Summit in April, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated that it is Trump’s “right” to suggest targets for investigation — a stance he has echoed repeatedly since settling into his role at the top of the department. “Certainly if the leader of the Free World learns about something or hears about something or wants us to focus on something, a certain area, that is, of course, what every Department of Justice has done,” Blanche told Semafor at the time. “This idea that President Trump has some sort of outsized control because of things that he says, that that’s absolutely his right and his duty to do that,” Blanche added. Notable Legal experts view the antitrust probe as a potential rationale for the DOJ to secure internal records from TV networks, Axios reported .

events.title: Fridge hack costing millions and sparking fires stemmed from poor security
events.summary: Earlier this week, a mass hack of refrigeration systems at an estimated 700 supermarkets throughout France caused them to suddenly malfunction, causing spoilage of untold tons of perishables and, in some cases, fires. As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). By the time the mass compromise was discovered, food was spoiled, and in some cases their electrical systems caught fire. The hacks that didn't have to happen Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident—sold by Danfoss of Denmark and Dixell and its parent company Copeland in the US—contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators. Until recently, Danfoss controllers, for instance, used a credential that changes each day. The password is generated by the publicly available firmware based on the date. A hacker who takes the time to analyze the code can do the same thing on any device that hasn’t received a recent update. Daily passwords are identical across models located in hundreds or thousands of stores. Read full article Comments

events.title: ICE says no to automatic body-cams
events.summary: ICE is rejecting a Government Accountability Office recommendation for technology that automatically activates body cameras when weapons are drawn and safeguards to ensure agents record arrests, searches and detentions when required. Why it matters: The GAO warns that ICE risks losing crucial evidence on what happened during incidents involving force amid growing distrust over agent accountability in the wake of multiple fatal ICE shootings . The big picture: The GAO report found both CBP and ICE are struggling to manage their body-camera programs during the agencies' shifting deployment plans. CBP and ICE haven't updated their camera plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively. The plans fail to account for funding changes, expanded deployment needs and pauses in camera rollouts following one of Trump's executive orders that rescinded a Biden-era federal body-camera mandate. ICE's camera activation dispute is the central flashpoint in the GAO review, as DHS accepted all six other recommendations. CBP uses technology that automatically activates body cameras when officers draw firearms or turn on emergency lights, but ICE doesn't. Zoom in: At six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed, CBP and ICE personnel said they were unsure when they had to turn on their cameras. Some said camera use is "not mandated," "up to interpretation," and "has gray areas." Agents specifically reported uncertainty about whether they should record during "subpoena issuance, in-custody interviews, vehicle searches, undercover operations, and detainee transports." At five sites, people said they weren't sure how to use a newer camera model. The other side: DHS rejected the recommendation, arguing that automatic activation "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." DHS warned that accidental activation could expose sensitive interactions with informants and victims or record people engaged in protected First Amendment activities. GAO pushed back, noting that DHS offered no alternative safeguards despite the risks of critical encounters going unrecorded. "ICE has acquired devices to equip all ICE officers and agents nationwide with body cameras," a DHS spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement. "Training required to equip individual officers remains ongoing and we expect to complete this training soon." Worth noting: ICE issued no written reprimands for failing to comply with camera policies from the program's launch through September 2025. CBP issued just one. The bottom line: Both CBP and ICE say their body-camera programs are meant to improve public trust, officer safety and accountability. But without clear standards, the agencies can't determine whether their programs are meeting those goals, GAO found. events.title: Ukraine's Starlink restrictions raise suspicions of Musk, Trump retaliation
events.summary: The rupture between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over last week's diesel deal deepened Wednesday after an Elon Musk -owned satellite system used by Ukraine unexpectedly restricted service — undercutting Ukraine's fight against Russia. Why it matters: The Ukrainian military uses SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system to control and operate its reconnaissance and intercept drones. When Starlink doesn't operate at full capacity, Ukraine's ability to gather intelligence, use interceptor drones and conduct long-range strikes against Russia is impeded. Service was partially restored Wednesday, but Ukrainian officials were still searching for answers about why the service was throttled and who was responsible. The limitations came days after a new crisis erupted between the U.S. and Ukraine over Trump's agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil sales. Zelensky criticized the move, then Trump called for Ukraine to elect a new president. A senior U.S. official said the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink service constraints. But Ukrainian officials remain suspicious. Driving the news: Ukrainian officials said SpaceX imposed the restrictions Tuesday night. The system turned off, they said, when a drone exceeded 160 kph. In some cases, it disconnected when the speed went over 80 kph. The Starlink restrictions came several hours after the Ukrainian military did not receive an early warning about a Russian ballistic missile attack. Ukrainian officials said the U.S. has provided such alerts over the last several years as part of intelligence sharing between the countries. U.S. officials pointed to a technical malfunction in the system, but Ukrainian officials suspect that it was a warning shot from the Trump administration. "We had massive [Russian] attacks today, and it's a pity that we also had difficulties ... about Starlink and about intelligence and a lot of different surprises," Zelensky said at the start of a meeting in London with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. "We count on the partnership with the U.S., but we just want to be very honest and very clear and be a strong partner." The latest: The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense said SpaceX continues to restrict Starlink to 160 kph — significantly higher than earlier but still well below its normal speeds. The ministry said it remains in communication "with partners and SpaceX regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions." "The situation is better than it was this morning, but 160 kph is not enough for intercepting" some Russian jet drones, a Ukrainian official added. The intrigue: Ukrainian officials think the restrictions were imposed intentionally by SpaceX to press Ukraine to accept Trump's demand not to attack Russian oil refineries. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski wrote to Musk on X on Wednesday: "Hey, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you." Between the lines: Ukraine relies on two satellite systems. One is SpaceX's Starlink, which it uses for communications, ground forces, logistics and defensive drones — ones that shoot down incoming drones. The other is Starshield, which is controlled by the U.S. government and used for offensive military purposes. Both systems were restricted, according to Ukraine. What they're saying: In a post on X , Musk did not directly address the throttling of Starlink, but he did indirectly comment on which entity would have been responsible for the limitations imposed on Ukraine. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote. "Starlink," he added, "is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." Behind the scenes: Zelensky's top advisers spoke with their White House counterparts Wednesday and asked whether there'd been a decision to shut down Starlink services and what could be done to fix the situation, two sources said. Ukrainian officials made similar calls to the CIA and the Pentagon. White House officials told the Ukrainians they don't have control over SpaceX, the sources said. One of the sources said the Trump administration is going to reach out to SpaceX to figure out what happened. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

events.title: AI tools are aiding would-be spies
events.summary: AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers. Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them. Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI. Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from." Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit . Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room." Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved. The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded. The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes. Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in August. Last year, authorities said a man used ChatGPT to help plot the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside of the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. Flashback: Alfozan's case has caught viral attention across news sites and social media, but it isn't the first time a tech employee has been arrested for allegedly stealing AI trade secrets. In 2024, the Justice Department indicted ex-Google software engineer Linwei Ding for stealing AI technology secrets and sharing them with two Chinese companies. Earlier this year, a federal jury found Ding guilty on several counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets. Threat level: Now, AI tools are adding a new dimension to corporate espionage, potentially making it easier for less-sophisticated actors to build spying devices while giving investigators new ways to retrace their steps. The bottom line: AI models are creating security headaches for companies not only when they break out of containment , but also when people use them to plan and carry out crimes — including espionage against their own internal workings.

events.title: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
events.summary: Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence . Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI. As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down. “Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson. Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun , a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them. Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online. The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry. In September, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes , which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU—who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress. OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI , warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer. As with math, Thompson says, we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way. Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science , and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound. “We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.” This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter . events.title: IEEE Continues Preparations for the Realignment of Its Regions
events.summary: Progress continues in restructuring IEEE’s geographic regions, as outlined in The Institute’s February 2023 article “ IEEE Is Realigning Its Geographic Regions .” The “Region 1” designation will no longer be used. The new Region 2 will merge what is currently Region 1 (Northeastern U.S.) with the current Region 2 (Eastern U.S.). It will be called Region 2 (Northeastern and Eastern U.S.). The current Region 10 (Asia Pacific) will be divided into two separate regions. The new Region 10 will encompass North Asia, and the new Region 11 will cover South Asia and the Pacific. The restructuring is defined in the image of the redrawn map in this article. What’s underway Although the new regional alignment will not officially take place until 1 January 2028, several activities have begun within IEEE Member and Geographic Activities (MGA) and across other IEEE organizational units. Within MGA, volunteers and staff have been actively addressing system enhancements, director/director-elect elections , governance updates, communications, and regional finances and offerings. No changes to membership Work will continue from now until the effective date of realignment in 2028. The change will not affect your IEEE membership, nor will it change either your local IEEE section or chapter. If you have any questions regarding the realignment, contact Reg-Realignment@ieee.org .

events.title: Xbox leans into AI with Xbox Labs
events.summary: In the span of weeks, AI altered the video game industry with mashups, which allow people to combine multiple popular games into one — and Xbox is leaning in. AI-coding models have crossed new capability thresholds that allow users to reverse-engineer and recreate complex game code that would have taken humans years to do. People have created mashups that allow characters to play in , or skateboard through . “These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry,” an Xbox executive said in a memo sent to employees and posted Tuesday on the company’s website, adding that the viral mashups mean gamers have become creators. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes ) they challenge our existing business models.” The video game giant announced Xbox Labs, which will aim to work with users as well as its own developers and engineers to make games and experiences stemming from the new AI-fueled creations. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
events.summary: Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years. Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10. Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City. The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly". The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives". The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers". "We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC. "Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do." The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year. None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC. It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports. Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest Published 23 July Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport. "Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports. She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution". The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports. Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households. Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? events.title: Bünyamin Aydın’s new collection, “From Earth to Sky,” soars with iPad Pro
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support We were working on high‑resolution images, creating multiple layers and playing with textures. That’s usually when things start to slow down. But that never happened on iPad Pro. It felt just like working on a desktop. Bünyamin Aydın, Les Benjamins designer Text of this article October 14, 2026 UPDATE Bünyamin Aydın’s new collection, “From Earth to Sky,” soars with iPad Pro The Les Benjamins designer brought together Turkish heritage, 1970s rock ’n’ roll influences, and futurism for a landmark fashion show in Cappadocia shot on iPhone 18 Pro Max Long before the sun rises in Cappadocia, Türkiye’s Rose Valley is already awake. Crews are on the move, models refresh their makeup, and three giant hot-air balloons — neon green, yellow, and pink — float above a landscape that looks like it belongs on Mars. The scene is set for Les Benjamins designer Bünyamin Aydın’s most ambitious project yet. “From Earth to Sky” celebrates 15 years of the Istanbul-based lifestyle brand and brings together Anatolian heritage, avant-garde design, and the magic of iPad Pro with Apple Pencil Pro. Shot on iPhone 18 Pro Max by French filmmaker Neels Castillon, this fashion show is like no other. The project began to take shape during a research trip to Cappadocia in early 2026. Aydın used iPad Pro and Apple Pencil Pro, alongside iPhone 17 Pro Max to record the extraordinary terrain, shooting photographs and 4K video at 60 fps. Aydın’s creative process seldom takes place behind a desk, so he appreciates the flexibility iPad Pro offers with its thin, light form factor and battery life that can last him up to two days. “It’s the ultimate workstation on the go,” Aydın says. “That gives me freedom.” Three native flowers he encountered in the region — spiky green Echinops, flutelike pink trumpets, and wild yellow tulips — became the heart of this latest collection, inspiring 10 striking looks and three custom-built hot-air balloons. For Aydın, Les Benjamins represents the intersection of people and their cultures, and “From Earth to Sky” is no different. Born in Germany, the designer was raised with what he describes as “German discipline and Turkish heart” — a duality that runs through his work. “The canvas is the West; the paint is the East,” he says of a collection that combines contemporary silhouettes with Turkish fabrics and Silk Road influences. iPad Pro with the powerful M5 chip became the creative nexus for the entire project. After research trips, Aydın would assemble photographs, fabric references, and early designs in the Freeform app, where evolving mood boards could be easily shared or exported to keep work ticking along. “Freeform allowed me to bring my team into my creative journey instead of simply giving them finished ideas,” he says. The multitasking features on iPad Pro became integral as the workflows multiplied. Aydın could use its intuitive windowing system to work on an active sketch in Procreate, refer to photos from his travels, and research local flora in Safari, all while Background Tasks exported files for his collaborators. And then there were the hot-air balloons. Working in Procreate, Aydın and his team designed a single structure as a starting point, then rapidly duplicated, altered, and redrew it until three final forms emerged from dozens of variations. To bring the designs to life, Aydın collaborated with Pasha Balloons, one of Cappadocia’s hot-air balloon pioneers. “I would send my sketches to them, and they would use their engineering know-how to make sure they could actually fly,” he says with a smile. These technical drawings would then go straight back into Procreate for review and refinement. Finding the right colors was vital. In addition to the electric hues of the balloons, Aydın also worked with cream, blue, and natural tones. “These are the colors of the earth and the sky,” he explains. The Ultra Retina XDR display on iPad Pro — which uses tandem OLED technology — became a key tool, while True Tone helped Aydın achieve the saturation he wanted, regardless of ambient lighting. Apple Pencil Pro helped draw the line from idea to iterative design. “Working with regular pen and paper feels very natural, but the hover feature on Apple Pencil Pro lets me preview every stroke before I even make it, so I can see any mistakes beforehand,” he says. “It’s like a supernatural tool.” An avid gamer, Aydın compares his relationship with Apple Pencil Pro to the muscle memory he developed while playing his favorite titles. Squeezing, double-tapping, and switching to the eraser now feel like reflexive actions, which enabled him to move quickly through variations without the tool interrupting the idea. And the low latency made the creative experience feel more immersive and responsive than ever. “We were working on high-resolution images, creating multiple layers and playing with textures. That’s usually when things start to slow down,” he says. “But that never happened on iPad Pro. It felt just like working on a desktop.” Back in Rose Valley, months of planning and work are finally coming to life. Even before the sun touches the horizon, Castillon’s iPhone 18 Pro Max is already rolling. Three runways, gigantic hot-air balloons, and natural light that continues to change with every passing minute mean there is little room for error. The new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture allows Castillon to begin filming in low light before narrowing the aperture as the sun comes up. Camera operators use Pro controls like histogram and white balance to keep the look consistent across multiple cameras as the sky changes from pink to blue. Working with iPhone 18 Pro Max brings the immediacy Castillon loves as a director. “When I see something beautiful, I want to film it right away,” he says. The A20 Pro chip and improved thermal management also give the production the sustained performance and reliability it needs to capture heavy 4K video throughout the event. Just as Aydın’s show travels from past to future, movement drives Castillon’s visual treatment. Custom-built drones each carry two iPhone 18 Pro Max models, with their 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide cameras focused on enhancing the sense of vertiginous speed while fitting the massive balloons into frame. Footage captured at 4K 120 fps allows Castillon to highlight elements like rippling fabric in cinematic slow motion, while a slower shutter speed turns quick drone passes into a painterly impressionistic motion blur. Castillon’s treatment also creates a dreamlike, psychedelic look. He uses ProRes RAW to preserve flexibility for color grading in post-production, as Cappadocia’s pale hues meet saturated pinks, yellows, and greens. “I’m a huge nerd for color, and the tones are really accurate on iPad Pro,” he says.

events.title: Exclusive: White House probes claims of missing Kennedy Center money in "MAGA blood feud"
events.summary: President Trump has directed his White House counsel to examine explosive allegations dropped on him Friday in the Oval Office: Former Trump attorney Alina Habba told the president that another one of his top advisers — former Kennedy Center leader Ric Grenell — failed to deposit a multimillion-dollar donation that her billionaire husband made to the center a year ago, according to four senior administration officials and three insiders briefed on the controversy. Grenell denied the accusations as "absurd" and a "lie." Habba and her husband, Turhan Mildon, declined to comment through a spokesperson. Why it matters: The extraordinary row between the two top-tier presidential advisers and former allies provides a rare and acrimonious behind-the-scenes glimpse into the intersection of power, influence and money in Trump's Washington. The total value of the contribution in question: nearly $6 million, White House sources said Habba told them. A senior administration official cautioned that "these are only allegations. We don't know if they're true. This could be a misunderstanding." Said another: "POTUS doesn't want to deal with this. Of course, he's concerned. But if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem." Just a few months ago , Grenell was friends with Mildon and Habba. But he was notably absent from their $10 million wedding that was attended by Trump world officials, power brokers and luminaries last month. "This is the ultimate MAGA blood feud," said one Trump world insider with knowledge of the conflict. Zoom in: The dispute grew out of a friendship between Grenell and Mildon, sources familiar with the conflict say. The men had mutual interests in Venezuela in early 2025, immediately after Trump returned to the White House. Grenell, as a Trump special envoy, was advocating for normalizing U.S. relations with Venezuela's leader at the time, Nicolas Maduro. Mildon, a Turkish national, had extensive Venezuelan business interests that were threatened by Secretary of State Marco Rubio's hardline pressure campaign targeting Maduro. The intrigue: In the spring of 2025, Grenell persuaded Mildon to include a multimillion-dollar Kennedy Center donation in a lump-sum $17.6 million payment for a business deal involving a U.S. company, Habba told the president and White House staffers, two sources said. Habba's attorneys plan to give the White House documentation — reviewed by Axios — to support her allegations about Grenell soliciting a Kennedy Center donation from Mildon to go to a private company in the spring of 2025. "The White House counsel has asked for documents and proof. None has come so far," a White House official said. Grenell called the statements from Habba to Trump "Absurd. I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all. Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations." When Habba initially leveled her accusations against Grenell, she said the total amount of the Kennedy Center contribution was $17 million, the sources said. But as she learned of the specifics from her husband, she said the amount of the contribution in question was $5.6 million. "This has been hard to track because numbers have changed," the White House official said. After making his alleged contribution , Mildon never checked to see if it was deposited. He believed it had been credited because he was treated like a VIP donor at the Kennedy Center, where he met Habba in late 2025 before their whirlwind romance and marriage, those sources said. Friction point: Mildon and Habba, the sources said, discovered the issue after their business relationship frayed with Grenell, who lost an internal administration power struggle with Rubio that culminated in the U.S. seizing Maduro on Jan. 3 and taking him to New York City to face narcotics charges. In June, Maduro's successor, Delcy Rodriguez, issued an order revoking one of Mildon's company contracts to operate state-owned cement plants in Venezuela, the New York Times reported Monday. A source familiar with the situation told Axios this summer that her action was partly due to the U.S. government's prodding. Rodriguez then reversed herself, the Times reported, after learning of Mildon's new relationship with Habba because the Venezuelan leader believed Mildon therefore had Trump's backing. Amid the Times' reporting into Mildon's contract, Habba discovered that Mildon's supposed donation never made it to the Kennedy Center, the sources said. Inside the room: Habba then headed to the White House last Friday to tell the president about the situation. "Alina hit the roof" when her husband told her that he hadn't donated the money directly to the Kennedy Center, whose records indicate that Mildon actually owed a $270,000 pledged donation. There was no record of Mildon giving anything close to $5.6 million, officials said. Mildon on Tuesday paid the $270,000, records show, to the Kennedy Center. In partial confirmation of Habba's story , Kennedy Center staff reported that late last year there was a search for Mildon's contribution — then thought to be $6 million — but that it couldn't be found, an official said. But Lisa Dale, who handled finances for the Kennedy Center then, said the only record in her books connected to Mildon showed he owed $270,000. "There was nothing about $6 million," she told Axios. "I would have heard about that." Context: Habba and Grenell trace their roots to Trump's first administration. Grenell was Trump's ambassador to Germany and then his acting director of national intelligence. Habba was Trump's private attorney and briefly was U.S. attorney in New Jersey during this term. Between the lines: The Kennedy Center has been an ongoing sore spot for Trump, beset by controversy over his efforts to put his name on the building and fundraising woes. If Habba's allegations of missing money are true, it could prove particularly galling to Trump, who views the center and its fundraising personally. Those who know the president's thinking say he is particularly disapproving of people who use his name or misuse positions he has given them. His dismissal Tuesday of Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle was the latest reminder of that. Two top Trump world figures being engaged in such a bitter feud adds to the complexity. "Nobody wants to get in the middle of Alina Habba and Ric Grenell going to war," one official said.

events.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
events.summary: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals. The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce. Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to". The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers. In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation". Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount . Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". TV series Below, starring Josh Hartnett, is one of Netflix's most popular shows The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October. Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series. It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films. However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer. He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau. "Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said. The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade. Are you affected by issues covered in this story? events.title: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters
events.summary: Data: Gallup ; Chart: Axios Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a new Gallup survey. The big picture: Americans' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism. By the numbers: 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments, per Gallup. That's the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974. The distrust cuts across party lines: 53% of Democrats, 51% of Republicans and 49% of independents trust Americans' ability to make democratic decisions. Flashback: Trust stood at 86% in 1976 and 78% in both 2002 and 2005. Trust has stayed below 60% since 2018, according to Gallup. State of play: Americans have more trust in their local government (67%) and state government (55%) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51%). The survey also found that 42% of Americans trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33% trust the news media. Zoom out: Americans' confidence in major U.S. institutions, including Congress, the presidency and the banking system, has also fallen to historically low levels. Methodology: Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1–17, 2026; the weighting-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 4 percentage points.

events.title: Trump returns to Ohio as Democrats try to claw back his advantage
events.summary: David’s view YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Toward the end of Monday night’s MAGA rally, after Jon Husted heard Donald Trump compliment his jawline and his “ass,” he thanked the president for making Ohio so much easier for Republicans to win. “The Youngstown area, for decades, used to vote Democrat,” the Republican senator said. “And then you ran for office in 2016, and flipped it red forever.” For a decade after that, Youngstown has become the first stop on what media critics derided as “Trump voter safaris,” journeys into the working-class counties that never voted Republican until he showed up. Husted’s claim of a permanently red state, however, isn’t adding up for Democrats: As soon as I arrived this week, they insisted that MAGA’s advance was over. This isn’t because Democrats have snapped back to the image and values they ran on in the 1970s, when they had a lock on this state. No, the party insists that Republicans are in charge, making voters angry with their handling of the economy and the Middle East, so the culture-war politicking that worked for a decade won’t be as potent in November. “People aren’t buying that again because they’ve realized you can’t deposit culture war into your bank account,” said Chris Anderson, the chairman of the Mahoning County Democrats, who’d spent years trying to limit their losses and defections. “You can’t fill your gas tank with it.” Campaigns have a queasy rhythm to them — hype followed by panic followed by hype. We’ve reached the time in the cycle where the party that built a post-Labor Day polling lead begins to question its own confidence. “They’re undersampling Republicans,” Speaker Mike Johnson told the faithful in South Texas on Tuesday, a part of that state that seemed to be following the same rightward march as northeast Ohio — and before that, Appalachia. Republicans around Youngstown expected the trend of underestimating their vote to hold this year, but not accelerate. They agreed that Democrats would at least be competitive. Rep. Michael Rulli, who represents the Mahoning Valley in Congress, said that the GOP got an opening when “Clinton came in and lied about NAFTA,” which made local Democrats thrash around in search of a populist alternative. “When Trump came around, the people just took to it, and so they’re giving us a shot,” Rulli added. “This area will not always stay Republican or Democrat.” This year’s Democrats are making hard plays for northeast Ohio, at least to trim the GOP margins. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost the five most Democratic counties east of Cleveland for the first time in 2024, has painted Husted as a “Big Tech” shill, captured by the next industry that’ll threaten working-class jobs. Amy Acton, the party’s gubernatorial nominee, takes every chance to talk about her Youngstown roots; her ads often portray Vivek Ramaswamy, the billionaire GOP nominee, playing tennis as he daydreams about cutting Medicare and Social Security. “I know what it’s like to not have the heat on, or live in a tent in the winter and experience a lot of neglect and abuse,” Acton told me on Tuesday, when I asked her to respond to the president rallying in Youngstown — specifically, about him telling voters they’d get rebate checks and energy bill relief only if Republicans won. “And I can also tell you that I wouldn’t be here today if it wasn’t for the institutions that gave me a chance.” A Democratic comeback in Ohio is unlikely to look like the winning maps of Barack Obama’s campaigns, much less Bill Clinton’s. While losing to Bernie Moreno two years ago, Brown ran stronger in the suburbs of Cleveland and Cincinnati than he had in elections he actually won. On Monday, the standard Trump rally scene of MAGA-hatted voters in line and liberals yelling at them from free speech zones showed how the coalitions had changed. The protesters skewed older; the younger they were, the more profanity they were comfortable putting on cardboard. A “progress pride” flag was hoisted on a pole, right under an American flag. Any Trump fan who objected got an earful about the “pedophile president” they were lined up for. Trump, at this point, was not the rebel candidate who first showed up in Youngstown 10 years ago, with rally speeches about the threat of mass Muslim immigration. He was the party leader every Republican wanted to borrow some aura from, by communing with his superfans. Ramaswamy posed for selfies a few steps away from MAGA activist Vince Fusca . Blake Marnell , who wears a brick-patterned suit to every Trump rally, got a seat near the main stage. Both men were at the 2024 Trump rally in Butler, Pa., where a failed assassin’s bullet clipped his ear; neither needed convincing that he was saving eastern Ohio, where they didn’t live, from neoliberalism. The Covelli Centre, where Trump had rallied before, was a bit more than half-full when the president got onstage. Like Democrats used to, he described all the investments he was bringing to the region. Submarine construction was coming to Cleveland; nearby Warren was getting a new ​​Kimberly-Clark plant ; he would figure out how to save the local heating utility company. The applause thinned out when he talked about how he’d rebranded artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” Notable David Skolnick covered the rally for the Youngstown Vindicator. Richard Cowan went to Warren, Ohio, for Reuters, to take the temperature of its Obama-Trump voters: “We ⁠believe our Christian ​values are more than gas prices.”

events.title: NVIDIA and Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI Across Chip Design and Manufacturing for AI-Defined Fabs
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA introduces cuPotential, a new NVIDIA CUDA-X library developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact, accelerating already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x in early-access testing. NanoVDB, an open source library for working with 3D data, accelerates chipmaking simulation for AI-defined fabs, helping Lam Research achieve 30x faster simulation. NVIDIA NPP, a library for processing images on GPUs, accelerates chipmaking inspection for AI-defined fabs, helping KLA accelerate inspection. Applied Materials, Cadence, KLA, Lam Research, Siemens, Synopsys and other semiconductor leaders are using NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI stack across chip design, manufacturing and testing, helping drive faster development, better yield and greater production capacity. NVIDIA today announced semiconductor leaders are adopting NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ libraries — including the new NVIDIA cuPotential library, which developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact — to advance AI-defined fabs. AI-defined fabs are semiconductor factories where AI helps engineers optimize processes, solve production issues and improve production efficiency. As demand for advanced chips rises, such fabs must expand production while managing increasingly complex manufacturing processes. Engineers need new ways to model materials, analyze inspection data and test process changes in digital twins before applying them in production. The expanded CUDA-X portfolio gives AI agents and engineering applications accelerated tools for semiconductor simulation, 3D data processing and image analysis, helping automate more engineering work across chip design and manufacturing so fabs can predict process behavior and improve yield. “The semiconductor industry made the AI revolution possible. Now, AI is transforming how chips are built,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “As fabs race to meet demand for advanced chips, NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries give AI agents accelerated simulation and inspection tools to help engineers manage complexity, improve yield and advance AI-defined fabs.” NVIDIA cuPotential Accelerates How Researchers Model Atomic Interactions Understanding how atoms and molecules interact is critical to modeling semiconductor materials and manufacturing processes, but these calculations can take significant amounts of time, even in software already optimized for GPUs. NVIDIA cuPotential accelerates atomic-scale simulation with specialized GPU-accelerated functions developers can add to existing software. It helps researchers model electrical forces and other interactions across large numbers of atoms to test and refine simulations faster. Synopsys is among the early adopters using cuPotential to accelerate materials simulations. By making these modeling capabilities available to AI agents, cuPotential helps agents run, evaluate and iterate on advanced molecular simulations. In early-access testing, the library accelerated already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x. Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI-Defined Fabs With NVIDIA CUDA-X AI-defined fabs require faster ways to model chip designs, materials behavior and manufacturing processes before changes reach production. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries — including NVIDIA cuPotential for simulating atomic interactions, NVIDIA cuEST for modeling electronic behavior and NVIDIA cuDSS for solving complex engineering simulations — accelerate these workloads to help make fabs more autonomous. Synopsys is using cuPotential, cuEST and cuDSS to accelerate semiconductor simulations, with early QuantumATK results showing a potential 30x speedup using cuEST, and S-Device benchmarks showing a 12x speedup using cuDSS. The company’s AgentEngineer solutions interoperate with NVIDIA Nemotron ™ open models and NVIDIA NeMo ™ to support AI agents for chip design and verification. Cadence is using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Nemotron open models and CUDA-X libraries to bring agentic AI to the design and simulation of electromechanical systems — from semiconductors to advanced packaging and printed circuit boards. Examples include Cadence AuraStack AI Super Agent optimizing advanced packages for heat and stress 8x faster using cuDSS with Cadence Celsius, and Nemotron with ChipStack AI Super Agent for semiconductor design and verification. COMSOL is accelerating semiconductor multiphysics simulations with NVIDIA cuDSS, delivering up to 10x faster simulations to help engineers optimize equipment and processes. Its upcoming COMSOL MCP Server will use the NVIDIA Nemotron Ultra open model to enable AI-assisted modeling and design exploration. Voltai accelerates advanced chip packaging with Voltaire, its agentic multiphysics platform for 3D-IC design and simulation. Voltaire combines AI agents with GPU-accelerated solvers powered by NVIDIA cuDSS and CUDA-X libraries, compressing complex electro-thermal-mechanical simulation workflows from months to a day. ChipAgents uses NVIDIA AI infrastructure and NVIDIA model-training and optimization software to develop specialized AI models for chip design. The company is also working with NVIDIA to develop Build-A-Chip Bench , a new AI benchmark that evaluates agents across end-to-end workflows from specification to graphic data system. The benchmark gives the industry a comprehensive measure of progress toward fully autonomous semiconductor engineering. NVIDIA Open Libraries Help Prepare and Optimize Manufacturing Workflows Fabs depend on thousands of process steps that must be modeled, refined and validated before production. The NVIDIA cuLitho library accelerates calculations for printing chip patterns; NanoVDB — an open source library for working with 3D data — accelerates chipmaking simulations; and the open NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo ™ framework helps train physics AI models to predict how physical systems behave. Siemens is using cuLitho to speed up Calibre software for chip-pattern refinement and mask preparation. Its Solido team is also developing agent-driven characterization workflows with Nemotron open models and NVIDIA NeMo open libraries. Lam Research intends to integrate NanoVDB into its advanced semiconductor process modeling platform SEMulator3D , part of the company’s Semiverse Solutions family of virtual products. The addition of NanoVDB is expected to accelerate select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x, while using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo has been demonstrated to assist in reducing plasma-prediction simulation time to as little as milliseconds instead of days. events.title: New inflation warning sign
events.summary: America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy . Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further. What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note. The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote. By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month. Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%. The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening. Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge. Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs. "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months. The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest rate hike later this month. But Wednesday's inflation data swiftly revived bets that the central bank will have to act sooner than the following meeting, in December. The two-year Treasury yield — particularly sensitive to Fed policy expectations — jumped roughly 12 basis points after the report. Traders now see a 47% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Oct. 27–28 policy meeting, up from 22.1% yesterday (and 18% this time last week), according to CME FedWatch. What to watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg Tuesday that rising Treasury yields could help cool the economy, potentially reducing the need for another rate hike. But the inflation report complicates that argument — showing that underlying price pressures remain stubbornly elevated. Instead, the report lends support to more hawkish policymakers like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who warned Monday that inflation was "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component." Hammack cited tariffs, the AI investment boom and rising services prices as additional sources of price pressures. The bottom line: For American consumers, the risk is that another bout of inflation proves harder to shake — prolonging the affordability squeeze while keeping borrowing costs elevated. The squeeze is already showing up in paychecks, with inflation outpacing wage growth for six consecutive months. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in September and were down 0.7% from a year earlier.

events.title: Why one spoiler candidate is now trying to replicate his work nationwide
events.summary: The News Aaron Day’s third-party campaign cost Republican Kelly Ayotte her Senate reelection bid in 2016. Now he’s trying to take his spoiler project national. With several Senate races tight enough for an alternate candidate to make a real difference, whether they’re Libertarian or another third party, Day is looking to spend as much as $2.5 million — or perhaps less, if his effort works as designed — to cost the GOP the Senate. Day’s strategy is simple: Use his Stark Freedom PAC to spend relatively small amounts on online ads made with AI that boost name ID for spoiler candidates, figuring he can do just enough to hand those races to the Democrats. Republican leaders are highly skeptical of Day’s efforts, but he sees a real chance at disrupting races across the country. What’s more remarkable is how open he is about his goal of ending the Senate Republican majority. “You call it a spoiler campaign, I call it holding Republicans accountable,” Day told Semafor in an interview. His website is equally explicit: “We fund the margin. It costs the GOP the Senate.” Day is targeting eight states where he’s deduced that boosting third-party candidates would hurt the Republican nominee: Texas, Iowa, New Hampshire, Minnesota, South Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, and Kansas. It’s a “Moneyball” theory of modern politics, banking on a relatively small amount of cash to mess up the margins in close contests. Nudging a third candidate’s vote share up by a couple of percentage points higher, as he explained, takes a lot less money than the obscene amount needed to actually win a race. “People are going to be shocked after the fact at how effective this is,” Day said. “Most voters don’t know that the third-party option exists, and a lot of these candidates don’t actually have money, and they’re not allowed to participate in the debates.” In addition to Ayotte’s 2016 New Hampshire campaign , Libertarian candidates’ support boosted former Democratic Sen. Jon Tester in his 2006 and 2012 Montana races. The effect was clear in Nevada’s 2024 Senate race, which Democrats narrowly won as nearly 5 percent of voters picked a candidate outside the two major parties. And no one can forget Jill Stein’s Green Party spoiler effect on Hillary Clinton’s presidential chances in 2016. It’s hard to see how giving Democrats the Senate helps advance Day’s causes — which include concerns over centralized digital currencies and government surveillance via cryptocurrency legislation. But Day says he wants to check President Donald Trump through “gridlock” and that with Democrats in charge, the crypto market structure bill and other legislation he dislikes will continue to stall. Several Republican groups, including the National Republican Senatorial Committee and Senate Leadership Fund, declined comment. While third-party hopefuls appreciate his support, their goals are different. Ted Brown, the Libertarian candidate in Texas, said he’s running to win, not to cost Republicans Senate control. “I’m running to defeat the corrupt two-party system,” Brown told Semafor. “But I would say this, if the Republicans lose the Senate on November 3: The good news is, the Republicans lost control of the Senate. The bad news is, the Democrats won control of the Senate.” Day said his model would be replicable to punish a Democratic majority in the future as well, by boosting Green Party candidates to eat into their candidates’ margins: “I actually view this, if it works, as something that can be used to hold both major parties accountable.” Know More So, why do this? Day was originally planning to be a candidate himself this fall, even fighting to get ballot access in New Hampshire to take out former Sen. John Sununu, R-N.H. But he said he didn’t run, in part because he was in negotiations with Republicans and the Trump administration over a list of demands that weren’t fulfilled: “I was told something definitive was going to happen, and it did not.” He declined to go into further detail; the White House did not comment. After the schism, he threw his support behind Edmond Laplante, a Constitution Party candidate in New Hampshire. He then decided to “duplicate” his 2016 bid against Ayotte by boosting anti-war candidates to reach the small percentage of “disaffected voters in these swing states.” “People do not want to vote for the Republican, but a lot of people still don’t want to vote for the Democrat,” Day said. “Texas is in play, Kansas is in play, South Carolina is potentially in play. I mean, who would have ever thought? But it’s true, and this really could make the difference.” Day’s ads are unique to each race, but most have peppy AI music critiquing the GOP candidate. They knock Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., for her pro-war votes and boost Libertarian Kasie Whitener; in New Hampshire, they hit Sununu for supporting the Wall Street bailout; in Texas, they whack state attorney general Ken Paxton for being a “mouthpiece for DC” and dub Brown the “voice of Texas.” Republicans are more worried about Day’s machinations in New Hampshire and don’t believe he’ll be effective anywhere else. Burgess’s view I’m a skeptic, and so naturally lean a bit bearish on the idea of a national spoiler campaign funded by the political equivalent of spare change. I watched a bunch of Day’s ads, as well, and found them somewhat tedious but also relentlessly on-message in driving the name ID of these somewhat obscure candidates. (It’s possible that AI-generated music just isn’t for me.) But Day is onto something with the spoiler effect, whether it’s induced by him or not. It’s undeniable that disaffected Republicans who cast primary votes for, say, Sen. John Cornyn in Texas or Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina may struggle with voting for Paxton and Graham — but not want to support their Democratic counterparts either. It just won’t be clear until Election Day how big of a threat these candidates are. The percentages they are drawing in polls are small enough to be a rounding error; given how tight the polls are, a rounding error still could cost Republicans multiple Senate seats. Notable Brown is courting jilted Cornyn voters , Houston Public Media reported earlier this year.
